I am initiating a Data Science project to investigate the reporting of greenhouse gas emissions in the USA, with the tentative end goal of creating a framework that will reliably evaluate corporate GHG emissions and provide a credibility score of voluntary climate claims by corporate companies. This framework will combine the historical EPA GHGRP record with voluntary disclosures, and independent satellite-derived emissions via statistical, NLP, and machine-learning methods, to deliver both a corporate emissions assessment and a Corporate Climate Credibility Score for selected U.S. industrial parent company, along with a detailed report and a dashboard for visualization. 


This report will be assessed by data professionals, executives, and faculty members of the Harvard Business School (HBS). 

 For getting a fuller context of the project and my current plan to execute the project, please read the attached documents in the following order

* HBS_Senior-Data-Scientist_Takehome-Prompt_Optimized.docx
* short_summary.docx
* PROJECT_CHARTER.md
* Master-System-Orchestration-Charter.docx
* project_outline_for_agent.md

Once you have read all the documents and have a solid understanding, let me know your comprehensive understanding of the project, and your suggestions in an honest, non-sycophantic manner as a Principal Data Scientist and business strategist. Always remember the ultimate goal and the target audience. 

You can ask me any clarifying questions you have to execute the project. Once I approve your understanding, I would like to know your suggested workflow for this project. Once I approve the workflow, we shall start working on this project. 

 Remember, we are in a strict time constraint of 3-4 days.

You can access the preliminary GHGRP dataset in the filepath "/Users/souvikmandal/Documents/S00_Career-development/20260318_HBS_Sen-Data-Scientist/task/data/raw/epa_ghgrp"

Objective
Identify and analyze a real-world problem using publicly available data. Your goal is to generate meaningful insights and/or build a predictive or analytical solution that demonstrates your ability to think critically, work with real data, and communicate results effectively.

Prompt
Choose a real-world question or problem that can be explored using publicly available data. You may use a dataset of your own choosing or select the following:
Climate & Sustainability (bonus — emerging D^3 focus)
EPA Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program: https://www.epa.gov/ghgreporting/data-sets
You are responsible for:
Defining the problem clearly
Identifying and acquiring relevant dataset(s)
Applying appropriate data science techniques
Communicating your findings
Your work should reflect how you would approach an ambiguous, real-world data science problem in a production or business setting.

Guidelines
Problem Definition
Clearly articulate the question you are trying to answer
Explain why the problem is meaningful (business, societal, or technical relevance)
2. Data Acquisition
Source one or more publicly available datasets
Provide links and a brief description of the data
Justify why the data is appropriate for your problem
3. Data Understanding & Preparation
Perform exploratory data analysis (EDA)
Handle missing values, inconsistencies, or biases as needed
Perform feature engineering if applicable
Leverage embeddings, dimensionality reduction, etc. as needed
4. Analysis / Modeling
Use some (but not necessarily all) of the following:
Statistical analysis (hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, etc.)
Machine learning (supervised or unsupervised)
Time series analysis
Natural language processing tools
Networks or knowledge graphs
Causal inference or experimentation framing
Be sure to explain:
Why you chose your approach
Trade-offs or alternative methods you considered
5. Evaluation
Define appropriate evaluation metrics
Evaluate your results rigorously
Discuss limitations and assumptions
6. Communication
Present findings clearly (visualizations encouraged)
Summarize key insights for a non-technical audience
Provide actionable recommendations

Deliverables
A well-documented notebook or repository that includes all code written for the project
Report of all LLM prompts (ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) used at any stage of the project
A short, written summary (1–2 pages or equivalent) including:
Problem statement
Approach
Key findings
Limitations and next steps

What We’re Evaluating
Problem framing and clarity of thought
Ability to work with ambiguous, real-world data
Technical depth and correctness
Judgment in choosing appropriate methods, NOT just using everything.
Communication and storytelling

Optional Extensions (Bonus)
Deploy a simple app or dashboard
Create a reproducible data pipeline
Incorporate multiple data sources
Perform error analysis or robustness checks

content.text:
Insuring Against the Dismantling of GHGRP:
A Predictive Climate Intelligence Framework for Corporate Decarbonization Credibility
Souvik Mandal
Candidate for “Senior Data Scientist, HBS AI Institute (formerly D^3 Institute)”; Email: drsouvikmandal@gmail.com

Problem statement:
On September 12, 2025, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed to eliminate the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP) for all 47 source categories ( Federal Register, 2025 1, 2, the bedrock of U.S. industrial emissions reporting since 2010, covering ~8,000 facilities and 85–90% of national GHG emissions. If finalized in mid-2026, the rule would dismantle the authoritative public baseline.
The voluntary reporting by corporates is not reliable: 74% of S&P 500 firms have restated emissions, under-reporting 135 million tons of emissions 3, 4; Nearly one-third of companies that announced 2020 targets never disclosed outcomes 5, 6. Moreover, ESG ratings by major providers, which rely heavily on the EPA GHGRP, correlate poorly on the same companies 7, 8.
In case of the elimination of GHGRP by EPA, no public framework would exist to reliably assess corporate GHG emissions or evaluate the credibility of voluntary climate claims. This will create a structural gap that will impair ESG capital allocation, regulatory enforcement, and public accountability. Environment, Social and Governance (ESG) factors are considered by 89% of investors when they are deciding where to put their money, according to the Center for Sustainability and Excellence. ESG-focused institutional investments are expected to reach $33.9 trillion globally in 2026, up from $18.4 trillion in 2021, according to the global consulting firm PwC 9. Therefore, without accurate and consistent GHGRP reporting or an alternative assessment system, businesses, investors and the public can't make informed decisions about where to expand, invest, shop and work.
This project proposes to mitigate that gap through monitoring with dashboard visualization and predictive modeling to assess credibility of the corporate voluntary reporting using other data sources.
Approach:
We build an emissions credibility framework for parent companies of facilities producing electricity by combusting fossil fuels and/or biomass. I chose to begin with this sector as a proof-of-concept as 
it is the largest contributor to U.S. stationary emissions, offering a universal baseline of continuous direct measurement to rigorously calibrate satellite-derived proxies, 
the power-sector implementation benefits from a second ground truth (CEMS) that lets us validate the calibration model against an independent measurement.
The methodology can generalize to sectors where no CEMS analog exists (refining, cement, chemicals);
and the short execution window of a week for the project. 
The framework integrates five independent data sources across three distinct analytical dimensions:
Corporate Pledge (Stated Intent). A pledge quality score from voluntary corporate disclosures, scored across five pillars — Ambition, Specificity, Time Horizon, Mechanism Clarity, and Verification — drawn from SBTi commitments and NLP analysis of climate-related disclosures in SEC 10-K filings.
Empirical Ground-Truth (Direct & Certified Action). A dual physical baseline combining annual EPA GHGRP regulatory reporting (2011–2023) with continuous direct stack measurements of GHG emission from EPA AMPD CEMS, where the GHGRP–CEMS divergence would flag reporting-integrity issues. This step also separates real operational decarbonization of parent companies from accounting effects of mergers and divestitures.
Satellite Proxy (External Estimation). Independent facility-level emissions estimates from Climate TRACE, derived from satellite imagery and activity data.
The framework delivers four artifacts: 
Statistical Analysis: A Linear Mixed-Effects Model analysis evaluating how satellite telemetry deviates from empirical ground-truth data across the historical overlap window (2015–2023), establishing how reliably independent remote sensing can substitute for the GHGRP data.
Predictive Modeling: A supervised machine learning pipeline that predicts a corrected, ground-truth-equivalent emissions baseline for parent companies using satellite telemetry and voluntary corporate reporting from overlapping timelines. In tandem with feature-level explanations, this calibrated baseline enables the systemic categorization of parent companies into distinct performance quadrants (Credible Leaders, Quiet Achievers, Greenwashers, or Laggards).
A Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS) per parent company, keeping the three underlying analytical dimensions explicitly visible so users see why each score is what it is, ensuring full auditability.
A live executive-facing dashboard with company, sector, and geographic breakdowns. Companies are additionally labeled by their joint Pledge × Performance position — credible leaders, greenwashers, quiet achievers, or laggards.
Moreover, unlike proprietary ESG ratings that combine voluntary and authoritative inputs into one opaque score, this framework keeps the three signals inspectable and publishes its full methodology and code.
Key Findings:
{Yet to be filled.}
Limitation of the project and Next steps: 
To ensure absolute data integrity and eliminate entity-matching latency, this framework prioritizes the power sector where continuous physical stack monitoring (CEMS) provides an absolute baseline. 
Future iterations will scale this calibration architecture to less-instrumented sectors (e.g., heavy manufacturing, refineries) as independent remote-sensing methodologies mature.

1	# The Corporate Climate Credibility Audit
2	## Project Charter and Problem Definition
3	
4	| | |
5	|---|---|
6	| **Project name** | The Corporate Climate Credibility |
7	| **Author** | Souvik Mandal (drsouvikmandal@gmail.com) |
8	| **Drafted** | May 19, 2026 |
9	| **Status** | Locked — guides Day 1–4 execution |
10	| **Version** | 1.0 |
11	
12	---
13	
14	### Document Purpose
15	
16	This document is the canonical scoping artifact for the project "Corporate Climate Credibility Audit". Any collaborator — human or LLM — should be able to read this end-to-end and reach full clarity on what we are doing, why we are doing it, how we are doing it, and what falls outside the current scope, *without consulting any external context*. It is intended as the project's "north star": every analytical decision, file, and figure in the repository should be traceable back to a paragraph in this document.
17	
18	---
19	
20	## Table of Contents
21	
22	1. Background and Strategic Context
23	2. The Problem
24	3. Why This Matters
25	4. Research Questions
26	5. The Conceptual Framework: Talk × Walk × Verify
27	6. Data Inventory
28	7. Methodology and Methods Mapping
29	8. Scope Decisions
30	9. Deliverables
31	10. Timeline
32	11. Limitations and Honest Risks
33	12. Success Criteria
34	13. Project Structure
35	14. References
36	15. Appendix A: Day 0 Empirical Findings
37	16. Appendix B: Glossary
38	
39	---
40	
41	## 1. Background and Strategic Context
42	
43	### 1.1 Project Origin
44	
45	This project is the response to a Senior Data Scientist take-home prompt issued by Harvard Business School (HBS). The prompt invites a candidate to choose a real-world problem, source publicly available data, apply appropriate data science techniques, and communicate findings — with explicit emphasis on problem framing, judgment in choosing methods (rather than using everything), and the ability to work with ambiguous, real-world data. The prompt offers four candidate datasets and explicitly flags climate/sustainability as an "emerging D^3 focus."
46	
47	### 1.2 Audience and Intended Outcome
48	
49	The proximate audience is the HBS evaluator who will read the deliverable. The substantive audience — the people whose intellectual interests this work must engage — is HBS's **Climate and Sustainability Impact Lab**, co-led by Professors **George Serafeim**, **Michael Toffel**, and **Peter Tufano**. The lab sits inside the *HBS AI Institute* (formerly the Digital, Data, and Design Institute, renamed in April 2026), and its work concentrates on:
50	
51	- Corporate environmental disclosure quality (Toffel; Marquis, Toffel & Zhou)
52	- Sustainable investing, ESG materiality, impact-weighted accounts (Serafeim)
53	- Climate finance (Tufano)
54	- Application of AI and machine learning to climate adaptation and mitigation (Toffel & Chaudhry, 2025)
55	
56	The intended outcome of this project — beyond satisfying the take-home rubric — is to position the author as a credible Senior Data Scientist whom the Lab would want to engage as a consultant or hire as a permanent senior IC. The deliverable must therefore *speak the Lab's language*, engage its active research lines, and produce an artifact that members of the Lab can immediately use in their own research, teaching, or executive education.
57	
58	### 1.3 What We Are Demonstrating
59	
60	Across the deliverable, the author intends to demonstrate the full spectrum of Senior Data Science capabilities required for this kind of role:
61	
62	- Exploratory data analysis on real-world, messy, multi-source data
63	- Data preparation and harmonization across heterogeneous public sources
64	- Statistical analysis grounded in domain context, not just methodological reflex
65	- Supervised and unsupervised machine learning, applied with judgment
66	- Natural language processing on regulatory disclosures (10-K filings)
67	- Time-series analysis of multi-decade panel data
68	- Light causal inference framing where the data supports it
69	- ML interpretability (SHAP) so that black-box models become consulting-grade evidence
70	- Reproducibility (version-controlled repo, pinned environment, end-to-end build targets)
71	- Communication: a working paper formatted in HBS style, a dashboard, and an LLM-prompt provenance log
72	
73	---
74	
75	## 2. The Problem
76	
77	### 2.1 The Accountability Crisis
78	
79	The decade 2015–2025 saw an enormous expansion of corporate climate pledges. Thousands of companies committed to net-zero, validated targets via the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), and published sustainability reports referencing climate ambition. Capital markets responded: roughly **$30 trillion** in assets are now managed under Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) mandates that depend on corporate emissions data and target disclosures.
80	
81	Yet the empirical foundation underneath all of this is demonstrably weak:
82	
83	- A March 2025 paper by **Jiang, Kim, and Lu** published in *Nature Climate Change* ("Limited Accountability and Awareness of Corporate Emissions Target Outcomes") established that *roughly one-third of global companies that announced a 2020 emissions target never disclosed whether they hit it*. Wall Street analysts do not follow up the way they would about earnings. There is no enforcement mechanism for self-set climate targets, and corporate communications selectively highlight only favorable outcomes.
84	
85	- A 2025 working paper by **Shirley Lu** and colleagues at HBS established that **74% of S&P 500 companies have restated their reported emissions** at some point, with **over 135 million tons of CO₂-equivalent emissions going unreported initially** before later corrections. The voluntary disclosure channel that ESG investors and ratings agencies depend on is unstable.
86	
87	- Major ESG ratings agencies — MSCI, Sustainalytics, Refinitiv — produce ESG scores that correlate at only **roughly 0.5** with one another on the same companies. Two reputable ratings agencies frequently disagree about whether a given company is well-run on climate.
88	
89	- A 2024 paper by **Marquis, Toffel, and Zhou** ("Scrutiny, Norms, and Selective Disclosure: A Global Study of Greenwashing") documents how firms under pressure to disclose environmental impacts strategically reveal benign information while obscuring true performance — a behavior termed "selective disclosure."
90	
91	Against this voluntary-channel unreliability, the United States Environmental Protection Agency's **Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP)** has, since 2010, collected legally mandated, third-party-verifiable emissions data from approximately 8,000 large industrial facilities — those emitting more than 25,000 metric tons of CO₂-equivalent per year. GHGRP is the closest thing US industry has to an authoritative baseline. But it has historically been underused in business research because (a) it is facility-level and not parent-company-aggregated, (b) it is published in a series of Excel workbooks with non-trivial structure that requires data engineering to harmonize across the 13-year panel, and (c) most business researchers, ESG analysts, and investors lack the data pipeline tooling to connect it cleanly to voluntary disclosures and other public sources.
92	
93	### 2.2 Active HBS Research Lines
94	
95	This project explicitly engages with at least four active HBS research lines:
96	
97	1. **Environmental disclosure quality and greenwashing** (Toffel; Marquis, Toffel & Zhou). Our framework's "Talk" axis operationalizes the disclosure-quality construct these papers describe, by scoring corporate pledges on dimensions including specificity, mechanism clarity, and verification.
98	
99	2. **Emissions target accountability** (Jiang, Kim & Lu 2025). Our "Pledge-Performance Gap" — the quantitative divergence between what a company committed to and what EPA-verified data shows them doing — is the metric these authors call for but did not themselves construct at scale.
100	
101	3. **AI/ML for climate mitigation** (Toffel & Chaudhry 2025; Toffel et al. 2024). The HBS AI Institute's explicit research positioning rewards work that uses ML in climate-relevant ways. Our predictive model layer, our NLP-based pledge-quality scoring, and our use of satellite-derived emissions data all sit squarely in this line.
102	
103	4. **Sustainable investing methodology** (Serafeim). Our EPA-grounded analog of the **Weighted Average Carbon Intensity (WACI)** metric — the industry-standard portfolio carbon-intensity measure used by S&P, MSCI, and most ESG funds — frames our work as a methodological contribution to the construction of next-generation sustainability indices.
104	
105	### 2.3 The GHGRP Sunset Risk
106	
107	On **September 12, 2025**, the EPA proposed under Executive Order 14192 ("Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation") to **permanently eliminate reporting obligations for 46 of the 47 source categories** in the GHGRP. The single remaining source category — petroleum and natural gas systems — is exempted only to the extent needed to administer the Inflation Reduction Act's Waste Emissions Charge, and even those reporting obligations are suspended until 2034 because the Charge itself was postponed by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Reporting year 2024 will be the **last year of mandatory reporting** for the 46 affected source categories if the proposal is finalized.
108	
109	The public comment period closed on November 3, 2025, with over 50,000 comments submitted. EPA has stated that a final rule will be issued by mid-2026 — within weeks of this project's completion. The 2025-reporting-year deadline has already been extended from March 31 to October 30, 2026, in what some observers read as a slow-walking of remaining data collection.
110	
111	The implication is profound. The 13-year GHGRP panel (2011–2023) that this project analyzes is, with high probability, **the most complete authoritative public record of US industrial emissions that will ever exist for this era**. Whatever data flows after 2024 will be voluntary, fragmented, and — per the research cited above — unreliable. The methodological framework we build here therefore has dual value: it audits the past, *and* it provides the empirical benchmark against which the patchier voluntary disclosure data of the post-mandatory-reporting era must be evaluated.
112	
113	---
114	
115	## 3. Why This Matters
116	
117	### 3.1 Business Relevance
118	
119	The credibility of corporate climate claims is materially financial. Decisions that depend on this credibility include:
120	
121	- *Capital allocation in ESG funds.* Roughly $30 trillion globally sits in funds with ESG mandates that use corporate emissions data and target disclosures as inputs. Even small improvements in capital-allocation accuracy translate to hundreds of billions of dollars moving toward (or away from) genuine decarbonizers.
122	
123	- *Climate stress testing in banking.* The Federal Reserve, ECB, and Bank of England now require large banks to perform climate stress tests. Bank capital requirements are partly determined by climate transition risk in their loan and investment portfolios, and that risk depends on knowing which borrowers are genuinely decarbonizing.
124	
125	- *Insurance pricing for industrial firms.* Directors & Officers, casualty, and property insurance increasingly price climate transition exposure. Underwriters need facility-level signals.
126	
127	- *Procurement and Scope 3 emissions management.* Fortune 500 companies committed to Scope 3 targets need to evaluate their suppliers' climate performance. Self-reported supplier emissions are precisely the weakly accountable data this project audits.
128	
129	- *Regulatory disclosure compliance.* The SEC's climate-disclosure rule (finalized 2024, partially stayed pending litigation), California's SB 253 and SB 261 (effective 2026), and the EU CSRD all require some form of standardized emissions reporting. A verified independent baseline is the natural reference for compliance assessment.
130	
131	### 3.2 Societal Relevance
132	
133	If voluntary corporate climate disclosure is unreliable *and* mandatory reporting is being dismantled, society loses its ability to know whether the largest emitters are decarbonizing or simply claiming to. This is not a theoretical concern. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) AR6 made clear that the trajectory of large industrial emitters in the OECD is decisive for the global 1.5°C and 2°C pathways. Independent third-party verification of corporate climate performance — the kind that satellite-based emissions estimation now makes possible — becomes the only remaining mechanism for public accountability.
134	
135	This project explicitly builds the bridge between the (potentially) about-to-disappear authoritative mandatory data and the satellite-based independent verification regime. The credibility framework we develop is a public-goods artifact even before it is a commercial one.
136	
137	### 3.3 Technical Relevance to Data Science as a Discipline
138	
139	From a pure data science standpoint, this project sits at the intersection of several methodological challenges that are unusually well-suited to a Senior IC demonstration:
140	
141	- *Multi-source data harmonization at scale.* Joining the EPA GHGRP panel (113,581 facility-year records, ~2,500 parent companies) to SBTi targets (~5,000 companies), 10-K filings (~9,000 large filers), and Climate TRACE satellite-derived estimates (millions of source-month observations) requires entity resolution and fuzzy joining done well.
142	
143	- *Composite index construction with sensitivity analysis.* The 5-pillar Pledge Quality Score, the EPA Performance Score, and the composite Credibility Score are all composite indices. Building them defensibly — with explicit weighting decisions, sensitivity testing, and transparent communication of the weighting choices — is a methodological exercise that the academic finance and sustainability literature actively struggles with.
144	
145	- *Anomaly detection on emissions trajectories.* Identifying facilities whose reporting patterns are suspicious (sudden drops, restatements, hockey-stick recoveries) is exactly the kind of anomaly-detection problem unsupervised ML handles well.
146	
147	- *NLP on regulatory text.* SEC 10-K filings have a specific structural grammar. Extracting climate-related content from the risk factors and MD&A sections, then scoring it for specificity and mechanism clarity, is a non-trivial NLP application.
148	
149	- *Honest small-N causal inference.* The Inflation Reduction Act passed in August 2022, leaving only 2024 and 2023 as post-treatment years in our panel. Doing causal inference under that constraint *responsibly* — being explicit about identification assumptions and limitations — is itself a marker of senior methodological maturity. (This analysis is deferred to "Next Steps" in the current scope but flagged here as a future direction.)
150	
151	---
152	
153	## 4. Research Questions
154	
155	### 4.1 Central Question
156	
157	> **Which US industrial companies are decarbonizing for real, which are merely making claims, and how do we know — using a transparent, replicable framework that triangulates voluntary pledges against EPA-verified emissions data against independent satellite-derived emissions estimates?**
158	
159	This question is operationalized as the construction of a **Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS)** for the top ~100–250 US industrial parent companies — the universe that, per Day 0 empirical analysis, accounts for 66–83% of total US industrial emissions.
160	
161	### 4.2 Subsidiary Questions
162	
163	The central question decomposes into seven analytically separable sub-questions, each of which is independently interesting and produces its own artifact in the deliverable.
164	
165	1. **EPA Performance** — How have US industrial emissions actually evolved at facility, sector, and parent-company level from 2011 to 2023? Where is the decline concentrated, and where has it stalled?
166	
167	2. **Pledge Quality Scoring** — Using SBTi's public targets database and SEC EDGAR 10-K filings, can we systematically score the quality of corporate climate pledges across five structural pillars (Ambition, Specificity, Time Horizon, Mechanism Clarity, Verification and Governance)? What does the resulting quality distribution look like?
168	
169	3. **Pledge–Performance Gap** — For companies with public pledges, what is the quantitative gap between the trajectory they committed to and the trajectory their EPA-verified emissions actually show? Where are the gaps concentrated by sector, size, or geography?
170	
171	4. **Satellite Cross-Validation** — Does independent satellite-derived emissions data from Climate TRACE corroborate EPA's reported emissions? Where do they systematically diverge, and what does that divergence tell us about reporting quality or sub-threshold coverage gaps?
172	
173	5. **The Talk × Walk × Verify Diagnostic Matrix** — When the three measurement axes are combined into a single diagnostic, which companies cluster as Credible Leaders, Greenwashers, Quiet Achievers, and Laggards? Which companies show a fourth-quadrant red flag (consistent talk-and-walk story but satellite contradicts both)?
174	
175	6. **EPA-Grounded WACI** — Can we compute an EPA-grounded analog of the industry-standard Weighted Average Carbon Intensity metric (Scope 1 emissions from EPA divided by revenue from 10-K), and how does it compare with published S&P/MSCI WACI for the companies where both exist?
176	
177	7. **Predictive Modeling** — Given a company's observable features (sector, fuel mix, geography, parent characteristics, prior trajectory, pledge structure), can we predict whether its next-period emissions will be on track for its own pledge? What features drive that prediction, per SHAP interpretation?
178	
179	A further question — *Did the Inflation Reduction Act cause an inflection in the trajectory of treated sectors?* — is explicitly **deferred** to the "Next Steps" section because the available post-treatment window (2 years) is too short for robust causal identification, and pursuing it within the four-day scope would crowd out higher-confidence analytical work.
180	
181	---
182	
183	## 5. The Conceptual Framework: Talk × Walk × Verify
184	
185	### 5.1 Framework Overview
186	
187	The framework triangulates corporate climate credibility across three measurement axes:
188	
189	- **Talk** — what a company publicly commits to. Measured by the Pledge Quality Score.
190	- **Walk** — what a company has actually done in measured emissions. Measured by the EPA Performance Score.
191	- **Verify** — what *independent* satellite-derived emissions data shows. Measured by the Satellite Cross-Validation Score.
192	
193	The diagnostic value of triangulation is twofold. First, the joint distribution of Talk and Walk identifies the four classical archetypes of corporate climate behavior — credible leaders, greenwashers, quiet achievers, and laggards. Second, the Verify axis introduces an independent check on both Talk and Walk: when Climate TRACE's satellite-derived estimates disagree with EPA's reported numbers, that disagreement is a separate signal of reporting quality regardless of what the company publicly claims.
194	
195	### 5.2 EPA Performance Score (EPS) — the Walk Axis
196	
197	The EPS scores each parent company's actual EPA-verified emissions performance over 2011–2023. The score is built from four components, each normalized to 0–100 and combined into a composite:
198	
199	1. *Absolute trajectory slope* — the linear regression slope of annual attributed emissions, in tons per year. Negative slopes (declining emissions) score higher.
200	
201	2. *Relative percentage decline* — the percent change from a baseline (e.g., the 2015–2017 average) to a recent period (2021–2023). Larger declines score higher.
202	
203	3. *Sectoral percentile rank* — the parent's trajectory slope expressed as a percentile within its primary sector, so that a parent in a structurally challenged sector (e.g., refining) is not penalized relative to a parent in a structurally easier sector (e.g., waste).
204	
205	4. *Recent acceleration* — whether the post-2020 trajectory shows acceleration of decline relative to the pre-2020 trend. This captures companies that are responding to the policy and capital environment of the last several years.
206	
207	The composite is the weighted geometric mean of the four components, which is more resistant to outliers than the arithmetic mean and penalizes weakness on any single dimension. Default weighting is equal; sensitivity analysis on weighting is part of the robustness checks.
208	
209	### 5.3 Pledge Quality Score (PQS) — the Talk Axis
210	
211	The PQS scores each parent company's *publicly stated climate commitment* across five structural pillars, each scored 0–10 and combined into a 0–100 composite. The five pillars are designed to be theoretically defensible (each captures a distinct, well-recognized dimension of pledge quality from the literature), operationalizable from public data, and orthogonal enough that the composite has discriminating power.
212	
213	1. **Ambition (0–10).** Magnitude of claimed reduction and pathway alignment. Inputs: SBTi target percent reduction, SBTi pathway alignment classification (1.5°C / well-below-2°C / 2°C), scope coverage (Scope 1, Scope 1+2, Scope 1+2+3), absolute vs. intensity-based target.
214	
215	2. **Specificity (0–10).** Whether the pledge is pinned down rigorously. Inputs: presence of a defined base year, presence of a defined target year, absence of ambiguous ranges or qualitative phrasing.
216	
217	3. **Time Horizon Structure (0–10).** Whether the company has near-term as well as long-term targets, and whether interim milestones are committed to. A near-term (≤2030) target sitting in front of a long-term (2050) target scores higher than a 2050-only target.
218	
219	4. **Mechanism Clarity (0–10).** Does the company specify *how* it will achieve the target? This pillar is operationalized through NLP analysis of the climate-related sections of the company's most recent 10-K filing. We score the prevalence of language naming specific mechanisms (fuel switching, electrification, carbon capture and storage, efficiency upgrades, offsets), the presence of capex commitments tied to the pledge, and the explicit disclosure (versus obscuring) of offset reliance. This is the pillar where the NLP layer earns its keep.
220	
221	5. **Verification and Governance (0–10).** Whether the company submits to external accountability. Inputs: SBTi validation status (validated targets carry external scientific review); third-party assurance of emissions reporting (disclosed in 10-K or sustainability report); linkage to executive compensation (disclosed in proxy statement); board-level climate oversight (disclosed in 10-K governance section).
222	
223	The composite PQS is the equal-weighted sum of the five pillars scaled to 0–100. Weight sensitivity is part of robustness checking.
224	
225	### 5.4 Satellite Cross-Validation Score (SCVS) — the Verify Axis
226	
227	The SCVS scores the *agreement* between a company's EPA-reported emissions and an independent satellite-derived emissions estimate from **Climate TRACE**. The score is inversely related to divergence: tight agreement scores high, large systematic divergence scores low.
228	
229	The construction proceeds in three stages:
230	
231	1. *Facility matching.* Climate TRACE assets (each with latitude, longitude, sector classification) are matched to EPA GHGRP facilities via k-nearest-neighbor spatial join with a per-sector radius constraint (~500 m for point sources, larger for distributed assets), restricted to compatible sector mappings.
232	
233	2. *Facility-level divergence computation.* For each matched facility, we compute Δ = Climate TRACE estimate − EPA reported emissions, both in tons of CO₂-equivalent and as a percent of EPA reported. A Bland-Altman plot characterizes the distribution; a one-sample t-test or median-based test characterizes systematic bias by sector.
234	
235	3. *Parent-level aggregation.* Facility-level divergences are aggregated to the parent company via the same ownership-share weighting used for the EPS. The SCVS is a transformation that yields high scores when EPA and Climate TRACE agree closely (within methodological uncertainty) and low scores when they disagree systematically.
236	
237	A separate flag — distinct from the SCVS — identifies parents whose EPA *and* Climate TRACE both report a particular trajectory but whose voluntary disclosure tells a different story. That is the "suspicious agreement" fourth-quadrant pattern and is investigated qualitatively in the working paper.
238	
239	### 5.5 Composite Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS)
240	
241	The CCCS combines PQS, EPS, and SCVS into a single 0–100 number per parent company. The construction philosophy is:
242	
243	- We *do not* collapse the three axes irrevocably; instead, every reported CCCS comes with the underlying PQS, EPS, and SCVS visible so that a user can see *why* a given company scores where it does.
244	- The composite uses a weighted geometric mean rather than an arithmetic mean. Geometric mean is sensitive to weakness on any single axis (a company cannot offset a low score on one dimension with a high score on another), which matches the credibility construct: if a company looks bad on any one of the three axes, the credibility story has a hole.
245	- Default weights are 0.4 (EPS), 0.4 (PQS), 0.2 (SCVS). The lower weight on SCVS reflects that Climate TRACE estimates carry their own model uncertainty and should serve as a verification check rather than a primary measurement. Sensitivity to weights is reported.
246	
247	### 5.6 The Talk × Walk × Verify Diagnostic Matrix
248	
249	The headline visualization of the working paper is the diagnostic scatter of PQS (x-axis, "Talk") against EPS (y-axis, "Walk"), with each point sized by 2023 attributed emissions and colored by SCVS. The plot is partitioned into four quadrants by median splits:
250	
251	| | Low Walk (flat or rising emissions) | High Walk (declining emissions) |
252	|---|---|---|
253	| **High Talk** (ambitious, well-structured pledge) | **Greenwashers** — talk big, deliver nothing | **Credible Leaders** — talk big, deliver |
254	| **Low Talk** (vague, weak, or no pledge) | **Laggards** — neither claim nor deliver | **Quiet Achievers** — actually decarbonizing without public claim |
255	
256	Color (SCVS) introduces the third dimension: a credible leader whose Climate TRACE estimate diverges sharply from EPA carries a red flag despite scoring well on Talk and Walk.
257	
258	### 5.7 EPA-Grounded WACI Analog
259	
260	The Weighted Average Carbon Intensity (WACI) is the industry-standard portfolio-level carbon-intensity metric used by S&P Dow Jones Indices, MSCI, and most large ESG funds. It is computed as the portfolio-weighted average of company-level (Scope 1 + Scope 2 emissions / revenue) values. The published WACI used in commercial indices is built on purchased data — primarily from Trucost (an S&P subsidiary).
261	
262	We construct an **EPA-grounded WACI analog** by using EPA GHGRP Scope 1 emissions in the numerator (the most authoritative public source) and revenue extracted from 10-K filings in the denominator. The result is a methodologically transparent, publicly replicable carbon-intensity metric for the universe of publicly traded US industrial parent companies. Where a company has a published S&P or MSCI WACI, we compare the two; the EPA-grounded version serves as a verification check on the vendor-derived version, and the comparison is itself a finding of methodological interest.
263	
264	---
265	
266	## 6. Data Inventory
267	
268	### 6.1 Data Already in Hand (EPA GHGRP)
269	
270	The following EPA GHGRP files are pre-positioned in `data/raw/epa_ghgrp/` and have been validated against EPA's published totals:
271	
272	| File | Contents | Shape (verified Day 0) |
273	|---|---|---|
274	| `ghgp_data_by_year_2023.xlsx` | Facility × year emissions panel, 2011–2023, multiple subsector sheets | 8,737 facilities × 13 years = 113,581 long-form rows |
275	| `ghgp_data_2023.xlsx` | 2023 annual snapshot with gas-by-gas (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, fluorinated) breakdown | Same facility universe |
276	| `ghgp_data_parent_company.xlsb` | Facility → parent company mapping with ownership percentages, multi-year (2010–2023) | 9,060 facility-year rows, 14 yearly sheets, ~2,500 distinct 2023 parents |
277	| `emissions_by_unit_and_fuel_type_c_d_aa.xlsb` | Unit-level and fuel-level emissions detail | UNIT_DATA: 268,778 rows; FUEL_DATA: 323,495 rows |
278	| `ghgrp_oris_power_plant_crosswalk_12_13_21.xlsx` | GHGRP-to-ORIS power plant ID crosswalk | ~3,000 power plant matches |
279	
280	Loaders live in `src/data/load_epa.py` and produce tidy long-form DataFrames with consistent snake_case column naming.
281	
282	### 6.2 Public Data to Acquire
283	
284	The following public sources must be downloaded before Day 1 begins. The sandbox environment cannot reach the bulk-download endpoints, so these require manual download by the author to `data/raw/...`:
285	
286	| Source | File / Endpoint | Purpose | Access |
287	|---|---|---|---|
288	| **Climate TRACE v5.6.0** (April 2026 release) | US country package or Manufacturing + Power sector packages, downloaded from [climatetrace.org/data](https://climatetrace.org/data) | Satellite Cross-Validation Score (SCVS) | Free, CC BY 4.0 license; requires browser interaction |
289	| **SBTi Public Target Database** | `companies-excel.xlsx`, `targets-excel.xlsx`, `Alpha-Dashboard-Data-Dictionary.xlsx` from [sciencebasedtargets.org/target-dashboard](https://sciencebasedtargets.org/target-dashboard) | Pledge Quality Score (PQS) — Ambition, Specificity, Time Horizon, Verification pillars | Free public |
290	| **SEC EDGAR 10-K filings** | Programmatically fetched via the `sec-edgar-downloader` Python package, targeting the top ~250 US industrial parent companies | Pledge Quality Score (PQS) — Mechanism Clarity pillar; revenue for the WACI analog | Free public; no API key needed |
291	
292	### 6.3 Optional Auxiliary Sources
293	
294	Available if useful but not required for the core scope:
295	
296	| Source | Use case |
297	|---|---|
298	| EIA Form 923/860 (power plant generation) | Emissions intensity (tCO₂/MWh) for the power sector via the ORIS crosswalk |
299	| Public stock ticker / SEC CIK mappings | Link EPA parent names to financial identifiers for WACI revenue denominator |
300	| Net Zero Tracker public dataset | Cross-validation of pledge metadata for companies not in SBTi |
301	| TROPOMI Sentinel-5P methane data | Methane super-emitter cross-validation for oil and gas — **deferred to Next Steps** |
302	| EPA EJScreen | Environmental justice overlay — **deferred to Next Steps** |
303	| Public 10-K-derived governance data (compensation linkage, board oversight) | Verification & Governance pillar of PQS |
304	
305	---
306	
307	## 7. Methodology and Methods Mapping
308	
309	### 7.1 Methods by Sub-Question
310	
311	| Sub-question | Primary methods | Senior DS skill demonstrated |
312	|---|---|---|
313	| 1. EPA Performance | EDA across 13-year panel; entity resolution; threshold-effect handling; ownership-share-weighted parent rollup; trajectory regression; sector-normalized percentile ranking | EDA, data preparation, statistical analysis |
314	| 2. Pledge Quality Scoring | Multi-pillar composite index construction; sensitivity analysis on pillar weights; NLP-based mechanism-clarity extraction from 10-K filings | NLP, statistical analysis, index methodology |
315	| 3. Pledge–Performance Gap | Difference between linear trajectory slope and pledged trajectory; bootstrap confidence intervals; hypothesis testing on systematic gap by sector | Statistical analysis, hypothesis testing |
316	| 4. Satellite Cross-Validation | Spatial join with KNN matching; Bland-Altman analysis; one-sample tests for systematic bias by sector; aggregation to parent level | Statistical analysis, geospatial join |
317	| 5. Talk × Walk × Verify Matrix | Quadrant classification via median splits; visualization with size and color encoding the three axes | Visualization, diagnostic analytics |
318	| 6. EPA-grounded WACI | Multi-source merge (EPA emissions + 10-K revenue); comparison with published S&P/MSCI values where available; sector-normalized intensity comparison | Data engineering, statistical analysis |
319	| 7. Predictive Modeling | Gradient boosting (LightGBM); time-based train/validation split; SHAP interpretation; out-of-time evaluation | Supervised ML, ML interpretability |
320	
321	Cross-cutting throughout: time-series clustering of facility/parent trajectories via k-shape, producing decarbonization archetype labels that feed into the predictive model and the dashboard.
322	
323	### 7.2 Senior Data Scientist Skill Showcase
324	
325	The skills explicitly demonstrated across the deliverable map to the assignment rubric as follows:
326	
327	| Skill on rubric | Demonstrated in |
328	|---|---|
329	| EDA | Day 0 notebook (`00_data_quality_report.ipynb`) and Day 2 sector/parent analyses |
330	| Data preparation | EPA panel unpivot; ownership-share-weighted parent rollup; multi-source entity resolution; NLP preprocessing of 10-Ks |
331	| Statistical analysis | EPS, PQS, SCVS, CCCS construction; Bland-Altman; bootstrap CIs; hypothesis tests on systematic gaps |
332	| Machine learning | k-shape time-series clustering; LightGBM predictive model with SHAP |
333	| Time series analysis | 13-year trajectory regression; trajectory clustering; forward forecasting for the Pledge-Performance Gap |
334	| NLP | 10-K climate-section extraction; mechanism-clarity scoring via regex + sentence classification |
335	| Networks / knowledge graphs | Parent → facility → fuel/unit structural map embedded in the dashboard |
336	| Causal inference framing | Acknowledged in scope; deferred to "Next Steps" with explicit identification-assumption discussion |
337	| Communication | HBS-style working paper, interactive Streamlit dashboard, and the prompts.md provenance log |
338	
339	---
340	
341	## 8. Scope Decisions
342	
343	### 8.1 In-Scope (Days 0–4)
344	
345	The four-day work plan delivers the following analytical artifacts:
346	
347	- EPA Performance Score (EPS) for the top ~250 parents
348	- Pledge Quality Score (PQS) for the SBTi-overlap subset, with 5-pillar composite
349	- Satellite Cross-Validation Score (SCVS) using Climate TRACE
350	- Talk × Walk × Verify diagnostic matrix
351	- EPA-grounded WACI analog
352	- k-shape trajectory clustering producing decarbonization archetypes
353	- Sector and geographic pattern analyses
354	- Predictive model with SHAP interpretability
355	- Streamlit dashboard surfacing the credibility scorecard
356	- HBS-style working paper
357	
358	### 8.2 Deferred to "Next Steps"
359	
360	The working paper's "Next Steps" section explicitly proposes these extensions, framing them as natural Phase-2 work the author is ready to execute:
361	
362	- **TROPOMI methane super-emitter cross-validation** for the oil and gas subset, leveraging Sentinel-5P methane column data
363	- **IRA causal Diff-in-Differences analysis** as more post-treatment years accumulate
364	- **Full Log-Mean Divisia Index (LMDI) mechanism decomposition** of sectoral emissions changes into fuel-switching, efficiency, scale, and exit components
365	- **Event-study analysis** around pledge announcement dates, testing whether pledges shift trajectories
366	- **Decarbonization premium analysis** linking CCCS to stock returns
367	- **Environmental Justice audit** combining emissions data with EPA EJScreen demographics
368	- **RAG-based chatbot** layer on the dashboard, grounded in the working paper and processed data
369	- **Extension to voluntary post-2024 data** when GHGRP reporting sunsets, demonstrating that the framework is the natural bridge
370	
371	Each of these is sketched with enough specificity in the report that an HBS reader sees an obvious ongoing engagement path.
372	
373	---
374	
375	## 9. Deliverables
376	
377	The final deliverable package consists of:
378	
379	1. **HBS-style working paper** (PDF, 10–15 pages plus appendix). Structure: executive summary on page 1, problem framing, data, methodology, findings, discussion, policy implications, limitations and assumptions, next steps. Type B "Executive Brief" formatting with charts on every page and technical methodology in an appendix.
380	
381	2. **Reproducible GitHub repository** with: README documenting motivation and reproduction steps, Makefile providing end-to-end build targets, pinned `requirements.txt`, modular `src/` package, four numbered notebooks (`00_data_quality_report`, `01_pledge_quality_score`, `02_statistical_analyses`, `03_predictive_model`), and an optional `04_supplementary_analyses` notebook for Next-Steps explorations.
382	
383	3. **Detailed Jupyter notebooks** with end-to-end narrative documentation, hyperlinks from in-notebook references to specific source-code files in the GitHub repository for full reproducibility.
384	
385	4. **Streamlit dashboard** (`dashboard/app.py`) surfacing the credibility scorecard, the Talk × Walk × Verify matrix, sector benchmarking, and predictive-model SHAP explanations. RAG chatbot deferred to Next Steps.
386	
387	5. **Comprehensive `prompts.md` log** documenting every meaningful LLM interaction across the project lifecycle, including the problem-framing conversations that produced this charter.
388	
389	6. **This Project Charter** (`docs/PROJECT_CHARTER.md`) preserved as the canonical scoping document.
390	
391	---
392	
393	---
394	
395	## 10. Limitations and Honest Risks
396	
397	A senior data scientist's mark of maturity is naming limitations explicitly rather than discovering them in review. The headline limitations of this project are:
398	
399	- **Entity resolution noise.** Joining ~2,500 EPA parent names to ~5,000 SBTi companies to ~9,000 10-K filers is a fuzzy-matching exercise. We will use RapidFuzz with a manual override list for the top 50 parents and explicitly report the coverage rate of the joined universe in the final report. Unmatched parents are excluded from CCCS construction but reported separately.
400	
401	- **Sub-threshold facilities are invisible to GHGRP.** Facilities below 25,000 mt CO₂e/year are absent from the EPA panel. Climate TRACE's broader coverage partially fills this gap, and the comparison itself is a finding in the SCVS section.
402	
403	- **Climate TRACE estimates carry model uncertainty.** Climate TRACE is peer-reviewed and methodologically transparent, but its estimates have their own confidence intervals. The SCVS should not be interpreted as "ground truth versus EPA" but as "independent verification versus EPA reporting." We weight SCVS at 0.2 in the composite to reflect this.
404	
405	- **Pledge data coverage is biased toward larger and more-disclosed companies.** Smaller private firms are systematically missing from SBTi and have only the basic 10-K filer subset. The credibility universe is therefore a *publicly traded, large-cap* universe. This is appropriate for the audience but should be stated.
406	
407	- **The post-IRA window is short.** Only 2022 and 2023 are post-treatment for any causal claim about the Inflation Reduction Act. This is why we explicitly defer the causal analysis. Mentioning it in the report as a planned Phase-2 deliverable demonstrates methodological honesty rather than weakness.
408	
409	- **10-K language has structural patterns that NLP must respect.** Legal language hedges aggressively. Our mechanism-clarity NLP scoring must be calibrated to recognize that "we may consider transitioning some operations to renewable energy" is not the same as "we will spend $2B by 2028 to convert coal to gas." We use a small labeled training set of ~50 hand-annotated 10-K passages to calibrate.
410	
411	- **The reporting-rule change in 2016 reduced the GHGRP facility count by ~900 (12%).** This is documented in the EDA notebook and is *not* facility closure; we will not treat the resulting coverage shift as decarbonization.
412	
413	- **GHGRP itself may not survive 2026.** The September 2025 EPA proposal would dismantle 46 of 47 source categories. Our analysis ends at 2023 regardless, but the *generalizability* of our framework to future years depends on whether mandatory reporting persists. This is acknowledged in the report's discussion section as a structural feature of the work.
414	
415	---
416	
417	## 12. Success Criteria
418	
419	The project succeeds if all three criteria below are met:
420	
421	**Technical success.** The repository runs end-to-end via `make all` on a clean environment. The credibility scores for the top 250 parents are computed, sensitivity-tested, and documented. The dashboard launches and displays the headline matrix and the predictive-model explanations. No notebook fails to execute on a re-run.
422	
423	**Communication success.** A reader who is technically literate but not an emissions-data specialist can read the working paper executive summary in under five minutes and come away with a clear sense of the central finding, the methodology, and one or two specific actionable recommendations. The same reader, looking at the dashboard, can identify their company of interest, see its position on the Talk × Walk × Verify matrix, and understand why it is positioned where it is.
424	
425	**Strategic success.** A reader from HBS's Climate and Sustainability Impact Lab — Toffel, Serafeim, Tufano, or one of their post-docs — finishes the working paper with the reaction that this work directly engages their research agenda, that the methodology is a contribution rather than a redundancy, and that the author of this work is the kind of person they would either hire or commission for a follow-on engagement.
426	
427	---
428

430	
431	The repository layout is:
432

436	
437	The work cites or builds directly on the following recent literature and public sources. Full citations are in the working paper's references section; this charter cites them by author and year:
438	
439	- *Jiang, X., Kim, S., & Lu, S.* (March 2025). "Limited Accountability and Awareness of Corporate Emissions Target Outcomes." *Nature Climate Change*. [HBS faculty profile](https://www.hbs.edu/faculty/Pages/item.aspx?num=66916)
440	- *Lu, S. et al.* (2025). Working paper on S&P 500 emissions restatement, summarized at [HBS Institute for Business in Global Society](https://www.hbs.edu/bigs/harvard-study-74-percent-sp-500-companies-revise-emissions-data)

442	- *Toffel, M. W., & Chaudhry, N.* (April 2025, revised March 2026). "Climate Change Adaptation with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning." Harvard Business School Background Note.
443	- *Toffel, M. W., Carter, K., Chambers, A., Park, A., & Pinckney, S.* (August 2024). "Mitigating Climate Change with Machine Learning."
444	- [HBS Climate and Sustainability Impact Lab](https://d3.harvard.edu/labs/climate-and-sustainability-impact-lab/)
