85	### 2.1 The accountability crisis we are addressing
86	
87	- Roughly $30 trillion in global assets are managed under ESG mandates that depend on corporate emissions data and target disclosures.
88	- 74% of S&P 500 firms have restated their reported emissions, with over 135 MtCO₂e initially under-reported (Lu et al., HBS, 2025).
89	- Roughly one-third of global companies that announced 2020 emissions targets never disclosed whether they hit them (Jiang, Kim & Lu, *Nature Climate Change*, 2025).
90	- Major ESG ratings (MSCI, Sustainalytics, Refinitiv) correlate at roughly 0.5 with one another on the same companies.
91	- A 2024 paper by Marquis, Toffel & Zhou documents "selective disclosure" — firms strategically reveal benign environmental information while obscuring true performance.
92	
93	Against this voluntary-disclosure unreliability, the EPA Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP) has been the closest U.S. industry has to an authoritative baseline since 2010. Roughly 8,000 large facilities, third-party verifiable, legally mandated. **If the September 2025 rule is finalized, this baseline disappears for 46 of 47 source categories.**
94	
95	### 2.2 Why this audience cares
96	
97	The HBS AI Institute, formerly known as Digital Data Design (D^3) Institute at Harvard Business School (HBS), especially the Climate and Sustainability Impact Lab at HBS (Toffel, Serafeim, Tufano) is publishing actively on greenwashing, emissions target accountability, AI/ML for climate mitigation, and sustainable-investing methodology. 99	- **Disclosure quality and greenwashing**: our Talk axis operationalizes pledge quality across five structural pillars.
100	- **Emissions target accountability**: our Pledge–Performance Gap is the quantitative metric these authors called for but did not construct at scale.
101	- **AI/ML for climate mitigation**: our predictive virtual-baseline model and our NLP layer over 10-K filings sit squarely in this line.
102	- **Sustainable-investing methodology**: our EPA-grounded analog of the Weighted Average Carbon Intensity (WACI) metric is a methodological contribution to next-generation sustainability indices.
103

105	
106	1. *Audit the past.* We produce per-parent decarbonization velocity and pledge-quality scores grounded in the most authoritative public record that will ever exist for this era.
107	
108	2. *Bridge to the post-mandatory-reporting future.* We build a calibrated virtual baseline — using only features that survive the regulatory rollback (satellite, voluntary disclosures, exogenous drivers) — that demonstrates how independent verification can substitute for GHGRP once it sunsets.

112	## 3. Conceptual Framework: Talk × Walk × Verify
113	
114	The framework triangulates corporate climate credibility across three measurement axes:
115	
116	| Axis | Measurement | Source | Score |
117	|---|---|---|---|
118	| **Talk** | What the company publicly commits to | SBTi targets + SEC 10-K text | Pledge Quality Score (PQS) — 5 pillars, 0–100 |
119	| **Walk** | What the company has measurably done | EPA GHGRP self-reports (2011–2023), validated against EPA CEMS continuous stack measurement | EPA Performance Score (EPS) — 0–100, headline metric is per-parent trajectory slope |
120	| **Verify** | What independent estimation shows | Climate TRACE asset-level emissions estimates (satellite + activity-data hybrid model) | Satellite Cross-Validation Score (SCVS) — 0–100, inverse of EPA-vs-Climate-TRACE divergence |
121	
122	The three scores are combined into a single per-parent **Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS)** via weighted geometric mean (default weights 0.2 PQS / 0.4 EPS / 0.4 SCVS). The composite is sensitive to weakness on any single axis (a company cannot offset a low Walk with a high Talk). Underlying components remain inspectable so a user can always see *why* a parent scores where it does.

354	A senior data scientist's mark of maturity is naming limitations explicitly. The working paper's Limitations section will include:

356	1. **Entity resolution noise.** Joining ~2,500 EPA parent names to ~5,000 SBTi companies to ~10k SEC registrants is fuzzy. We use RapidFuzz with explicit overrides for known parents and a `DO_NOT_MATCH` set for known non-registrants. Coverage rate reported.
357	2. **Sub-threshold facilities invisible to GHGRP.** Facilities below 25,000 mt CO₂e/year are absent from the panel. Climate TRACE partially fills this gap, but the comparison itself is a finding in the SCVS section.
358	3. **Climate TRACE is a hybrid model, not pure satellite.** Estimates use activity data and emission factors heavily, especially for power. We weight SCVS at 0.2 in the composite to reflect this. The working paper labels Climate TRACE as "independent model-based, remote-sensing-informed estimate" — not "pristine remote sensing."
359	4. **Pledge data biased toward larger and more-disclosed companies.** Smaller private firms and cooperatives are systematically absent from SBTi and have no 10-Ks. 28 of our 50 cohort parents are non-registrants. The credibility universe is publicly-traded large-cap industrial; we say so explicitly.
360	5. **2023 ownership applied retroactively.** M&A and divestitures across the 2011–2023 window are not tracked. Notable cases (e.g., Vistra emerging from Energy Future Holdings, Talen spin-off) are flagged in the report.

362	7. **GHGRP itself may not survive 2026.** Our analysis ends at 2023 regardless, but the generalizability of the framework to future years depends on whether mandatory reporting persists. Acknowledged in discussion section.
363	8. **CEMS coverage is power-sector-only.** The calibration architecture we propose to extend to refining, cement, and chemicals does not yet have an equivalent ground-truth source in those sectors — Phase 2 work.
364	9. **OLS trajectory slopes in Notebook 01 are coarse summaries.** Per-parent slopes on 13 data points without covariates are noisy. Bootstrap CIs reflect sampling uncertainty only, not measurement uncertainty in the underlying GHGRP values. The proper LME with random effects + AR(1) is in Notebook 03.

489	## 16. Glossary
490	
491	| Term | Definition |
492	|---|---|
493	| **GHGRP** | EPA Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program. Mandatory annual self-reporting by U.S. facilities emitting ≥25,000 mt CO₂e/year, since 2010. |
494	| **Subpart D** | The GHGRP source category covering Electricity Generation (fossil-fuel and biomass combustion at power plants). |
495	| **CEMS** | Continuous Emissions Monitoring System. Direct, continuous, in-stack measurement of pollutant mass. Required for fossil power plants under Acid Rain / Cross-State Air Pollution rules. |
496	| **AMPD / CAMPD** | Air Markets Program Data / Clean Air Markets Program Data. EPA's portal for CEMS data. |
497	| **Climate TRACE** | Public emissions inventory project (https://climatetrace.org) that publishes asset-level emissions estimates derived from satellite imagery, activity data, and emission factors. |
498	| **SBTi** | Science Based Targets initiative. Independent body that validates corporate climate targets against 1.5°C / well-below-2°C / 2°C pathway alignment. |
499	| **CCCS** | Corporate Climate Credibility Score. The headline output per parent — a 0–100 weighted-geometric-mean composite of PQS, EPS, SCVS. |
500	| **PQS** | Pledge Quality Score. The Talk axis. 5 pillars: Ambition, Specificity, Time Horizon, Mechanism Clarity, Verification & Governance. |
501	| **EPS** | EPA Performance Score. The Walk axis. Decarbonization velocity + sector-normalized rank + recent acceleration. |
502	| **SCVS** | Satellite Cross-Validation Score. The Verify axis. Inverse of EPA-vs-Climate-TRACE divergence at parent level. |
503	| **LME** | Linear Mixed-Effects model. Used as the Diagnostic Instrument to quantify Climate TRACE's structural bias vs EPA/CEMS, with nested random effects (Facility ⊂ Parent) and AR(1) within-facility residual structure. |
504	| **GroupKFold** | Cross-validation scheme that holds out entire groups (here: parent companies) across folds. Tests whether the predictive model generalizes to unseen corporate systems. |
505	| **SHAP** | SHapley Additive exPlanations. Per-prediction feature-contribution attribution used to make black-box ML interpretable for the audit dashboard. |
506	| **WACI** | Weighted Average Carbon Intensity. Industry-standard portfolio carbon-intensity metric (Scope 1 + 2 / revenue). Our EPA-grounded WACI analog uses GHGRP Scope 1 and 10-K revenue. |
507	| **ORIS** | Office of Regulatory Information Systems plant identifier. Used by EIA. The GHGRP↔ORIS crosswalk bridges GHGRP to CEMS. |
508	| **NO_PARENT_RECORD** | Placeholder label for facilities whose parent record is missing from the 2023 parent workbook. Excluded from cohort. |

## How to Use This Document

This file complements rather than duplicates `docs/PROJECT_CHARTER.md`. The charter is the strategic scoping document — it states *what* we are building and *why*. This workplan is the operational document — it states *how* we are building, *what is currently true*, and *what every executor (human or AI) needs to know to keep the work aligned*.

Read top-to-bottom on first visit. On subsequent visits, jump to the section you need:

- New collaborator joining? Read sections 1–4.
- Checking if a decision has been locked? Section 5.
- Wondering what a notebook is supposed to produce? Section 7.
- Looking at today's work? Section 8.
- Wondering whether to add a feature? Sections 5 and 11.

The Change Log at the bottom is updated whenever a substantive decision changes.

---

## Table of Contents

1. Project at a Glance
2. Strategic Context
3. Conceptual Framework
4. The Headline Question and the Deliverable
5. Locked Scope Decisions
6. Data Sources and Acquisition Status
7. Notebook-by-Notebook Plan

## 1. Project at a Glance

We are building a defensible, reproducible, public-goods framework that triangulates three independent signals — corporate climate **Talk** (pledges), regulator-verified **Walk** (EPA emissions), and independent **Verify** (CEMS continuous stack measurement and Climate TRACE remote-sensing-derived estimates) — to produce a **Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS)** for the top 50 U.S. fossil-fuel power-generating parent companies. The framework outputs a per-parent scorecard plus a 2×2 quadrant taxonomy (Credible Leaders, Greenwashers, Quiet Achievers, Laggards).

The work is urgent because on 12 September 2025 the EPA proposed to dismantle reporting obligations for 46 of the 47 GHGRP source categories, with the final rule expected mid-2026. The 2011–2023 GHGRP record we are analyzing is, with high probability, the most complete authoritative public emissions panel that will ever exist for this era of U.S. industry.

### The deliverable that HBS asked for is 
- A well-documented notebook or repository that includes all code written for the project
- Report of all LLM prompts (ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) used at any stage of the project
- A short, written summary (1-2 pages or equivalent) including
    - Problem statement
    - Approach
    - Key findings
    - Limitations and next steps

    - Optional Extensions (Bonus)
        - Deploy a simple app or dashboard
        - Create a reproducible data pipeline
        - Incorporate multiple data sources
        - Perform error analysis or robustness checks

For the final decision on the delverables, see the section "## 4. The Headline Question and the Deliverable".

### Evaluation Criteria
- Problem framing and clarity of thought
- Ability to work with ambiguous, real-world data
- Technical depth and correctness
- Judgment in choosing appropriate methods, NOT just using everything.
- Communication and storytelling

---

## 2. Strategic Context

### 2.1 The accountability crisis we are addressing

- Roughly $30 trillion in global assets are managed under ESG mandates that depend on corporate emissions data and target disclosures.
- 74% of S&P 500 firms have restated their reported emissions, with over 135 MtCO₂e initially under-reported (Lu et al., HBS, 2025).
- Roughly one-third of global companies that announced 2020 emissions targets never disclosed whether they hit them (Jiang, Kim & Lu, *Nature Climate Change*, 2025).
- Major ESG ratings (MSCI, Sustainalytics, Refinitiv) correlate at roughly 0.5 with one another on the same companies.
- A 2024 paper by Marquis, Toffel & Zhou documents "selective disclosure" — firms strategically reveal benign environmental information while obscuring true performance.

Against this voluntary-disclosure unreliability, the EPA Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP) has been the closest U.S. industry has to an authoritative baseline since 2010. Roughly 8,000 large facilities, third-party verifiable, legally mandated. **If the September 2025 rule is finalized, this baseline disappears for 46 of 47 source categories.**

### 2.2 Why this audience cares

The HBS AI Institute, formerly known as Digital Data Design (D^3) Institute at Harvard Business School (HBS), especially the Climate and Sustainability Impact Lab at HBS (Toffel, Serafeim, Tufano) is publishing actively on greenwashing, emissions target accountability, AI/ML for climate mitigation, and sustainable-investing methodology. Our framework engages each of those lines:

- **Disclosure quality and greenwashing**: our Talk axis operationalizes pledge quality across five structural pillars.
- **Emissions target accountability**: our Pledge–Performance Gap is the quantitative metric these authors called for but did not construct at scale.
- **AI/ML for climate mitigation**: our predictive virtual-baseline model and our NLP layer over 10-K filings sit squarely in this line.
- **Sustainable-investing methodology**: our EPA-grounded analog of the Weighted Average Carbon Intensity (WACI) metric is a methodological contribution to next-generation sustainability indices.

### 2.3 The dual value of this work

1. *Audit the past.* We produce per-parent decarbonization velocity and pledge-quality scores grounded in the most authoritative public record that will ever exist for this era.

2. *Bridge to the post-mandatory-reporting future.* We build a calibrated virtual baseline — using only features that survive the regulatory rollback (satellite, voluntary disclosures, exogenous drivers) — that demonstrates how independent verification can substitute for GHGRP once it sunsets.

## 3. Conceptual Framework: Talk × Walk × Verify

The framework triangulates corporate climate credibility across three measurement axes:

| Axis | Measurement | Source | Score |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Talk** | What the company publicly commits to | SBTi targets + SEC 10-K text | Pledge Quality Score (PQS) — 5 pillars, 0–100 |
| **Walk** | What the company has measurably done | EPA GHGRP self-reports (2011–2023), validated against EPA CEMS continuous stack measurement | EPA Performance Score (EPS) — 0–100, headline metric is per-parent trajectory slope |
| **Verify** | What independent estimation shows | Climate TRACE asset-level emissions estimates (satellite + activity-data hybrid model) | Satellite Cross-Validation Score (SCVS) — 0–100, inverse of EPA-vs-Climate-TRACE divergence |

The three scores are combined into a single per-parent **Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS)** via weighted geometric mean (default weights 0.2 PQS / 0.4 EPS / 0.4 SCVS). The composite is sensitive to weakness on any single axis (a company cannot offset a low Walk with a high Talk). Underlying components remain inspectable so a user can always see *why* a parent scores where it does.

The headline visualization is the **2×2 quadrant matrix**:

|  | Low Walk | High Walk |
|---|---|---|
| **High Talk** | Greenwashers — talk big, deliver nothing | Credible Leaders — talk big, deliver |
| **Low Talk** | Laggards — neither claim nor deliver | Quiet Achievers — actually decarbonizing without public claim |

Color overlays the SCVS so cases where satellite contradicts both Talk and Walk are visually flagged as red-flag suspicious-agreement candidates.

## 5. Scope Decisions

Each row below was decided on the indicated date and should not be revisited without an explicit unlock in Section 17 (Change Log).

| # | Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Scope:** Power POC only — top 50 U.S. fossil-fuel power-generating parents | CEMS provides an independent ground truth available *only* for power. Multi-sector scope is infeasible in 4 days and would weaken the calibration argument. |
| 2 | **Cohort selection:** Deterministic from GHGRP — top 50 by 2023 Subpart-D attributed CO₂e | Replicable. No judgment calls. |
| 3 | **Decarbonization velocity:** Hybrid — GHGRP slope is the headline metric; CEMS shown as a validation panel | Avoids circularity from using the ML virtual baseline as both predictor and target. CEMS validates GHGRP; satellite is a separate Verify axis. |
| 4 | **Ownership rule:** 2023-locked ownership applied across full 2011–2023 panel | M&A timeline reconstruction is ~hours of manual work per parent. Phase-2 item. Acknowledged limitation. |
| 5 | **Pledge Quality Score NLP layer:** Tiered — regex / keyword-density first; embeddings only if Day 3 has slack | SBTi data alone supports 4 of 5 PQS pillars. NLP earns the 5th (Mechanism Clarity). Embedding-based scoring is calibration-heavy and the tail risk doesn't fit the 4-day window. |
| 6 | **LME implementation:** Full nested random-effects + AR(1) spec via `pymer4` or `rpy2`+`lme4` | Methodological purity matters to the HBS audience. `statsmodels` cannot fit the joint specification cleanly. |
| 7 | **Dashboard format:** Single self-contained HTML + Plotly file (not Streamlit) | Durability for an HBS reviewer opening the artifact on their own laptop weeks after submission. No backend dependency. |
| 8 | **Data acquisition mode:** Fully programmatic via reproducible notebook | Changed from Chrome-driven scraping after Day 0 to make the pipeline reproducible end-to-end. |
| 9 | **Orphan handling in cohort:** `NO_PARENT_RECORD` placeholder facilities excluded from cohort, backfilled from rank 51+ | Retired plants without parent records are not parent companies. Treating them as such would inflate the cohort total share and misattribute emissions. |
| 10 | **CEMS endpoint:** EPA `streaming-services/emissions/apportioned/annual` (not `camd-services/bulk-files`) | Bulk-files endpoint serves raw ECMPS submissions with a 15-minute manifest timeout. Streaming-services endpoint serves clean facility-unit-annual CSV with no record limit. |
| 11 | **CEMS pull strategy:** One year per request, idempotent per-year files, exponential backoff on HTTP 429 | EPA's effective short-window rate limit is tighter than the documented 1,000/hr. Year-by-year is robust to transient rate-limits. |
| 12 | **Notebook 01 scope:** All 8 sections (panel construction, headline trajectory, fuel mix, per-parent slope, hand-labeled exit register, geography, CEMS visual peek, save deliverables) | Per user direction after structured-question review. |
| 13 | **Notebook 01 threshold-effect handling:** Option A — hand-label top 20 dropouts with public-sourced exit causes | The HBS audience expects this distinction. Cost ~1 hour. |
| 14 | **Notebook 01 CEMS peek depth:** Visual side-by-side for top 10 parents; no statistics, no Bland-Altman | Proper LME comparison is Notebook 03's job. Notebook 01 just gives a sanity-check eyeball. |

### Acquisition issues encountered and resolved

1. **CAMD bulk-files endpoint silently returned a 1-entry sample on query-param auth.** Pivoted to header auth (`x-api-key`) AND switched endpoint from `bulk-files` to `streaming-services/emissions/apportioned/annual`. Resolved 2026-05-23.
2. **EPA streaming-services rate-limits at ~5 requests / 10 sec despite documented 1,000/hr.** Patched with 2-second inter-call sleep and exponential backoff on HTTP 429. Resolved 2026-05-23.
3. **Climate TRACE auto-download URLs all 404'd** (v04/v05 sector-package paths I guessed don't exist on the current CDN). Switched to user-manual download with explicit save-path convention. Resolved 2026-05-23.

5. **Fuzzy CIK matching produced false positives** (`GENON ENERGY INC` → `MGE ENERGY INC`; `UNS ENERGY CORP` → `US ENERGY CORP`). Patched with a `DO_NOT_MATCH` blocklist, tighter fuzzy cutoff (0.92), and first-token gate that operates on punctuation-normalized titles. Resolved 2026-05-23.

## 11. Limitations (To Be Stated Honestly in the Working Paper)

A senior data scientist's mark of maturity is naming limitations explicitly. The working paper's Limitations section will include:

1. **Entity resolution noise.** Joining ~2,500 EPA parent names to ~5,000 SBTi companies to ~10k SEC registrants is fuzzy. We use RapidFuzz with explicit overrides for known parents and a `DO_NOT_MATCH` set for known non-registrants. Coverage rate reported.
2. **Sub-threshold facilities invisible to GHGRP.** Facilities below 25,000 mt CO₂e/year are absent from the panel. Climate TRACE partially fills this gap, but the comparison itself is a finding in the SCVS section.
3. **Climate TRACE is a hybrid model, not pure satellite.** Estimates use activity data and emission factors heavily, especially for power. We weight SCVS at 0.2 in the composite to reflect this. The working paper labels Climate TRACE as "independent model-based, remote-sensing-informed estimate" — not "pristine remote sensing."
4. **Pledge data biased toward larger and more-disclosed companies.** Smaller private firms and cooperatives are systematically absent from SBTi and have no 10-Ks. 28 of our 50 cohort parents are non-registrants. The credibility universe is publicly-traded large-cap industrial; we say so explicitly.
5. **2023 ownership applied retroactively.** M&A and divestitures across the 2011–2023 window are not tracked. Notable cases (e.g., Vistra emerging from Energy Future Holdings, Talen spin-off) are flagged in the report.
6. **Short post-treatment window for any IRA causal analysis.** Only 2022 and 2023 are post-IRA. Causal analysis is explicitly deferred to Phase 2.
7. **GHGRP itself may not survive 2026.** Our analysis ends at 2023 regardless, but the generalizability of the framework to future years depends on whether mandatory reporting persists. Acknowledged in discussion section.
8. **CEMS coverage is power-sector-only.** The calibration architecture we propose to extend to refining, cement, and chemicals does not yet have an equivalent ground-truth source in those sectors — Phase 2 work.
9. **OLS trajectory slopes in Notebook 01 are coarse summaries.** Per-parent slopes on 13 data points without covariates are noisy. Bootstrap CIs reflect sampling uncertainty only, not measurement uncertainty in the underlying GHGRP values. The proper LME with random effects + AR(1) is in Notebook 03.
10. **Regex-based Mechanism Clarity NLP is the floor, not the ceiling.** Embedding-based scoring is deferred to Phase 2 if Day 3 is on track to slip the budget.

## 16. Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **GHGRP** | EPA Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program. Mandatory annual self-reporting by U.S. facilities emitting ≥25,000 mt CO₂e/year, since 2010. |
| **Subpart D** | The GHGRP source category covering Electricity Generation (fossil-fuel and biomass combustion at power plants). |
| **CEMS** | Continuous Emissions Monitoring System. Direct, continuous, in-stack measurement of pollutant mass. Required for fossil power plants under Acid Rain / Cross-State Air Pollution rules. |
| **AMPD / CAMPD** | Air Markets Program Data / Clean Air Markets Program Data. EPA's portal for CEMS data. |
| **Climate TRACE** | Public emissions inventory project (https://climatetrace.org) that publishes asset-level emissions estimates derived from satellite imagery, activity data, and emission factors. |
| **SBTi** | Science Based Targets initiative. Independent body that validates corporate climate targets against 1.5°C / well-below-2°C / 2°C pathway alignment. |
| **CCCS** | Corporate Climate Credibility Score. The headline output per parent — a 0–100 weighted-geometric-mean composite of PQS, EPS, SCVS. |
| **PQS** | Pledge Quality Score. The Talk axis. 5 pillars: Ambition, Specificity, Time Horizon, Mechanism Clarity, Verification & Governance. |
| **EPS** | EPA Performance Score. The Walk axis. Decarbonization velocity + sector-normalized rank + recent acceleration. |
| **SCVS** | Satellite Cross-Validation Score. The Verify axis. Inverse of EPA-vs-Climate-TRACE divergence at parent level. |
| **LME** | Linear Mixed-Effects model. Used as the Diagnostic Instrument to quantify Climate TRACE's structural bias vs EPA/CEMS, with nested random effects (Facility ⊂ Parent) and AR(1) within-facility residual structure. |
| **GroupKFold** | Cross-validation scheme that holds out entire groups (here: parent companies) across folds. Tests whether the predictive model generalizes to unseen corporate systems. |
| **SHAP** | SHapley Additive exPlanations. Per-prediction feature-contribution attribution used to make black-box ML interpretable for the audit dashboard. |
| **WACI** | Weighted Average Carbon Intensity. Industry-standard portfolio carbon-intensity metric (Scope 1 + 2 / revenue). Our EPA-grounded WACI analog uses GHGRP Scope 1 and 10-K revenue. |
| **ORIS** | Office of Regulatory Information Systems plant identifier. Used by EIA. The GHGRP↔ORIS crosswalk bridges GHGRP to CEMS. |
| **NO_PARENT_RECORD** | Placeholder label for facilities whose parent record is missing from the 2023 parent workbook. Excluded from cohort. |

2. **Sub-threshold facilities invisible to GHGRP.** Facilities below 25,000 mt CO₂e/year are absent from the panel. Climate TRACE partially fills this gap, but the comparison itself is a finding in the SCVS section.

-3. **Climate TRACE is a hybrid model, not pure satellite.** Estimates use activity data and emission factors heavily, especially for power. We weight SCVS at 0.2 in the composite to reflect this. The working paper labels Climate TRACE as "independent model-based, remote-sensing-informed estimate" — not "pristine remote sensing."

+3. **Climate TRACE is a hybrid model, not pure satellite.** Estimates use activity data and emission factors heavily, especially for power. The working paper labels Climate TRACE as "independent model-based, remote-sensing-informed estimate" — not "pristine remote sensing." Despite this model uncertainty, we weight SCVS at **0.4** in the composite (equal to EPS, double PQS) because in a post-GHGRP world the independent-estimation axis is the only durable credibility anchor: corporate self-disclosure has a 74% restatement track record and mandatory reporting is being dismantled. The framework's defensibility rests on making this weighting choice explicit and presenting full sensitivity analysis across alternative weight combinations.

4. **Pledge data biased toward larger and more-disclosed companies.** Smaller private firms and cooperatives are systematically absent from SBTi and have no 10-Ks. 28 of our 50 cohort parents are non-registrants. The credibility universe is publicly-traded large-cap industrial; we say so explicitly.

5. **2023 ownership applied retroactively.** M&A and divestitures across the 2011–2023 window are not tracked. Notable cases (e.g., Vistra emerging from Energy Future Holdings, Talen spin-off) are flagged in the report.
6. **Short post-treatment window for any IRA causal analysis.** Only 2022 and 2023 are post-IRA. Causal analysis is explicitly deferred to Phase 2.

### Notebook 06 — Dashboard

**Status:** Pending.
**Purpose:** Assemble the self-contained HTML dashboard. (The working paper itself is a separate `.ipynb` in `Deliverables/` — see below.)
**Planned sections:**
- (1) **Macro view** — cohort-wide 2×2 quadrant scatter (PQS × EPS, sized by 2023 emissions, colored by SCVS), geospatial map, aggregate divergence over time. Includes the interactive CCCS weight sliders described below; the quadrant labels and ranking recompute live as the user changes weights.

  - re-renders the Macro quadrant scatter and the leaderboard table,
  - updates the per-parent panels in Drilldown view,
  - displays the current weights and a "default (Anthropic recommended)" reset button.
  Implementation is vanilla JavaScript driving Plotly `restyle`/`relayout` calls, no Python backend. All component-score data is embedded at notebook-render time as a JSON blob.
- (5) Working-paper figure pack (PNG + SVG) — exec summary chart, methodology figures, findings panels — produced at the default weights.
- (6) Save `dashboard/index.html` and `outputs/figures/working_paper/`.

## Quick UX Question Before We Build

You said "a slider between 0-1 to choose different weights from PQS, EPS, and SCVS" and "the 3rd weight will be deduced from the first two." That implies a **two-slider** setup, but I want to confirm the UX detail because it determines a small implementation choice:

questions.question: How should the two CCCS-weight sliders behave when the user moves them?

options.label: Constrained — second slider's range shrinks based on first

content.subject: Build 00_Data_Acquisition.ipynb skeleton
content.description: Create the notebook scaffold with title, imports, paths, helper functions (download_with_retry, sha256, manifest writer), and section markdown.

content.subject: Section 2: Top-50 cohort identification
content.description: Load GHGRP 2023 panel + parent-company workbook, filter to Subpart D / power generation, attribute by 2023 ownership share, rank by 2023 emissions, write data/processed/cohort_top50.csv.

content.subject: Section 3: EPA AMPD CEMS via CAMD easey API
content.description: Add cells that read CAMD API key from env, fetch facility-annual emissions for 2011-2024, save CSVs to data/raw/cems/, with graceful fallback instructions if key is missing.

content.subject: Section 4: Climate TRACE US power-sector package
content.description: Add cells to download Climate TRACE electricity-generation package (zip), unpack to data/raw/climate_trace/, with version probing.

content.subject: Section 5: SBTi public target dashboard
content.description: Add cells to fetch SBTi companies-excel.xlsx and targets-excel.xlsx, save to data/raw/sbti/, with manual-download fallback instructions.

content.subject: Section 6: SEC EDGAR 10-K fetch for cohort
content.description: Add cells that load SEC ticker→CIK map, fuzzy-match parent names → CIKs with manual override slot, and pull the most recent 10-K (full submission HTML) for each cohort parent into data/raw/sec_10k/{ticker}/.

content.subject: Section 7: data_manifest.json generator
content.description: Final cell that walks data/raw/ and writes a manifest with source URL, retrieved-at timestamp, file size, sha256, and notes for every acquired file.

content.subject: Verify notebook end-to-end (lint, JSON validity, smoke run plan)
content.description: Validate the .ipynb opens as valid JSON via nbformat, do a static read-through, and document which cells the user should run vs which require their API key/credentials.

content.subject: Read current state of 00_Data_Acquisition.ipynb
content.description: Read the notebook end-to-end as it currently exists after the user's fixes. Compare with the original generator script to identify what changed.

content.subject: Inspect downstream artifacts produced by the user's run
content.description: Inspect data/raw, data/processed, and data/external to see exactly what files exist, their sizes, and whether the cohort/manifest/10-K outputs are present and well-formed.

content.subject: Audit user's fixes for impact on plan assumptions
content.description: For each user edit, evaluate whether it violates a locked decision (Power POC, top 50, hybrid velocity, 2023 ownership, tiered NLP, HTML+Plotly, full LME) or is purely a bug fix. Flag anything that needs reversion or follow-up.

content.subject: Report findings + restate work plan
content.description: Write the review report: what changed, what is OK, what needs follow-up, and a clean restatement of the 4-day plan so the user can confirm or adjust before notebook 01.

content.subject: Patch notebook 00 — .env loading, orphan exclusion, fuzzy guard, CT URL probe
content.description: Four fixes: (1) explicit .env path resolution in cell 02 so CEMS section sees EPA_CAMD_API_KEY; (2) defensive NO_PARENT_RECORD exclusion + backfill in cell 13; (3) DO_NOT_MATCH set + fuzzy cutoff 0.92 + first-token gate in cell 27 to kill UNS-Energy / GenOn false positives; (4) env-overridable CLIMATE_TRACE_URL with broader candidate list in cell 21.

content.subject: Validate patched notebook syntactically
content.description: Run nbformat.validate and ast.parse over every code cell to confirm the four patches did not introduce syntax errors.

content.subject: User: re-run Sections 0, 2, 3, 4, 6 + verify CEMS & Climate TRACE land on disk
content.description: After my patches: user re-runs cell 02 (env), Section 2 (cohort with orphan exclusion), Section 3 (CEMS — now sees API key), Section 4 (Climate TRACE — may still fail; will need a working URL from the user if all candidates 404), Section 6 (10-K matching with tighter fuzzy). Verify data/raw/cems and data/raw/climate_trace are populated.

content.subject: Design Notebook 01 — EDA scope and structure
content.description: Define the cohort-focused EDA notebook: 13-year trajectories, fuel mix, geography, threshold-effect handling, restatement patterns, CEMS sanity peek. Per user's selection: top-50 only.

content.subject: Diagnose CEMS 0-match — auth or schema issue?
content.description: CAMD API returned only 1 manifest entry (dataType: EDR, 1995 filing) — strongly suggests auth failure. Need to switch from query-param to header auth (x-api-key) and re-test.

content.subject: Patch CEMS Section 3 — header auth + diagnostics + broader filter
content.description: Fix cell 17 to use `headers={'x-api-key': ...}` instead of query param. Add diagnostics that print unique dataType values and entries-per-year. Loosen cell 18 filter to dataType==Emissions for our years (drop dataSubType check which doesn't exist in schema).

content.subject: Patch fuzzy CIK — title punctuation normalization (EVERGY edge case)
content.description: EVERGY INC went from matched to unmatched after my fix because SEC's "Evergy, Inc." title has a comma after the first token, defeating the startswith("evergy ") gate. Normalize titles before the startswith check.

content.subject: Rewrite Section 3 to use streaming-services/emissions/apportioned/annual

## Good news: the leaders/laggards table DID run

Section 4 cells (4.1, 4.2, 4.3) all executed cleanly — execution counts 21, 22, 23 with valid outputs. You may have missed it because Section 3 prints `"Section 3 not yet implemented"` and that stub may have made you assume Section 4 was also stubbed. Section 4 is fully implemented and ran. Here's what it produced, pulled straight from cell 22's output:

### Section 1 validation — PASSED

- Cohort facility-year rows: 7,839
- Distinct cohort facilities: 578
- Distinct cohort parents: 50 (expected)
- parent_year panel shape: (650, 5) = 50 parents × 13 years
- **Worst 2023 reconciliation diff: -0.000% (LIGHTSTONE GENERATION LLC) — "All within 1%: True"** ✅

### Section 4 — Decarbonization Leaders (top 5 most-negative slope)

| Rank | Parent | Slope (Mt/yr) | % per year | Total % change 2011→2023 | Stat. significant |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|:---:|
| 1 | American Electric Power | −3.90 | −5.5% | **−50.4%** | ✓ |
| 2 | US Government (TVA) | −3.17 | −6.0% | −46.0% | ✓ |
| 3 | NRG Energy | −2.93 | −7.7% | **−63.1%** | ✓ |
| 4 | Duke Energy | −2.58 | −2.9% | −29.5% | ✓ |
| 5 | Talen Energy | −2.14 | −9.7% | **−70.0%** | ✓ |

### Section 4 — Largest Growers (top 5 most-positive slope)

| Rank | Parent | Slope (Mt/yr) | % per year | Total % change 2011→2023 | Stat. significant |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|:---:|
| 1 | Prairie State Energy Campus | +0.73 | +7.5% | **+69,352%** ⚠️ | ✓ |
| 2 | CPN Management (Calpine) | +0.50 | +1.2% | +37.9% | ✗ |
| 3 | LS Power Development | +0.45 | +5.7% | +156.6% | ✓ |
| 4 | Constellation Energy | +0.33 | +5.0% | +39.8% | ✓ |
| 5 | Entergy | +0.19 | +0.5% | +6.2% | ✗ |

### Cohort summary

- **27 parents** statistically distinguishable as decarbonizing
- **5 parents** statistically distinguishable as growing
- **18 parents** flat / not distinguishable from zero

## One Big Red Flag to Flag in the Working Paper

**Prairie State Energy Campus +69,352%** is not a real growth rate. Prairie State came online in 2012 (Unit 1) and 2013 (Unit 2). In 2011 it had essentially zero emissions (it didn't exist yet); by 2023 it's a ~9 MtCO₂e/yr coal plant. The trajectory regression treats the early near-zero baseline as a real measurement, producing a meaningless slope. This is a **young-plant artifact**, and we should either:
- Exclude facilities with <5 years of operating data from the trajectory regression, OR
- Flag them in the leaders/laggards table with a "started during panel" annotation.

Same caveat probably applies to **LS Power Development +156%** (PE-owned, facilities likely changed hands during the window) and possibly **Constellation Energy +39.8%** (the Exelon spin-off happened in Feb 2022, so the "Constellation Energy Corp" parent name didn't exist for most of the panel — its rising 2022/2023 emissions are accounting artifact of corporate structure, not real growth).

These three flagged cases are *interesting findings*, not bugs — they show how a naive trajectory metric can be misleading and motivate the more careful LME approach in Notebook 03.

## Proposed Plan for Today's Remaining Work

Build the four pending sections of Notebook 01 in this order:

**Step 1 — Section 3: Fuel-mix decomposition** (~30 min)
Load `emissions_by_unit_and_fuel_type_c_d_aa.xlsb`, filter to cohort facilities, decompose each parent's 2023 emissions into coal / gas / oil / biomass / other. Two charts: (a) stacked bar of fuel-mix per parent (2023 snapshot), (b) cohort-wide fuel-mix share over 2011–2023. Save `cohort_fuel_mix_panel.csv`.

**Step 2 — Section 5: Hand-labeled exit register** (~45 min)
Identify cohort facilities whose CO₂e went from >0 to NaN/zero before 2023. Rank by last-known emissions. For top 20, manually label `exit_reason ∈ {retirement, sub_threshold, rule_change, uncertain}` using domain knowledge of well-documented coal closures (Navajo 2019, Bruce Mansfield 2019, J M Stuart 2018, San Juan 2022, plus 16 others). Save `cohort_exit_register.csv` with `source_url` column. Then add a "young-plant exclusion" companion register for Prairie State / LS Power / Constellation cases.

**Step 3 — Section 6: Geographic concentration** (~30 min)
State-level rollup of 2023 cohort emissions. Two charts: (a) horizontal bar of top-15 states, (b) a state choropleth via Plotly. Note state×parent heatmap for top 10 parents.

**Step 4 — Section 7: CEMS sanity peek** (~45 min)
Load CEMS stitched panel. Aggregate unit → facility → parent for top-10 cohort parents (after short-ton→metric-ton conversion). Small-multiples chart: 10 panels, two lines each (CEMS vs GHGRP). Visual only, no statistics — proper LME comparison is Notebook 03.

**Step 5 — Validate and save** (~15 min)
Re-run notebook end-to-end, confirm all stubs are gone, regenerate `data_manifest.json` to include the new processed CSVs.

**Total: ~2.5–3 hours.** After this, I move to Notebook 02 (entity resolution + multi-source alignment).

## Approve Plan?

If you say "go" or "proceed", I start with Step 1 immediately. If you want to adjust scope (e.g., skip the choropleth, simplify the exit register, or change the young-plant handling), say so before I start.

def md_cell(src: str) -> dict:
    return nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(src.strip("\n"))

# ============================================================================

SECTION_3_MARKDOWN = '''## 3. Fuel-mix composition within the cohort

This section decomposes each cohort parent's emissions into the four conventional power-sector fuel categories — **Coal**, **Natural Gas**, **Oil**, **Biomass** — plus an **Other** catchall. The source is `emissions_by_unit_and_fuel_type_c_d_aa.xlsb` (FUEL_DATA sheet), which reports each Subpart D unit's annual CO2 emissions broken out by fuel.

**Why this matters for the framework:** the fuel-mix shape predicts how exposed a parent is to the coal-retirement decarbonization channel. Parents whose 2023 emissions are 80% coal have far more easy decarbonization runway than parents whose emissions are 80% natural gas — this is the conversation a Lab researcher will want to have when reading the working paper.

**Outputs:**
- `data/processed/cohort_fuel_mix_panel.csv` — parent × year × fuel-category CO2 attribution
- `outputs/figures/03_fuel_mix_2023_per_parent.png` — stacked horizontal bar, 2023 snapshot
- `outputs/figures/03_cohort_fuel_mix_over_time.png` — cohort-wide fuel-mix share, 2011-2023
'''

SECTION_3_CELLS = [
    code_cell('''
# --- 3.1 load FUEL_DATA from the xlsb workbook ---
fuel_xlsb = GHGRP_DIR / "emissions_by_unit_and_fuel_type_c_d_aa.xlsb"
try:
    import pyxlsb  # noqa: F401
except ImportError:
    import subprocess
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "pyxlsb"])

fuel_xl = pd.ExcelFile(fuel_xlsb, engine="pyxlsb")
print("Sheets in workbook:", fuel_xl.sheet_names)

# FUEL_DATA contains one row per (facility, unit, year, fuel-type) with CO2 mass.
fuel_data = pd.read_excel(fuel_xlsb, sheet_name="FUEL_DATA", engine="pyxlsb", header=0)
fuel_data.columns = [str(c).strip() for c in fuel_data.columns]
print(f"FUEL_DATA shape: {fuel_data.shape}")
print("First 15 columns:")
for c in list(fuel_data.columns)[:15]:
    print(f"  - {c}")
'''),

    code_cell('''
# --- 3.2 normalize columns + filter to cohort facilities ---
FUEL_ALIASES = {
    "facility_id":   ["GHGRP ID", "Facility Id", "GHGRP Facility ID", "Facility ID"],
    "year":          ["Reporting Year", "REPORTING YEAR", "Year"],
    "fuel_type":     ["Specific Fuel Type", "Fuel Type (specific)", "Fuel Type",
                       "SPECIFIC FUEL TYPE", "FUEL TYPE (SPECIFIC)"],
    "fuel_type_gen": ["Fuel Type (general)", "General Fuel Type", "FUEL TYPE (GENERAL)"],
    "co2_tons":      ["Fuel Methodology - CO2 emissions (non-biogenic) (metric tons)",
                       "CO2 emissions (non-biogenic) (metric tons)",
                       "Total CO2 emissions (metric tons)",
                       "CO2 emissions (metric tons)",
                       "CO2 emissions",
                       "Total Reported Direct Emissions from Fuel (metric tons)"],
}
fuel_data = rename_first_match(fuel_data, FUEL_ALIASES)

# Fall back: any column with "co2" and "metric" if alias miss
if "co2_tons" not in fuel_data.columns:
    co2_candidates = [c for c in fuel_data.columns
                      if re.search(r"co2", str(c), re.I) and re.search(r"metric|ton", str(c), re.I)]
    if co2_candidates:
        best = max(co2_candidates,
                   key=lambda c: pd.to_numeric(fuel_data[c], errors="coerce").notna().sum())
        fuel_data["co2_tons"] = pd.to_numeric(fuel_data[best], errors="coerce")
        print(f"[info] inferred co2_tons from column: {best}")

# Fall back: fuel_type if alias miss
if "fuel_type" not in fuel_data.columns:
    fuel_candidates = [c for c in fuel_data.columns if re.search(r"fuel", str(c), re.I)]
    if fuel_candidates:
        fuel_data["fuel_type"] = fuel_data[fuel_candidates[0]].astype(str)
        print(f"[info] inferred fuel_type from column: {fuel_candidates[0]}")

print(f"Resolved fuel columns: {[c for c in ['facility_id', 'year', 'fuel_type', 'co2_tons'] if c in fuel_data.columns]}")

assert_required("facility_id" in fuel_data.columns, "FUEL_DATA missing facility_id")
assert_required("year" in fuel_data.columns,        "FUEL_DATA missing year")
assert_required("fuel_type" in fuel_data.columns,   "FUEL_DATA missing fuel_type")
assert_required("co2_tons" in fuel_data.columns,    "FUEL_DATA missing co2_tons")

# Restrict to cohort facility-year keys via the panel we just built
panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_PROCESSED / "cohort_facility_year_panel.csv")
cohort_fac_ids = set(panel["facility_id"].astype(int).unique())
fuel_data["facility_id"] = pd.to_numeric(fuel_data["facility_id"], errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
fuel_data["year"]        = pd.to_numeric(fuel_data["year"], errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
fuel_cohort = fuel_data[fuel_data["facility_id"].isin(cohort_fac_ids)].copy()
print(f"Cohort fuel-rows: {len(fuel_cohort):,}  (of {len(fuel_data):,} total)")
'''),

    code_cell('''
# --- 3.3 categorize fuels into five buckets ---
def categorize_fuel(s: object) -> str:
    s = str(s).lower()
    if any(k in s for k in ["coal", "lignite", "anthracite", "bituminous", "subbituminous", "petroleum coke", "pet coke", "coke"]):
        return "Coal"
    if any(k in s for k in ["natural gas", "pipeline", "lng", "methane", "liquefied"]):
        return "Natural Gas"
    if any(k in s for k in ["oil", "diesel", "kerosene", "petroleum", "fuel oil", "distillate", "residual"]):
        return "Oil"
    if any(k in s for k in ["wood", "biomass", "biogas", "landfill", "biogenic", "agric", "manure", "msw", "muni"]):
        return "Biomass"
    return "Other"

# ============================================================================
# Surgical update logic
# ============================================================================
def find_markdown_index(cells: list, predicate) -> int:
    for i, c in enumerate(cells):
        if c.cell_type == "markdown" and predicate(c.source):
            return i
    raise ValueError("Markdown predicate not found")


def replace_section(cells: list, md_predicate, new_md_source: str, new_code_cells: list) -> list:
    """Find a markdown cell matching predicate, replace its source + all consecutive
    code cells after it (until next markdown or end) with new content."""
    md_idx = find_markdown_index(cells, md_predicate)
    end_idx = md_idx + 1
    while end_idx < len(cells) and cells[end_idx].cell_type == "code":
        end_idx += 1
    # Build the new markdown cell with updated source
    new_md = nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(new_md_source.strip("\n"))
    return cells[:md_idx] + [new_md] + new_code_cells + cells[end_idx:]


def main() -> None:
    nb = nbf.read(str(NB_PATH), as_version=4)
    cells = nb.cells

    # Process sections in REVERSE order so insertions do not shift earlier indices.
    cells = replace_section(
        cells,
        md_predicate=lambda src: src.startswith("## 7."),
        new_md_source=SECTION_7_MARKDOWN,
        new_code_cells=SECTION_7_CELLS,
    )
    cells = replace_section(
        cells,
        md_predicate=lambda src: src.startswith("## 6."),
        new_md_source=SECTION_6_MARKDOWN,
        new_code_cells=SECTION_6_CELLS,
    )
    cells = replace_section(
        cells,
        md_predicate=lambda src: src.startswith("## 5."),
        new_md_source=SECTION_5_MARKDOWN,
        new_code_cells=SECTION_5_CELLS,
    )
    cells = replace_section(
        cells,
        md_predicate=lambda src: src.startswith("## 3."),
        new_md_source=SECTION_3_MARKDOWN,
        new_code_cells=SECTION_3_CELLS,
    )

    nb.cells = cells
    nbf.write(nb, str(NB_PATH))

    # Validate
    import ast
    nb2 = nbf.read(str(NB_PATH), as_version=4)
    nbf.validate(nb2)
    errs = []
    for i, c in enumerate(nb2.cells):
        if c.cell_type == "code":
            try:
                ast.parse(c.source)
            except SyntaxError as e:
                errs.append((i, str(e)))
    n_code = sum(1 for c in nb2.cells if c.cell_type == "code")
    n_md   = sum(1 for c in nb2.cells if c.cell_type == "markdown")
    print(f"Second pass complete.")
    print(f"Total cells: {len(nb2.cells)} ({n_md} md, {n_code} code)")
    print(f"Syntax check: {n_code - len(errs)}/{n_code} OK")
    for i, e in errs:
        print(f"  [SYNTAX ERROR] cell {i}: {e}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# ============================================================================
# Surgical update logic
# ============================================================================
def find_markdown_index(cells: list, predicate) -> int:
    for i, c in enumerate(cells):
        if c.cell_type == "markdown" and predicate(c.source):
            return i
    raise ValueError("Markdown predicate not found")


def replace_section(cells: list, md_predicate, new_md_source: str, new_code_cells: list) -> list:
    """Find a markdown cell matching predicate, replace its source + all consecutive
    code cells after it (until next markdown or end) with new content."""
    md_idx = find_markdown_index(cells, md_predicate)
    end_idx = md_idx + 1
    while end_idx < len(cells) and cells[end_idx].cell_type == "code":
        end_idx += 1
    # Build the new markdown cell with updated source
    new_md = nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(new_md_source.strip("\n"))
    return cells[:md_idx] + [new_md] + new_code_cells + cells[end_idx:]


def main() -> None:
    nb = nbf.read(str(NB_PATH), as_version=4)
    cells = nb.cells

    # Process sections in REVERSE order so insertions do not shift earlier indices.
    cells = replace_section(
        cells,
        md_predicate=lambda src: src.startswith("## 7."),
        new_md_source=SECTION_7_MARKDOWN,
        new_code_cells=SECTION_7_CELLS,
    )
    cells = replace_section(
        cells,
        md_predicate=lambda src: src.startswith("## 6."),
        new_md_source=SECTION_6_MARKDOWN,
        new_code_cells=SECTION_6_CELLS,
    )
    cells = replace_section(
        cells,
        md_predicate=lambda src: src.startswith("## 5."),
        new_md_source=SECTION_5_MARKDOWN,
        new_code_cells=SECTION_5_CELLS,
    )
    cells = replace_section(
        cells,
        md_predicate=lambda src: src.startswith("## 3."),
        new_md_source=SECTION_3_MARKDOWN,
        new_code_cells=SECTION_3_CELLS,
    )

    nb.cells = cells
    nbf.write(nb, str(NB_PATH))

    # Validate
    import ast
    nb2 = nbf.read(str(NB_PATH), as_version=4)
    nbf.validate(nb2)
    errs = []
    for i, c in enumerate(nb2.cells):
        if c.cell_type == "code":
            try:
                ast.parse(c.source)
            except SyntaxError as e:
                errs.append((i, str(e)))
    n_code = sum(1 for c in nb2.cells if c.cell_type == "code")
    n_md   = sum(1 for c in nb2.cells if c.cell_type == "markdown")
    print(f"Second pass complete.")
    print(f"Total cells: {len(nb2.cells)} ({n_md} md, {n_code} code)")
    print(f"Syntax check: {n_code - len(errs)}/{n_code} OK")
    for i, e in errs:
        print(f"  [SYNTAX ERROR] cell {i}: {e}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

**Section 3 — Fuel-mix decomposition (6 cells).** Loads `FUEL_DATA` sheet from the unit-and-fuel xlsb (~323k rows), filters to cohort facilities, categorizes fuels into 5 buckets (Coal / Natural Gas / Oil / Biomass / Other) via keyword matching, attributes by 2023 ownership shares. **Section 5 — Hand-labeled exit register (3 cells).** Identifies cohort facilities that exit the panel before 2023, ranks by last-year emissions. Top-20 are labeled via regex name-matching against a curated `EXIT_REGISTRY` covering 20 well-documented coal retirements (Navajo, Bruce Mansfield, J M Stuart, San Juan, Big Sandy, Brayton Point, Allen, Paradise, Hammond, Conesville, Tanners Creek, Asheville, Sammis, Comanche, Sherco, Plant Crist, Crawford, Fisk, Will County, Killen) — each with exit date, source URL, and notes. Parent × state heatmap (top-10 × top-10) with in-cell value annotations — surfaces e.g. Vistra's Texas concentration, Southern's Georgia concentration, AEP's Ohio-WV-Indiana spread.

nb.cells[18].source = '''# --- 3.1 load FUEL_DATA + UNIT_DATA from the xlsb workbook ---
# Strategy: FUEL_DATA tells us the General Fuel Type per (facility, unit, year) but only
# has CH4 and N2O emissions (no CO2). UNIT_DATA at header=6 has the CO2 mass per unit.
# We determine each unit-year's *primary fuel* from FUEL_DATA (by which fuel has the

try:
    import pyxlsb  # noqa: F401
except ImportError:
    import subprocess
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "pyxlsb"])

# Both sheets have notes/preamble rows; the headers sit at row 5 (FUEL_DATA) and row 6 (UNIT_DATA).
def load_xlsb_sheet_probe(xl_path: Path, sheet: str, must_match: list[str],
                          probe_rows: tuple = (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7),
                          engine: str = "pyxlsb") -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, int]:
    last_df = None
    for header_row in probe_rows:
        df = pd.read_excel(xl_path, sheet_name=sheet, engine=engine, header=header_row)
        cols_lower = [str(c).lower() for c in df.columns]
        if all(any(tok in c for c in cols_lower) for tok in must_match):
            print(f"  loaded sheet={sheet!r} header={header_row}, shape={df.shape}")
            return df, header_row
        last_df = df
    raise RuntimeError(f"No header row found in {sheet!r}. Last cols: {list(last_df.columns)[:5]}")


print("Loading FUEL_DATA …")
fuel_data, _ = load_xlsb_sheet_probe(
    fuel_xlsb, "FUEL_DATA",
    must_match=["facility", "year", "fuel"],
)
fuel_data.columns = [str(c).strip() for c in fuel_data.columns]

print("\\nLoading UNIT_DATA …")
unit_data, _ = load_xlsb_sheet_probe(
    fuel_xlsb, "UNIT_DATA",
    must_match=["facility", "unit", "co2"],
)
unit_data.columns = [str(c).strip() for c in unit_data.columns]

print(f"\\nFUEL_DATA: {fuel_data.shape}  UNIT_DATA: {unit_data.shape}")

nb.cells[19].source = '''# --- 3.2 determine the primary fuel per (facility, unit, year) from FUEL_DATA ---
# We use CH4 + N2O emissions (both in mt CO2e) as a proxy for fuel-usage weight within
# each unit-year. The fuel category with the highest combined CH4+N2O is treated as
# that unit's primary fuel for that year. For ~95% of US power units this is a single
# unambiguous fuel; mixed-fuel units (e.g., coal+gas startup) get categorized by their
# dominant heat source.
FUEL_KEY_COLS = {
    "facility_id":   ["Facility Id", "GHGRP ID", "GHGRP Facility ID"],
    "year":          ["Reporting Year"],
    "unit_name":     ["Unit Name"],
    "fuel_general":  ["General Fuel Type"],
    "ch4_co2e":      ["Fuel Methane (CH4) emissions (mt CO2e)"],
    "n2o_co2e":      ["Fuel Nitrous Oxide (N2O) emissions (mt CO2e)"],
}
fuel_data = rename_first_match(fuel_data, FUEL_KEY_COLS)
for k in ["facility_id", "year", "unit_name", "fuel_general"]:
    assert_required(k in fuel_data.columns, f"FUEL_DATA missing {k}")

fuel_data["facility_id"] = pd.to_numeric(fuel_data["facility_id"], errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
fuel_data["year"]        = pd.to_numeric(fuel_data["year"],        errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
fuel_data["ch4_co2e"]    = pd.to_numeric(fuel_data.get("ch4_co2e", 0), errors="coerce").fillna(0)
fuel_data["n2o_co2e"]    = pd.to_numeric(fuel_data.get("n2o_co2e", 0), errors="coerce").fillna(0)
fuel_data["ghg_weight"]  = fuel_data["ch4_co2e"] + fuel_data["n2o_co2e"]

# Aggregate within (facility, unit, year, fuel_general) — there may be multiple rows

fuel_agg = (
    fuel_data.groupby(["facility_id", "year", "unit_name", "fuel_general"], as_index=False)["ghg_weight"]
    .sum()
    .dropna(subset=["unit_name", "fuel_general"])
)
# Pick the highest-weight fuel per (facility, unit, year). When ghg_weight ties at 0
# (small units), we fall back to the first non-null fuel_general encountered.
fuel_agg_sorted = fuel_agg.sort_values(

)

## Summary of Fixes Applied

**Section 3 — completely rewritten (cells 18-23):**

Root issue I missed in the first pass: FUEL_DATA has only CH4/N2O emissions, no CO2 column. The CO2 data lives in UNIT_DATA (a separate sheet in the same workbook) at header row 6. 

The new logic:
- **3.1** loads both `FUEL_DATA` (header probed → row 5) and `UNIT_DATA` (header probed → row 6) using a defensive probe that tries rows 0-7.
- **3.2** determines each unit-year's *primary fuel* by aggregating FUEL_DATA's CH4+N2O emissions per (facility, unit, year, General Fuel Type), then picking the fuel with the highest weight.
- **3.3** categorizes General Fuel Type into 5 buckets (Coal / Natural Gas / Oil / Biomass / Other).
- **3.4** attaches UNIT_DATA's `Unit CO2 emissions (non-biogenic)` to each unit-year, joins to the primary-fuel category, filters to cohort, attributes by 2023 ownership share, saves `cohort_fuel_mix_panel.csv`.
- **3.5 & 3.6** charts unchanged in logic — stacked horizontal bar (2023 per parent) and cohort-wide fuel-mix area chart over 2011-2023.

**Section 7 — patched cells 37-38:**

Root issue: the crosswalk xlsx has two sheets (`README` and `ORIS Crosswalk`) and pandas defaulted to the README sheet. Also, a single GHGRP facility can map to up to 5 ORIS codes (multi-unit plants).

The new logic:
- **7.1** reads `sheet_name="ORIS Crosswalk"`, header=0.
- **7.2** melts the 5 `ORIS CODE` / `ORIS CODE 2..5` columns into long form (one row per facility-ORIS pair), then joins to CEMS via `Facility ID`. Expected matching: ~97% of CEMS rows, 99.8% of cohort facilities.

## What You Do Now

**Project:** Corporate Climate Credibility Audit — power-sector POC
**Cohort:** Top 50 fossil-fuel power-generating parent companies, locked in `00_Data_Acquisition.ipynb`

- `data/processed/per_parent_trajectory_slopes.csv` — per-parent OLS slope + bootstrap CI
- `data/processed/cohort_exit_register.csv` — hand-labeled exit causes for top-20 dropouts (Section 5)
- `outputs/figures/*.png` — working-paper-ready visuals

**Reproducibility:** the notebook is restartable top-to-bottom; every analytical cell is idempotent.

---

## Sections

1. **Panel construction** — build the canonical 13-year cohort facility-year panel
2. **Cohort trajectory overview** — headline chart for the working paper
3. **Fuel-mix composition** — coal / gas / oil / biomass within the cohort
4. **Per-parent trajectory regression** — OLS slope + bootstrap CI per parent
5. **Threshold-effect handling** — hand-labeled exit register for top-20 dropouts

===== CELL 1 (markdown) =====
## 0. Environment

Imports, paths, and helpers. Run this first; everything below depends on these globals.

===== CELL 4 (markdown) =====
## 1. Panel construction — the canonical 13-year cohort facility-year panel

This is the most important output of this notebook. Every downstream notebook reads from `cohort_facility_year_panel.csv` (long-form, one row per facility-year) and `cohort_parent_year_panel.csv` (rolled up to parent-year).

**Construction logic:**

1. Load the `Direct Point Emitters` sheet from `ghgp_data_by_year_2023.xlsx`. This sheet contains one row per facility with separate columns for each year's emissions, plus stable facility metadata (id, name, lat/lon, state, subparts).
2. Filter to facilities reporting Subpart D (Electricity Generation) in any year.
3. Unpivot the year columns into a long form: one row per (facility, year).
4. Attach 2023-locked parent ownership from `ghgp_data_parent_company.xlsb`. Multiply each facility-year emission by the parent's ownership share to get attributed emissions.
5. Restrict to the locked top-50 cohort (read from `data/processed/cohort_top50.csv`).
6. Validate: every cohort parent has ≥1 facility-year; total cohort emissions in 2023 match the value in `cohort_top50.csv` within 1%.

===== CELL 13 (markdown) =====
## 2. Cohort trajectory overview — the headline chart

One small-multiples figure: each of the 50 parents as one panel, 2011–2023 attributed emissions trajectory. Sorted by 2023 emissions descending. This is the visual that anchors the working paper's executive summary.

===== CELL 17 (markdown) =====
## 3. Fuel-mix composition within the cohort

This section decomposes each cohort parent's emissions into the four conventional power-sector fuel categories — **Coal**, **Natural Gas**, **Oil**, **Biomass** — plus an **Other** catchall. The source is `emissions_by_unit_and_fuel_type_c_d_aa.xlsb` (FUEL_DATA sheet), which reports each Subpart D unit's annual CO2 emissions broken out by fuel.

**Why this matters for the framework:** the fuel-mix shape predicts how exposed a parent is to the coal-retirement decarbonization channel. Parents whose 2023 emissions are 80% coal have far more easy decarbonization runway than parents whose emissions are 80% natural gas — this is the conversation a Lab researcher will want to have when reading the working paper.

**Outputs:**
- `data/processed/cohort_fuel_mix_panel.csv` — parent × year × fuel-category CO2 attribution
- `outputs/figures/03_fuel_mix_2023_per_parent.png` — stacked horizontal bar, 2023 snapshot
- `outputs/figures/03_cohort_fuel_mix_over_time.png` — cohort-wide fuel-mix share, 2011-2023

===== CELL 24 (markdown) =====
## 4. Per-parent trajectory regression

OLS slope of attributed CO2e (Mt) on year, fitted per parent. Bootstrap 95% confidence interval (n=1000). Output: ranked table of decarbonization velocity (Mt/year and %/year) saved to `data/processed/per_parent_trajectory_slopes.csv`.

**Honest caveats:** OLS on 13 data points with no covariates is a coarse summary. Parents with a small number of facilities (n<3) have noisy slopes. Bootstrap CIs reflect sampling uncertainty in the slope only, not measurement uncertainty in the underlying GHGRP values. The proper LME with random effects + AR(1) lives in Notebook 03.

===== CELL 28 (markdown) =====
## 5. Threshold-effect handling — hand-labeled exit register

GHGRP requires reporting only for facilities emitting >=25,000 mt CO2e/year. When a cohort facility disappears from the panel before 2023, it can mean one of three different things:

1. **Plant retirement** — the facility physically closed. Real emissions reduction.
2. **Sub-threshold drop** — the facility reduced output but still operates, emitting <25k tCO2e/year. Real (partial) reduction, but the panel can no longer see the remaining emissions.
3. **Rule-change exit** — EPA changed reporting obligations; the facility wasn't required to report anymore but its operations may not have changed.

Treating all three the same systematically overstates cohort decarbonization. A senior data scientist's job is to label these correctly so downstream trajectory regressions and the LME don't mistake an accounting artifact for a real reduction.

Per locked Decision #13, we **hand-label the top 20 cohort dropouts** using public sources (Wikipedia plant-history pages, EIA-860 retirement records, parent-company press releases, S&P Global power-plant trackers). Facilities outside the top 20 receive an "uncertain" label.

We also include a **young-plant / young-parent register** flagging the three cases surfaced by Section 4's trajectory regression where extreme percent growth is a structural artifact (Prairie State, LS Power Development, Constellation Energy).

**Output:** `data/processed/cohort_exit_register.csv` with columns `facility_id, facility_name, parent_name, state, last_active_year, last_year_co2_mt, exit_reason, source_url, notes`.

===== CELL 32 (markdown) =====
## 6. Geographic concentration

Where is cohort emissions concentrated geographically? Two views:

1. **State-level rollup** — total 2023 cohort emissions per state, ranked. Tells the working paper reader which states would be most affected by GHGRP sunset and which are the natural focus areas for any state-level decarbonization policy.
2. **Parent x state heatmap** — for the top-10 parents and top-10 states, the cell value shows attributed 2023 emissions. Reveals geographic concentration patterns (e.g., does Vistra dominate Texas, AEP dominate Ohio/WV).

We deliberately avoid a choropleth here to keep matplotlib-only dependencies; the dashboard (Notebook 06) does the proper geospatial layer with Plotly.

===== CELL 36 (markdown) =====
## 7. CEMS sanity peek - visual side-by-side for top-10 cohort parents

The CEMS panel (acquired by Notebook 00) is our independent ground truth: direct, continuous, in-stack measurement at every fossil power plant subject to Acid Rain/CSAPR rules. Notebook 03 uses CEMS as the anchor for the Linear Mixed-Effects diagnostic that quantifies Climate TRACE's structural bias.

In this notebook we only do the **first-look visual sanity check**: do the GHGRP self-reports and CEMS direct measurements tell roughly the same story at parent level for our top-10 cohort parents? If they diverge meaningfully even at this coarse level, that is itself a finding that motivates the more careful LME work.

**Three preparation steps before plotting:**
1. Convert CEMS CO2 from short tons (US customary) to metric tons (standard factor 0.907185).
2. Bridge CEMS Facility ID (which equals ORIS ID) to GHGRP facility_id using `ghgrp_oris_power_plant_crosswalk_12_13_21.xlsx`.
3. Apply the same 2023-ownership attribution we used for GHGRP to roll CEMS unit-rows up to parent-year.

The proper LME comparison (with random effects, AR(1) residuals, Bland-Altman, systematic-bias tests) is Notebook 03's job; do NOT compute statistics here.

===== CELL 41 (markdown) =====
## 8. Save deliverables

Persist the canonical panel CSVs that every downstream notebook depends on. The slope table is the headline analytic output of this notebook.

===== CELL 45 (markdown) =====
---

## Next steps

1. Verify the panel from Section 1 (row counts, parent coverage, 2023 reconciliation).
2. Inspect the Section 2 figures (`outputs/figures/01_cohort_total_trajectory.png` and `02_per_parent_trajectories.png`).
3. Sanity-check the Section 4 slope table (`per_parent_trajectory_slopes.csv`) — does the leaders/laggards list match your intuition?
4. If all three look right, send a thumbs-up and I'll implement Sections 3 (fuel mix), 5 (threshold-effect hand-labels), 6 (geography), 7 (CEMS visual).

## 1. Panel construction — the canonical 13-year cohort facility-year panel

This is the most important output of this notebook. Every downstream notebook reads from `cohort_facility_year_panel.csv` (long-form, one row per facility-year) and `cohort_parent_year_panel.csv` (rolled up to parent-year).

**Construction logic:**

1. Load the `Direct Point Emitters` sheet from `ghgp_data_by_year_2023.xlsx`. This sheet contains one row per facility with separate columns for each year's emissions, plus stable facility metadata (id, name, lat/lon, state, subparts).
2. Filter to facilities reporting Subpart D (Electricity Generation) in any year.
3. Unpivot the year columns into a long form: one row per (facility, year).
4. Attach 2023-locked parent ownership from `ghgp_data_parent_company.xlsb`. Multiply each facility-year emission by the parent's ownership share to get attributed emissions.
5. Restrict to the locked top-50 cohort (read from `data/processed/cohort_top50.csv`).

The source is `emissions_by_unit_and_fuel_type_c_d_aa.xlsb` (FUEL_DATA sheet), which reports each Subpart D unit's annual CO2 emissions broken out by fuel.

GHGRP requires reporting only for facilities emitting >=25,000 mt CO2e/year. When a cohort facility disappears from the panel before 2023, it can mean one of three different things:

2. **Sub-threshold drop** — the facility reduced output but still operates, emitting <25k tCO2e/year. Real (partial) reduction, but the panel can no longer see the remaining emissions.
3. **Rule-change exit** — EPA changed reporting obligations; the facility wasn't required to report anymore but its operations may not have changed.

Produces the canonical multi_source_facility_year_panel.csv that Notebook 03
(LME diagnostic + predictive ML) consumes.
"""

import nbformat as nbf

nb = nbf.v4.new_notebook()
cells: list = []


def md(src: str) -> None:
    cells.append(nbf.v4.new_markdown_cell(src.strip("\n")))


def code(src: str) -> None:
    cells.append(nbf.v4.new_code_cell(src.strip("\n")))


# ============================================================================

# ============================================================================
md(r'''
# 02 — Entity Resolution & Multi-Source Alignment

**Project:** Corporate Climate Credibility Audit — power-sector POC
**Cohort:** Top 50 fossil-fuel power-generating parent companies (578 facilities), locked in Notebook 00 and panelized in Notebook 01

**Notebook purpose:** Take three independently-collected emissions datasets — EPA GHGRP self-reports, EPA AMPD CEMS continuous-stack measurements, and Climate TRACE asset-level model-based estimates — and align them into a single facility-year panel. The output is the *direct* input to Notebook 03's Linear Mixed-Effects diagnostic, which quantifies the structural bias of Climate TRACE relative to the regulatory ground truths.

**Why entity resolution is hard for this project:**

- **GHGRP** uses its own internal `facility_id` (an EPA-assigned integer like `1004377`).
- **CEMS** uses **ORIS codes** (assigned by EIA / CAMD, like `3` for Plant Barry). One GHGRP facility can map to up to **5 different ORIS codes** if its units register separately.
- **Climate TRACE** identifies each asset by a `source_id` (an internal CT integer) plus `lat`/`lon` coordinates. Climate TRACE knows nothing about GHGRP or ORIS IDs, so the only bridge to GHGRP is **spatial proximity**.

The two bridges we therefore build:
1. **GHGRP ↔ CEMS** — deterministic via `ghgrp_oris_power_plant_crosswalk_12_13_21.xlsx`, the official EPA-published bridge. Long-form melt handles multi-ORIS facilities; ~97% CEMS row coverage, 99.8% cohort facility coverage (verified in Notebook 01 Section 7).
2. **Climate TRACE ↔ GHGRP** — spatial KNN using haversine distance. Each CT asset is matched to its nearest cohort facility within a 5-km radius; matches are aggregated to facility-year.

**Inputs:**

# ============================================================================
md(r'''
## 5. Climate TRACE asset → GHGRP facility spatial join

Climate TRACE doesn't carry any GHGRP or ORIS identifier — the only bridge is **geographic proximity**. The approach:

1. **Aggregate CT** from monthly per-asset rows to **annual per-asset** rows (sum `emissions_quantity` per `source_id` per year). Keep lat/lon and source_name for diagnostics.
2. **Build a haversine BallTree** indexed on the cohort's GHGRP facility coordinates (one entry per cohort facility; coordinates from the cohort panel).
3. **Query each CT asset** for its nearest cohort facility. Apply a **5-km radius threshold** — CT and GHGRP coordinates often differ by several hundred meters because they reference different points (stack vs plant gate vs centroid). 5 km is conservative enough to capture all reasonable matches without spurious cross-matches between adjacent independent plants.
4. **Aggregate matched CT emissions** to (GHGRP facility_id, year) by summing across all assets that matched to the same facility.

Implementation uses `sklearn.neighbors.BallTree(metric="haversine")` which expects radians.
''')

code(r'''
# --- 5.1 install scikit-learn if missing, then build per-asset annual rows ---
try:
    from sklearn.neighbors import BallTree  # noqa: F401
except ImportError:
    import subprocess
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "scikit-learn"])
    from sklearn.neighbors import BallTree  # noqa: F401

# Parse CT dates and aggregate monthly → annual per asset
ct_raw["start_time"] = pd.to_datetime(ct_raw["start_time"], errors="coerce")
ct_raw["year"]       = ct_raw["start_time"].dt.year
ct_raw["emissions_quantity"] = pd.to_numeric(ct_raw["emissions_quantity"], errors="coerce")

# Keep only the gas/sector slice we care about
ct = ct_raw[(ct_raw["sector"] == "power") & (ct_raw["iso3_country"] == "USA")].copy()
print(f"CT US power rows after sector/country filter: {len(ct):,}")
print(f"Distinct CT assets: {ct['source_id'].nunique():,}  years: {ct['year'].min()}-{ct['year'].max()}")

# Annualize
ct_asset_year = (
    ct.groupby(["source_id", "source_name", "source_type", "lat", "lon", "year"], as_index=False)
    ["emissions_quantity"].sum()
    .rename(columns={"emissions_quantity": "co2_ct_metric"})
)
ct_asset_year = ct_asset_year.dropna(subset=["lat", "lon", "year"])
print(f"CT asset-year rows: {len(ct_asset_year):,}  (one row per asset per year)")
''')

code(r'''
# --- 5.2 build BallTree on cohort facility coordinates ---
# Use the most-recent (2023) row per facility for stable coordinates; coordinates do not change.
fac_coords = (
    ghgrp.sort_values("year").drop_duplicates("facility_id", keep="last")
    [["facility_id", "facility_name", "state", "lat", "lon"]]
    .dropna(subset=["lat", "lon"])
)
print(f"Cohort facilities with coords: {len(fac_coords)} / {ghgrp['facility_id'].nunique()}")

# BallTree in radians (haversine metric)
fac_rad = np.radians(fac_coords[["lat", "lon"]].to_numpy())
tree = BallTree(fac_rad, metric="haversine")
print(f"BallTree built with {len(fac_rad)} cohort facility points.")
''')

code(r'''
# --- 5.3 query each CT asset for nearest cohort facility (with 5-km radius) ---
EARTH_R_KM     = 6371.0
RADIUS_KM      = 5.0
RADIUS_RAD     = RADIUS_KM / EARTH_R_KM

# CT asset coordinates (use the per-asset values; we already have lat/lon in ct_asset_year)
asset_coords = ct_asset_year.drop_duplicates("source_id")[["source_id", "lat", "lon"]].dropna()
asset_rad = np.radians(asset_coords[["lat", "lon"]].to_numpy())

# Nearest-neighbor query
dist_rad, idx = tree.query(asset_rad, k=1)
asset_coords = asset_coords.assign(
    nn_facility_id = fac_coords.iloc[idx.flatten()]["facility_id"].values,
    nn_distance_km = dist_rad.flatten() * EARTH_R_KM,
)
# Apply radius threshold
asset_coords["within_radius"] = asset_coords["nn_distance_km"] <= RADIUS_KM
matched = asset_coords[asset_coords["within_radius"]]
print(f"CT assets total: {len(asset_coords):,}")
print(f"CT assets matched to a cohort facility within {RADIUS_KM} km: {len(matched):,}  ({len(matched)/len(asset_coords):.1%})")
print(f"\\nDistance distribution (km) for matched assets:")
print(matched["nn_distance_km"].describe(percentiles=[0.5, 0.9, 0.99]).to_string())
''')

code(r'''
# --- 5.4 aggregate matched CT emissions to (GHGRP facility_id, year) ---
ct_asset_year = ct_asset_year.merge(
    asset_coords[["source_id", "nn_facility_id", "nn_distance_km", "within_radius"]],
    on="source_id", how="left",
)
ct_matched = ct_asset_year[ct_asset_year["within_radius"].fillna(False)]

ct_facility_year = (
    ct_matched.groupby(["nn_facility_id", "year"], as_index=False)
    .agg(
        co2_ct_metric=("co2_ct_metric", "sum"),
        n_ct_assets=("source_id", "nunique"),
        mean_match_distance_km=("nn_distance_km", "mean"),
    )
    .rename(columns={"nn_facility_id": "facility_id"})
)
ct_facility_year["facility_id"] = ct_facility_year["facility_id"].astype("Int64")
print(f"CT facility-year rows (cohort-matched): {len(ct_facility_year):,}")
print(f"Distinct cohort facilities with at least one year of CT data: {ct_facility_year['facility_id'].nunique()}")

# Persist intermediate
ct_facility_year.to_csv(DATA_PROCESSED / "climate_trace_facility_year.csv", index=False)
print(ct_facility_year.head(3).to_string(index=False))
''')

md(r'''
## 6. Multi-source panel construction

LEFT JOIN the GHGRP cohort facility-year panel against the CEMS-by-GHGRP table and the CT-by-GHGRP table. Result: one row per `(facility_id, year)` with three CO2 measurements (where available) plus parent attribution and coverage flags.

Schema of `multi_source_facility_year_panel.csv`:

| Column | Source | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `facility_id` | GHGRP | Primary key (with year) |
| `year` | GHGRP | 2011–2023 |
| `facility_name` | GHGRP | For human readability |
| `state`, `lat`, `lon` | GHGRP | Geography |
| `parent_name`, `ownership_share` | GHGRP | Parent attribution (2023-locked) |
| `co2_ghgrp_metric` | GHGRP | Self-reported facility CO2e, metric tons |
| `attributed_co2_ghgrp_metric` | GHGRP | After ownership weighting |
| `co2_cems_metric` | CEMS | Sum across all matched ORIS codes, metric tons |
| `cems_n_oris_codes` | CEMS | Number of ORIS codes summed for this facility |
| `co2_ct_metric` | Climate TRACE | Sum across all matched assets within 5 km |
| `ct_n_assets` | Climate TRACE | Number of CT assets summed |
| `ct_mean_match_distance_km` | Climate TRACE | Average asset-to-facility distance |
| `has_cems`, `has_ct` | derived | Boolean coverage flags |
''')

code(r'''
# --- 6.1 build the panel ---
multi = ghgrp.copy()
multi = multi.rename(columns={"co2e_tons": "co2_ghgrp_metric", "attributed_co2e": "attributed_co2_ghgrp_metric"})

multi = multi.merge(
    cems_with_ghgrp[["facility_id", "year", "co2_cems_metric", "n_oris_codes",
                      "gross_load_mwh", "heat_input_mmbtu"]]
    .rename(columns={"n_oris_codes": "cems_n_oris_codes"}),
    on=["facility_id", "year"], how="left",
)

multi = multi.merge(
    ct_facility_year[["facility_id", "year", "co2_ct_metric", "n_ct_assets", "mean_match_distance_km"]]
    .rename(columns={"n_ct_assets": "ct_n_assets", "mean_match_distance_km": "ct_mean_match_distance_km"}),
    on=["facility_id", "year"], how="left",
)

multi["has_cems"] = multi["co2_cems_metric"].notna()
multi["has_ct"]   = multi["co2_ct_metric"].notna()
multi["n_sources"] = (
    multi["co2_ghgrp_metric"].notna().astype(int)
    + multi["has_cems"].astype(int)
    + multi["has_ct"].astype(int)
)
print(f"Multi-source panel shape: {multi.shape}")
print(f"\\nCoverage by source (facility-year rows):")
print(f"  GHGRP: {multi['co2_ghgrp_metric'].notna().sum():,} / {len(multi):,}  ({multi['co2_ghgrp_metric'].notna().mean():.1%})")
print(f"  CEMS:  {multi['has_cems'].sum():,} / {len(multi):,}  ({multi['has_cems'].mean():.1%})")
print(f"  CT:    {multi['has_ct'].sum():,} / {len(multi):,}  ({multi['has_ct'].mean():.1%})")
print(f"\\nRows with all 3 sources: {(multi['n_sources'] == 3).sum():,}  ({(multi['n_sources']==3).mean():.1%})")
''')

md(r'''
## 7. Coverage and divergence diagnostics

Two complementary views before we hand off to Notebook 03:

1. **Coverage matrix** — for each cohort parent, count how many of its facility-years are covered by each of the three sources. Surfaces parents where one source is systematically missing (e.g., a parent dominated by sub-threshold facilities will show low CEMS coverage; a parent dominated by very young plants will show low GHGRP coverage in early years).

2. **Pairwise ratio plots** — for facility-years where two sources both have data, compute the ratio (CEMS / GHGRP, CT / GHGRP, CT / CEMS) and plot histograms. Ratio ≈ 1.0 means agreement; systematic skew away from 1.0 indicates structural bias that Notebook 03's LME will quantify rigorously.
''')

code(r'''
# --- 7.1 per-parent coverage report ---
cov = (
    multi.groupby("parent_name", as_index=False)
    .agg(
        n_facility_years=("facility_id", "count"),
        n_facilities=("facility_id", "nunique"),
        has_ghgrp_pct=("co2_ghgrp_metric", lambda s: s.notna().mean()),
        has_cems_pct=("has_cems", "mean"),
        has_ct_pct=("has_ct", "mean"),
        all_three_pct=("n_sources", lambda s: (s == 3).mean()),
    )
    .sort_values("n_facility_years", ascending=False)
)
cov.to_csv(DATA_PROCESSED / "multi_source_coverage_report.csv", index=False)
print("Top 15 parents — coverage by source:")
print(cov.head(15).to_string(index=False))
''')

code(r'''
# --- 7.2 pairwise ratio plots ---
# Compute facility-year ratios where both sources have data
multi["cems_over_ghgrp"] = multi["co2_cems_metric"] / multi["co2_ghgrp_metric"]
