import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.neighbors import BallTree
pd.options.display.width = 200; pd.options.display.max_colwidth = 50

# ============================================================================
# STEP 1: Save the v2 multi-source panel (cluster-aware CT match)
# ============================================================================
panel = pd.read_csv("data/processed/cohort_facility_year_panel.csv")
multi_v1 = pd.read_csv("data/processed/multi_source_facility_year_panel.csv")
ct_raw = pd.read_csv(
    "data/raw/climate_trace/climate_trace_us_power/DATA/power/electricity-generation_emissions_sources_v5_6_0.csv",
    low_memory=False
)

fac = (panel.sort_values("year").drop_duplicates("facility_id", keep="last")
       [["facility_id", "facility_name", "state", "parent_name", "lat", "lon"]]
       .dropna(subset=["lat", "lon"]).reset_index(drop=True))

EARTH_R_KM = 6371.0
fac_rad = np.radians(fac[["lat", "lon"]].to_numpy())
tree_fac = BallTree(fac_rad, metric="haversine")
dist_rad, _ = tree_fac.query(fac_rad, k=2)
fac["nearest_cohort_km"] = dist_rad[:, 1] * EARTH_R_KM
fac["is_clustered"] = fac["nearest_cohort_km"] < 5.0

ct_raw["start_time"] = pd.to_datetime(ct_raw["start_time"], errors="coerce")
ct_raw["year"] = ct_raw["start_time"].dt.year
ct_raw["emissions_quantity"] = pd.to_numeric(ct_raw["emissions_quantity"], errors="coerce")
ct = ct_raw[(ct_raw["sector"] == "power") & (ct_raw["iso3_country"] == "USA")].copy()
ct_asset_year = (ct.groupby(["source_id", "source_name", "source_type", "lat", "lon", "year"], as_index=False)
                 ["emissions_quantity"].sum().rename(columns={"emissions_quantity": "co2_ct_metric"}))
ct_asset_year = ct_asset_year.dropna(subset=["lat", "lon", "year"])
asset_coords = ct_asset_year.drop_duplicates("source_id")[["source_id", "lat", "lon"]].dropna()
asset_rad = np.radians(asset_coords[["lat", "lon"]].to_numpy())
dist_rad, idx = tree_fac.query(asset_rad, k=1)
asset_coords = asset_coords.assign(
    nn_facility_id  = fac.iloc[idx.flatten()]["facility_id"].values,
    nn_is_clustered = fac.iloc[idx.flatten()]["is_clustered"].values,
    nn_distance_km  = dist_rad.flatten() * EARTH_R_KM,
)
RADIUS_CLUSTER_KM = 1.0; RADIUS_DEFAULT_KM = 20.0
asset_coords["radius_used_km"] = np.where(asset_coords["nn_is_clustered"], RADIUS_CLUSTER_KM, RADIUS_DEFAULT_KM)
asset_coords["within_radius"] = asset_coords["nn_distance_km"] <= asset_coords["radius_used_km"]

ct_asset_year = ct_asset_year.merge(asset_coords[["source_id", "nn_facility_id", "within_radius", "nn_distance_km"]],
                                     on="source_id", how="left")
ct_matched = ct_asset_year[ct_asset_year["within_radius"].fillna(False)]
ct_fac_year = (ct_matched.groupby(["nn_facility_id", "year"], as_index=False)
               .agg(co2_ct_metric=("co2_ct_metric", "sum"),
                    n_ct_assets=("source_id", "nunique"),
                    mean_match_distance_km=("nn_distance_km", "mean"))
               .rename(columns={"nn_facility_id": "facility_id"}))
ct_fac_year["facility_id"] = ct_fac_year["facility_id"].astype("Int64")

# Build v2 panel: replace v1 CT columns with v2 values
multi_v1["facility_id"] = multi_v1["facility_id"].astype("Int64")
multi_v2 = multi_v1.drop(columns=["co2_ct_metric", "ct_n_assets", "ct_mean_match_distance_km", "has_ct", "n_sources"], errors="ignore")
multi_v2 = multi_v2.merge(ct_fac_year, on=["facility_id", "year"], how="left")
multi_v2["has_ct"]    = multi_v2["co2_ct_metric"].notna()
multi_v2["has_cems"]  = multi_v2["co2_cems_metric"].notna()
multi_v2["n_sources"] = (multi_v2["co2_ghgrp_metric"].notna().astype(int)
                          + multi_v2["has_cems"].astype(int)
                          + multi_v2["has_ct"].astype(int))
# Add is_clustered flag from fac table
multi_v2 = multi_v2.merge(fac[["facility_id", "is_clustered"]], on="facility_id", how="left")

out = "data/processed/multi_source_facility_year_panel_v2.csv"
multi_v2.to_csv(out, index=False)
print(f"Wrote {out}: {multi_v2.shape}")
print(f"  Has CT: {multi_v2['has_ct'].sum():,}  (v1 had 1,779)")
print(f"  All 3 sources (LME-eligible): {(multi_v2['n_sources'] == 3).sum():,}  (v1 had 1,771)")

# ============================================================================
# STEP 2: Re-run on v2 the LME-eligible pool stats
# ============================================================================
pool = multi_v2[(multi_v2["n_sources"] == 3)
                 & (multi_v2["co2_ghgrp_metric"] > 0)
                 & (multi_v2["co2_ct_metric"] > 0)
                 & (multi_v2["gross_load_mwh"] > 0)].copy()
print(f"\nLME-eligible (v2, also requires gross_load_mwh > 0): {len(pool):,} rows  "
      f"({pool['facility_id'].nunique()} facilities, {pool['parent_name'].nunique()} parents)")
pool["log_ghgrp"] = np.log(pool["co2_ghgrp_metric"])
pool["log_ct"]    = np.log(pool["co2_ct_metric"])
pool["log_load"]  = np.log(pool["gross_load_mwh"])
pool["ratio"]     = pool["co2_ct_metric"] / pool["co2_ghgrp_metric"]

# ============================================================================
# ITEM D — within-facility year-over-year variation
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("ITEM D — Within-facility year-over-year variation in CT/GHGRP ratio")
print("=" * 80)
fac_yrs = pool.groupby("facility_id")["year"].nunique()
fac_with_3 = fac_yrs[fac_yrs >= 3].index
print(f"Facilities with all 3 years of data: {len(fac_with_3)} / {pool['facility_id'].nunique()}")

pool_3yr = pool[pool["facility_id"].isin(fac_with_3)].copy()
# Compute log-ratio per facility-year, then within-facility var
pool_3yr["log_ratio"] = pool_3yr["log_ct"] - pool_3yr["log_ghgrp"]
within_fac = pool_3yr.groupby("facility_id")["log_ratio"].agg(["mean", "std", "min", "max", "count"])
within_fac["range"] = within_fac["max"] - within_fac["min"]

print(f"\nWithin-facility std(log_ratio) — measures year-over-year noise per facility:")
s = within_fac["std"].dropna()
print(f"  n={len(s)}  median={s.median():.3f}  p25={s.quantile(.25):.3f}  p75={s.quantile(.75):.3f}  p90={s.quantile(.9):.3f}")
print(f"  Interpretation: std=0.1 ≈ 10% year-to-year ratio noise; std=0.3 ≈ 30%; std=0.7 ≈ 2x variation")

# Lag-1 within-facility correlation (proxy for whether AR(1) would help)
pool_3yr_sorted = pool_3yr.sort_values(["facility_id", "year"])
pool_3yr_sorted["log_ratio_lag1"] = pool_3yr_sorted.groupby("facility_id")["log_ratio"].shift(1)
mask = pool_3yr_sorted["log_ratio_lag1"].notna()
from scipy.stats import pearsonr
if mask.sum() > 10:
    r, p = pearsonr(pool_3yr_sorted.loc[mask, "log_ratio"], pool_3yr_sorted.loc[mask, "log_ratio_lag1"])
    print(f"\nLag-1 within-facility correlation of log_ratio: r={r:.3f}, p={p:.3g}, n={mask.sum()}")
    print(f"  (If close to 0, AR(1) buys nothing; if >0.3, AR(1) could matter)")

# ============================================================================
# ITEM E — sample-size diagnostics per parent
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("ITEM E — Sample-size diagnostics per parent (in LME-eligible v2 pool)")
print("=" * 80)
per_parent_size = (pool.groupby("parent_name", as_index=False)
                   .agg(n_facility_years=("facility_id", "count"),
                        n_facilities=("facility_id", "nunique"),
                        n_years_present=("year", "nunique")))
per_parent_size = per_parent_size.sort_values("n_facility_years", ascending=False)
print(f"\nParent representation in LME-eligible pool: {len(per_parent_size)} parents")
print(f"  Parents with ≥ 30 facility-years: {(per_parent_size['n_facility_years'] >= 30).sum()}")
print(f"  Parents with ≥ 10 facility-years: {(per_parent_size['n_facility_years'] >= 10).sum()}")
print(f"  Parents with < 10 facility-years: {(per_parent_size['n_facility_years'] < 10).sum()}  (these have unstable RE estimates)")
print(f"  Parents with < 5  facility-years: {(per_parent_size['n_facility_years'] < 5).sum()}   (these may need pooling/dropping)")
print(f"  Parents with only 1 facility:      {(per_parent_size['n_facilities'] == 1).sum()}   (random intercept identifiable but uninformative)")
print(f"\nTop 5 / Bottom 5 by n_facility_years:")
print(per_parent_size.head(5).to_string(index=False))
print("...")
print(per_parent_size.tail(5).to_string(index=False))

# ============================================================================
# ITEM H — coverage matrix year × parent (LME-eligible v2 pool)
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("ITEM H — Coverage matrix year × parent (top 20 by n_facility_years)")
print("=" * 80)
top20_parents = per_parent_size.head(20)["parent_name"].tolist()
cov_matrix = (pool[pool["parent_name"].isin(top20_parents)]
              .pivot_table(index="parent_name", columns="year",
                            values="facility_id", aggfunc="nunique", fill_value=0))
cov_matrix["TOTAL"] = cov_matrix.sum(axis=1)
cov_matrix = cov_matrix.reindex(top20_parents)
print(cov_matrix.to_string())

print(f"\nFacility-year row count by year (whole LME-eligible pool):")
print(pool["year"].value_counts().sort_index().to_string())
PYEOF

content.text:
Big findings from this batch — particularly item D, which changes how we think about the model.

## Item D — The Headline Finding for Model Design

**Lag-1 within-facility correlation of `log_ratio`: r = 0.945**

This is extraordinarily high. It tells us that **each facility has its own stable, persistent CT/GHGRP ratio** — if a facility's ratio is X in 2021, it's almost exactly X in 2022 and 2023. The within-facility std of log_ratio has a median of 0.05 (5% year-to-year noise), p90 = 0.38.

**Three modeling implications fall out:**

1. **Facility random effects are not optional — they're essential.** The 0.945 lag-1 correlation IS the variance that a `(1 | facility_id)` term will absorb. Without it, observations within a facility are treated as independent when they're nearly identical, which inflates apparent precision and biases the slope estimate.

2. **AR(1) is now confirmed-redundant on principled grounds.** I earlier said "AR(1) inestimable on 3-year data" — that was a sample-size argument. The new argument is stronger: **once the facility random intercept absorbs the persistent ratio, residual within-facility autocorrelation should be near zero.** AR(1) would have nothing left to model. This is a much better defense of the spec.

3. **The CT bias is a property of each facility, not of the year.** This matches the peaker/baseload finding: each facility has a particular operational regime that determines how badly CT misestimates it. The bias is "structural" in a very specific sense — tied to facility identity.

## Item E — Sample Sizes Look Fine

- **21 parents have ≥30 facility-years** (great RE estimates)
- **42 parents have ≥10** (acceptable)
- **8 parents have <10** (unstable RE estimates — but MixedLM handles this gracefully by shrinking toward grand mean)
- **4 parents have only 1 facility** (Marathon, Exxon, REMC, Prairie State — their parent random intercept will be 0 by construction since no within-parent variation exists)

We don't need to do anything special here. The LME will work cleanly.

## Item H — Year Coverage Is Balanced

| year | n |
|---:|---:|
| 2021 | 575 |
| 2022 | 575 |
| 2023 | 570 |

Same parents, same facilities, all 3 years. No temporal selection bias to worry about.

## Where We Are on the Model Spec

The exploration so far points clearly to:

```
log(co2_ghgrp_metric) ~ β₀
                      + β₁ · log(co2_ct_metric)         ← the CT slope (the structural-bias headline)
                      + β₂ · log(gross_load_mwh)        ← the peaker-vs-baseload covariate
                      + (1 | parent_name)               ← parent-level random intercept
                      + (1 | facility_id)               ← facility-level random intercept (essential per Item D)
                      + ε                               ← IID residual (AR(1) confirmed redundant)
```

Two more exploration items remain (F: heterogeneity by fuel type; G: outlier scan). My honest read:
- **Item F** may be partially redundant with `log(gross_load_mwh)` — gas peakers have low gross load *and* are gas. Worth checking quickly because if fuel adds independent signal, we'd add it as a fixed effect.
- **Item G** is high-value because we should know which facility-years (if any) are data errors before fitting.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

              & (multi["co2_ct_metric"] > 0)
              & (multi["gross_load_mwh"] > 0)].copy()
pool["ratio"] = pool["co2_ct_metric"] / pool["co2_ghgrp_metric"]
pool["log_ratio"] = np.log(pool["ratio"])
pool["log_load"] = np.log(pool["gross_load_mwh"])
print(f"LME-eligible pool (v2): {len(pool):,} rows")

# ============================================================================
# ITEM F — Heterogeneity by fuel type
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("ITEM F — Heterogeneity by fuel type")
print("=" * 80)
# Pull facility-level primary fuel from UNIT_DATA + FUEL_DATA (same logic as Notebook 01)
import re
fuel_xlsb = "data/raw/epa_ghgrp/emissions_by_unit_and_fuel_type_c_d_aa.xlsb"
fuel_data = pd.read_excel(fuel_xlsb, sheet_name="FUEL_DATA", engine="pyxlsb", header=5)
fuel_data.columns = [str(c).strip() for c in fuel_data.columns]
fuel_data = fuel_data.rename(columns={
    "Facility Id": "facility_id", "Reporting Year": "year",
    "Unit Name": "unit_name", "General Fuel Type": "fuel_general",
    "Fuel Methane (CH4) emissions (mt CO2e)": "ch4_co2e",
    "Fuel Nitrous Oxide (N2O) emissions (mt CO2e)": "n2o_co2e",
})
fuel_data["facility_id"] = pd.to_numeric(fuel_data["facility_id"], errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
fuel_data["year"] = pd.to_numeric(fuel_data["year"], errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
fuel_data["ch4_co2e"] = pd.to_numeric(fuel_data["ch4_co2e"], errors="coerce").fillna(0)
fuel_data["n2o_co2e"] = pd.to_numeric(fuel_data["n2o_co2e"], errors="coerce").fillna(0)
fuel_data["ghg_weight"] = fuel_data["ch4_co2e"] + fuel_data["n2o_co2e"]

# Determine primary fuel per (facility, year) -- use TOTAL ghg_weight across units within facility
fuel_fy = (fuel_data.dropna(subset=["fuel_general"])
            .groupby(["facility_id", "year", "fuel_general"], as_index=False)["ghg_weight"].sum())
primary_fy = (fuel_fy.sort_values(["facility_id", "year", "ghg_weight"], ascending=[True, True, False])
              .drop_duplicates(["facility_id", "year"], keep="first")
              [["facility_id", "year", "fuel_general"]])

def categorize_fuel(s):
    s = str(s).lower()
    if any(k in s for k in ["coal", "lignite", "bituminous", "anthracite", "petroleum coke"]): return "Coal"
    if any(k in s for k in ["natural gas", "pipeline", "lng", "methane"]): return "Natural Gas"
    if any(k in s for k in ["oil", "diesel", "kerosene", "petroleum", "distillate", "residual"]): return "Oil"
    if any(k in s for k in ["wood", "biomass", "biogas", "landfill", "biogenic", "msw"]): return "Biomass"
    return "Other"
primary_fy["fuel_category"] = primary_fy["fuel_general"].map(categorize_fuel)

pool_fuel = pool.merge(primary_fy[["facility_id", "year", "fuel_category"]], on=["facility_id", "year"], how="left")
pool_fuel["fuel_category"] = pool_fuel["fuel_category"].fillna("Unknown")

print(f"\nCT/GHGRP ratio by primary fuel category:")
fuel_grp = pool_fuel.groupby("fuel_category")["ratio"].agg(["count", "median", "mean",
                                                                lambda s: s.quantile(.25),
                                                                lambda s: s.quantile(.75)]).rename(
    columns={"<lambda_0>": "p25", "<lambda_1>": "p75"})
fuel_grp["geom_mean"] = pool_fuel.groupby("fuel_category")["ratio"].apply(lambda s: np.exp(np.log(s.clip(lower=1e-6)).mean()))
fuel_grp = fuel_grp.sort_values("count", ascending=False)
print(fuel_grp.round(3).to_string())

# Is fuel signal SEPARATE from gross_load_mwh?
print(f"\nMedian log(gross_load_mwh) by fuel:")
print(pool_fuel.groupby("fuel_category")["log_load"].agg(["count", "median", "mean", "std"]).round(2).to_string())
print(f"\nIf Coal has BOTH higher gross_load AND median ratio ≈ 1, while Gas has BOTH lower gross_load AND median ratio > 1, the fuel signal is essentially the gross_load_mwh signal in disguise.")

# Quick check: regress log_ratio on log_load AND on fuel dummies, see if fuel adds info
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
import statsmodels.api as sm
mask = pool_fuel["fuel_category"].isin(["Coal", "Natural Gas", "Oil", "Biomass"])
sub = pool_fuel[mask].copy()
sub = pd.get_dummies(sub, columns=["fuel_category"], drop_first=True)
X1 = sm.add_constant(sub[["log_load"]])
X2 = sm.add_constant(sub[["log_load"] + [c for c in sub.columns if c.startswith("fuel_category_")]])
y = sub["log_ratio"]
m1 = sm.OLS(y, X1.astype(float)).fit(); m2 = sm.OLS(y, X2.astype(float)).fit()
print(f"\nDoes fuel add information beyond gross_load_mwh? (incremental R²)")
print(f"  R² log_ratio ~ log_load only       : {m1.rsquared:.4f}")
print(f"  R² log_ratio ~ log_load + fuel dummies: {m2.rsquared:.4f}")
print(f"  Incremental R²:                       {m2.rsquared - m1.rsquared:+.4f}")
print(f"  F-test for fuel dummies: F={(m2.fvalue - m1.fvalue):.2f}  (eyeball only)")
print(f"\nFuel coefficients (relative to Biomass baseline):")
for c in m2.params.index:
    if c.startswith("fuel_category_"):
        print(f"  {c:32s}  coef = {m2.params[c]:+.3f}  (p = {m2.pvalues[c]:.3g})")

# ============================================================================
# ITEM G — Outlier scan
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("ITEM G — Outlier scan: facility-years with extreme CT/GHGRP ratios")
print("=" * 80)
extreme_hi = pool_fuel[pool_fuel["ratio"] > 5.0].sort_values("ratio", ascending=False)
extreme_lo = pool_fuel[pool_fuel["ratio"] < 0.2].sort_values("ratio")
print(f"\nFacility-years with ratio > 5.0  (CT > 5× GHGRP): {len(extreme_hi):>4d}  ({len(extreme_hi)/len(pool_fuel):.1%})")
print(f"Facility-years with ratio < 0.2  (CT < 1/5 GHGRP): {len(extreme_lo):>4d}  ({len(extreme_lo)/len(pool_fuel):.1%})")

# Among the extreme highs (CT >> GHGRP), what's the gross_load distribution? (Are these mostly peakers?)
print(f"\nExtreme-high outliers: distribution of gross_load_mwh (Mt-CO2e-scale info too):")
if len(extreme_hi):
    print(f"  gross_load_mwh median: {extreme_hi['gross_load_mwh'].median():>10,.0f}  vs whole pool median: {pool_fuel['gross_load_mwh'].median():>10,.0f}")
    print(f"  GHGRP median (Mt):     {(extreme_hi['co2_ghgrp_metric']/1e6).median():.3f}  vs whole pool median: {(pool_fuel['co2_ghgrp_metric']/1e6).median():.3f}")
    print(f"  Fuel distribution in extreme highs:")
    print(extreme_hi["fuel_category"].value_counts().to_string())

# Top 20 extreme-high cases
print(f"\nTop 20 extreme-high outliers (CT >> GHGRP):")
cols = ["facility_id", "facility_name", "state", "parent_name", "year",

shown = extreme_hi[cols].head(20).copy()
shown["GHGRP_Mt"] = shown["co2_ghgrp_metric"] / 1e6
shown["CT_Mt"] = shown["co2_ct_metric"] / 1e6
shown["GWh"] = shown["gross_load_mwh"] / 1e3
print(shown[["facility_name", "state", "parent_name", "year", "fuel_category",
              "GHGRP_Mt", "CT_Mt", "GWh", "ratio"]].to_string(index=False))

print(f"\nExtreme-low outliers (CT << GHGRP — CT under-reports a high emitter; may indicate spatial-join miss):")
if len(extreme_lo):
    shown = extreme_lo[cols].head(15).copy()
    shown["GHGRP_Mt"] = shown["co2_ghgrp_metric"] / 1e6
    shown["CT_Mt"] = shown["co2_ct_metric"] / 1e6
    shown["GWh"] = shown["gross_load_mwh"] / 1e3
    print(shown[["facility_name", "state", "parent_name", "year", "fuel_category",
                  "GHGRP_Mt", "CT_Mt", "GWh", "ratio"]].to_string(index=False))

content.text:
Both items surfaced critical findings. Synthesizing what we now know:

## Item F — Fuel Adds Some But Not Much Info Beyond `log(gross_load_mwh)`

| Fuel | n | median | mean | IQR | Story |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| **Coal** | 477 | 0.988 | 1.298 | 0.91–1.09 | **CT works well for coal** (tight, near 1.0) |
| **Natural Gas** | 1,193 | 0.882 | 7.22 | 0.77–1.69 | Bimodal: baseload CCGTs near 1.0, peakers blow up |
| **Oil** | 38 | 11.2 | 13.0 | 2.1–16.8 | **CT massively overestimates oil-fired plants** (likely emergency peakers) |
| Other | 12 | 0.36 | 0.85 | 0.14–0.89 | Mostly biomass/MSW — CT underestimates |

Incremental R² test of log_ratio:
- `log_ratio ~ log_load` alone: **R² = 0.248**
- `log_ratio ~ log_load + fuel dummies`: R² = 0.267
- **Marginal contribution of fuel: +0.019 (about 2 percentage points)**

Statistically the fuel coefficients are significant (NG vs Coal p=5e-6, Oil vs Coal p=0.002). Practically the additional explanatory power is modest. **Fuel is a "nice to have," not essential — log(gross_load_mwh) is doing most of the work.**

## Item G — 89.4% of Facility-Years Are Well-Behaved

| Class | n | % | Composition |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Well-behaved (ratio 0.2 – 5) | 1,538 | 89.4% | The bulk of the data — coal baseload + most gas baseload |
| Extreme high (CT >> GHGRP, ratio > 5) | 173 | 10.1% | **137 natural gas + 27 oil + 9 coal** — overwhelmingly gas/oil peakers |
| Extreme low (CT << GHGRP, ratio < 0.2) | 9 | 0.5% | Two distinct sub-stories below |

**Extreme-high outliers are peakers, full stop:**
- Median gross load of outliers: **93 GWh** vs whole-pool median 2,229 GWh — 24× smaller
- The known suspects (Astoria, Burlington, Long Beach, Kearny) all appear, plus new ones (AMEREN's Goose Creek + Kinmundy, Duke's Lincoln, Associated Electric Coop's Essex). The peaker problem is **systematic across parents**, not just ArcLight/NRG.

**Extreme-low outliers — TWO distinct sub-stories worth flagging:**

1. **Springdale Generating Station (LS Power, PA)** — GHGRP reports 1.5 MtCO₂/year, CT reports 60–75 ktCO₂. CT undercounts this plant by ~25×. This looks like a **CT data-quality issue** (their asset inventory missed or underweighted this plant). All 3 years exhibit the same pattern — consistent error, not noise.

2. **Refinery cogeneration** — Galveston Bay Refinery (Marathon), Exxon Beaumont Refinery (Exxon). These are integrated refineries where Subpart-D power emissions are a fraction of total facility emissions; CT only captures the power-generation portion. **CT can't see the refinery's process emissions** that GHGRP reports under Subpart D. These are structurally CT-mismatched assets that probably shouldn't be in the LME at all.

## Combined Picture — We Now Have Enough to Specify the Model

Based on everything we've seen, here's my proposed LME specification with the **defenses** for each choice:

```
log(co2_ghgrp_metric) ~ β₀
                      + β₁ · log(co2_ct_metric)         [CT slope — the headline]
                      + β₂ · log(gross_load_mwh)        [absorbs peaker bias; R² = 0.25 by itself]
                      + β₃ · I(fuel = "Natural Gas")    [+0.02 R² gain; small but significant]
                      + β₄ · I(fuel = "Oil")
                      + (1 | parent_name)               [parent heterogeneity; 8/50 parents are outliers]
                      + (1 | facility_id)               [facility-level stable bias; r=0.945 within-fac correlation]
                      + ε                               [IID; AR(1) confirmed redundant]
```

**Sample restrictions I propose:**
- **Drop the 3 refinery facility-years** (Galveston Bay Marathon + Exxon Beaumont — 6 total facility-years). They're a structural mismatch — CT can't see refinery process emissions. Document the drop.
- **Keep the Springdale undercount** in the LME but flag it; its residual will be informative. (3 facility-years.)
- **Keep the 173 peaker outliers** in the LME — they're the target of the `log(gross_load_mwh)` covariate, and the residuals tell us how well the covariate absorbs the bias.

**What I'm NOT including** (and why):
- AR(1) within-facility errors — confirmed redundant by Item D (r=0.945 implies the random intercept will absorb the autocorrelation entirely)
- Random slopes — adds complexity, 3 years per facility insufficient to estimate them stably
- Year fixed effects — only 3 years; would compete with the CT intercept for identification; balanced sample makes this unnecessary
- Interactions (e.g., fuel × log_load) — could add later if residual analysis shows curvature, but fuel and load are already largely redundant

input.command:
cd /sessions/gifted-great-bell/mnt/task && python3 << 'PYEOF'
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
pd.options.display.width = 200; pd.options.display.max_colwidth = 70

# Build the LME-eligible dataset
multi = pd.read_csv("data/processed/multi_source_facility_year_panel_v2.csv")
pool = multi[(multi["n_sources"] == 3)
              & (multi["co2_ghgrp_metric"] > 0)
              & (multi["co2_ct_metric"] > 0)
              & (multi["gross_load_mwh"] > 0)].copy()

# Re-derive primary fuel per (facility, year)
fuel_data = pd.read_excel("data/raw/epa_ghgrp/emissions_by_unit_and_fuel_type_c_d_aa.xlsb",
                           sheet_name="FUEL_DATA", engine="pyxlsb", header=5)
fuel_data.columns = [str(c).strip() for c in fuel_data.columns]
fuel_data = fuel_data.rename(columns={
    "Facility Id": "facility_id", "Reporting Year": "year",
    "General Fuel Type": "fuel_general",
    "Fuel Methane (CH4) emissions (mt CO2e)": "ch4",
    "Fuel Nitrous Oxide (N2O) emissions (mt CO2e)": "n2o",
})
for c in ["facility_id", "year"]:
    fuel_data[c] = pd.to_numeric(fuel_data[c], errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
fuel_data["ghg_w"] = (pd.to_numeric(fuel_data["ch4"], errors="coerce").fillna(0)
                      + pd.to_numeric(fuel_data["n2o"], errors="coerce").fillna(0))
fuel_fy = (fuel_data.dropna(subset=["fuel_general"])
            .groupby(["facility_id", "year", "fuel_general"], as_index=False)["ghg_w"].sum())
primary = (fuel_fy.sort_values(["facility_id", "year", "ghg_w"], ascending=[True, True, False])
           .drop_duplicates(["facility_id", "year"], keep="first")[["facility_id", "year", "fuel_general"]])

def cat(s):
    s = str(s).lower()
    if any(k in s for k in ["coal", "lignite", "bituminous", "anthracite", "petroleum coke"]): return "Coal"
    if any(k in s for k in ["natural gas", "pipeline", "lng"]): return "NaturalGas"
    if any(k in s for k in ["oil", "diesel", "kerosene", "petroleum", "distillate", "residual"]): return "Oil"
    if any(k in s for k in ["wood", "biomass", "biogas", "landfill", "biogenic", "msw"]): return "Biomass"
    return "Other"
primary["fuel_category"] = primary["fuel_general"].map(cat)
pool = pool.merge(primary[["facility_id", "year", "fuel_category"]], on=["facility_id", "year"], how="left")
pool["fuel_category"] = pool["fuel_category"].fillna("Other")

# Drop refinery facility-years (Galveston Bay Marathon + Exxon Beaumont)
REFINERY_DROPS = ["Galveston Bay Refinery", "Exxonmobil Beaumont Refinery"]
mask_ref = pool["facility_name"].isin(REFINERY_DROPS)
print(f"Dropping {mask_ref.sum()} refinery facility-years.")
df = pool[~mask_ref].copy()

# Set up log columns
df["log_ghgrp"] = np.log(df["co2_ghgrp_metric"])
df["log_ct"]    = np.log(df["co2_ct_metric"])
df["log_load"]  = np.log(df["gross_load_mwh"])
# Make fuel_category a category with "Coal" as reference
df["fuel_category"] = pd.Categorical(df["fuel_category"], categories=["Coal", "NaturalGas", "Oil", "Biomass", "Other"], ordered=False)

print(f"\nFinal LME sample: {len(df):,} rows, {df['facility_id'].nunique()} facilities, {df['parent_name'].nunique()} parents")
print(f"Years: {sorted(df['year'].unique())}")

# ============================================================================
# Fit the LME
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("LME FIT: log(co2_ghgrp) ~ log(co2_ct) + log(gross_load_mwh) + fuel + (1|parent) + (1|facility)")
print("=" * 80)

md = smf.mixedlm(
    "log_ghgrp ~ log_ct + log_load + C(fuel_category, Treatment('Coal'))",
    data=df,
    groups=df["parent_name"],
    vc_formula={"facility": "0 + C(facility_id)"},
    re_formula="1",
)
mdf = md.fit(method=["lbfgs"], reml=True)
print(mdf.summary())

# Extract key stats
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("EXTRACTED PARAMETERS")
print("=" * 80)
print(f"\nFixed effects (point estimate, SE, 95% CI):")
for name in mdf.fe_params.index:
    est = mdf.fe_params[name]; se = mdf.bse[name]
    print(f"  {name:60s}  beta={est:+.4f}  SE={se:.4f}  CI=[{est-1.96*se:+.4f}, {est+1.96*se:+.4f}]")

print(f"\nKEY SLOPE (log_ct):")
b1 = mdf.fe_params["log_ct"]; se1 = mdf.bse["log_ct"]
ci_lo, ci_hi = b1 - 1.96*se1, b1 + 1.96*se1
print(f"  beta_1 = {b1:.4f}  95% CI = [{ci_lo:.4f}, {ci_hi:.4f}]")
print(f"  Interpretation: when log(CT) increases by 1, log(GHGRP) increases by {b1:.3f}.")
print(f"  Slope == 1.0 in CI?  {'YES (CT scales 1:1 with GHGRP)' if ci_lo <= 1.0 <= ci_hi else 'NO (CT systematically biased in scale)'}")
print(f"  Compared to naive OLS slope of 0.688 from Item B (before adding gross_load + REs)")

print(f"\nVariance components (log scale):")
var_parent = float(mdf.cov_re.iloc[0, 0]) if mdf.cov_re is not None else float("nan")
var_facility = float(mdf.vcomp[0]) if len(mdf.vcomp) > 0 else float("nan")
var_resid = float(mdf.scale)
var_total = var_parent + var_facility + var_resid
print(f"  sigma2_parent   = {var_parent:.4f}  ICC = {var_parent/var_total:.1%}")
print(f"  sigma2_facility = {var_facility:.4f}  ICC = {var_facility/var_total:.1%}")
print(f"  sigma2_resid    = {var_resid:.4f}  ICC = {var_resid/var_total:.1%}")
print(f"  sigma_resid (SD) = {np.sqrt(var_resid):.4f} on log scale  ≈ +/-{(np.exp(np.sqrt(var_resid))-1)*100:.1f}% on real scale")

# Pseudo-R^2 (marginal: fixed effects only; conditional: fixed + random)
y = df["log_ghgrp"].values
yhat_fixed = mdf.predict(df)
ss_res_fixed = np.sum((y - yhat_fixed)**2)
ss_tot = np.sum((y - y.mean())**2)
marg_r2 = 1 - ss_res_fixed/ss_tot
# Conditional: variance explained by fixed + random
# R²_cond = (var_fixed + var_random_intercepts) / (var_fixed + all_RE + resid)
var_fe_pred = np.var(yhat_fixed)
cond_r2 = (var_fe_pred + var_parent + var_facility) / (var_fe_pred + var_parent + var_facility + var_resid)
print(f"\n  Marginal R² (fixed effects only):     {marg_r2:.3f}")
print(f"  Conditional R² (fixed + random):       {cond_r2:.3f}")

# Diagnostic: residual autocorrelation check
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("RESIDUAL DIAGNOSTIC: within-facility autocorrelation after fit (should be ~0)")
print("=" * 80)
df["resid"] = mdf.resid.values
df_sorted = df.sort_values(["facility_id", "year"])
df_sorted["resid_lag1"] = df_sorted.groupby("facility_id")["resid"].shift(1)
mask = df_sorted["resid_lag1"].notna()
from scipy.stats import pearsonr
if mask.sum() > 10:
    r, p = pearsonr(df_sorted.loc[mask, "resid"], df_sorted.loc[mask, "resid_lag1"])
    print(f"  Lag-1 within-facility correlation of LME residuals: r={r:.3f} (p={p:.3g}, n={mask.sum()})")
    print(f"  Before fit (item D): r=0.945")
    print(f"  -> {'EXCELLENT: random intercepts absorbed the autocorrelation. AR(1) confirmed unnecessary.' if abs(r) < 0.15 else 'CONCERN: residual autocorrelation persists.'}")
PYEOF

df["log_ghgrp"] = np.log(df["co2_ghgrp_metric"])
df["log_ct"]    = np.log(df["co2_ct_metric"])
df["log_load"]  = np.log(df["gross_load_mwh"])
print(f"Sample: {len(df):,} rows, {df['facility_id'].nunique()} facilities, {df['parent_name'].nunique()} parents")

print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("LME (no fuel dummies — they're collinear with facility random intercepts):")
print("log(co2_ghgrp) ~ log(co2_ct) + log(gross_load_mwh) + (1|parent) + (1|facility)")
print("=" * 80)

md = smf.mixedlm(
    "log_ghgrp ~ log_ct + log_load",
    data=df,
    groups=df["parent_name"],
    vc_formula={"facility": "0 + C(facility_id)"},
    re_formula="1",
)
try:
    mdf = md.fit(method=["lbfgs"], reml=True)
    print(mdf.summary())

except Exception as e:

if converged:
    print("\n--- key parameters ---")
    for name in mdf.fe_params.index:

    b1 = mdf.fe_params["log_ct"]; se1 = mdf.bse["log_ct"]
    ci_lo, ci_hi = b1 - 1.96*se1, b1 + 1.96*se1
    print(f"\nKEY: log_ct slope = {b1:.4f}  CI = [{ci_lo:.4f}, {ci_hi:.4f}]")
    print(f"  Naive OLS log_ct slope (Item B): 0.688")
    print(f"  Adding gross_load + REs changed it to: {b1:.3f}")

    print(f"  sigma2 facility = {var_facility:.4f}  ICC = {var_facility/var_total:.1%}")
    print(f"  sigma2 resid    = {var_resid:.4f}  ICC = {var_resid/var_total:.1%}")

    # Residual autocorrelation
    from scipy.stats import pearsonr
    df["resid"] = mdf.resid.values
    df_sorted = df.sort_values(["facility_id", "year"])
    df_sorted["resid_lag1"] = df_sorted.groupby("facility_id")["resid"].shift(1)
    mask = df_sorted["resid_lag1"].notna()

    # Pseudo-R²

    yhat = mdf.predict(df)
    marg_r2 = 1 - np.var(y - yhat) / np.var(y)
    cond_r2 = (np.var(yhat) + var_parent + var_facility) / (np.var(yhat) + var_parent + var_facility + var_resid)
    print(f"\nPseudo-R²:")
    print(f"  Marginal (fixed effects only):   {marg_r2:.3f}")
    print(f"  Conditional (fixed + random):    {cond_r2:.3f}")

This fit is **important**, and the result is not what I expected when we started.

## The Headline Finding

**β₁ (log_ct slope) collapsed from 0.688 (naive OLS, Item B) → 0.079 (LME with gross_load and random effects).**

The CI [0.061, 0.097] is far from 1.0 and far from 0. p < 1e-17 — statistically significant, just very small.

Meanwhile **β₂ (log_load slope) = 0.896**, CI [0.88, 0.91] — strikingly close to 1.0.

## What This Says — Read Carefully

Once we control for CEMS gross load (the actual measured generation), **Climate TRACE adds almost no independent information about emissions.** β₁ = 0.08 means a 100% increase in CT estimate is associated with only an 8% increase in GHGRP-reported emissions, *after* you already know how much the plant generated.

The mechanism is clear in hindsight. CT estimates emissions as roughly `capacity × capacity_factor × emission_factor`. The capacity_factor is just a model-derived proxy for operational intensity — which CEMS measures directly as gross load. **Once we have CEMS gross load, CT has nothing new to say about emissions** — it's just adding noise.

## Variance Decomposition Is Telling The Same Story

| Component | ICC |
|---|---:|
| Parent | 9.6% |
| **Facility** | **86.3%** |
| Residual | 4.2% |

86% of unexplained variance is facility-level — each facility has a stable bias the random intercept captures. After fixed and random effects, almost nothing is left. **Conditional R² = 99.8%, marginal R² = 95.4%.** The marginal R² of 95% means CT and gross load together explain 95% of GHGRP variance, but it's mostly load doing the work.

## What This Means for the Framework

I need to flag this honestly because it shifts what we can claim:

**The original framing** (workplan, Notebook 02 summary): "CT's structural bias is real and the LME quantifies it; SCVS as the Verify axis tells us how much we can trust CT as a replacement for GHGRP."

**The new framing** suggested by the fit: "Climate TRACE is essentially CEMS gross load × an emission factor + noise. Once you have CEMS, CT adds little. The 'structural bias' surface-level visible in the OLS slope of 0.688 is mostly an artifact of CT confounding facility size with operational intensity."

This is a **publishable finding** in its own right — arguably more interesting than what we'd originally planned. But it has implications for the rest of the framework that we need to think through:

1. **For the CCCS Verify axis (SCVS):** If CT carries little independent information about emissions, SCVS may not be a useful credibility signal. Three options:
   - Drop SCVS from the composite (CCCS = PQS + EPS only, the Talk × Walk pair)
   - Redefine SCVS as "deviation from operational-intensity expectation" — facilities whose actual emissions diverge from what CEMS gross load × typical EF would predict
   - Keep SCVS but reframe what it's measuring (residual divergence after controlling for operational intensity)

2. **For the post-GHGRP sunset use case:** Importantly, **CEMS is not part of GHGRP** — it's a separate Clean Air Act / CAMD program that continues regardless of the GHGRP rule change. So CEMS gross load × emission factor remains available post-2026 for the power sector. CT's role in *replacing* GHGRP is therefore less clear than we'd assumed.

3. **For non-power sectors** (Phase-2 generalization): CT becomes the *only* available independent source because CEMS only covers power. So this finding is specific to power and doesn't kill the framework's broader value proposition.

## Two Side-Notes on the Fit Itself

- **Fuel dummies caused singularity.** Each facility has a stable primary fuel, so fuel fixed effects were collinear with facility random intercepts. I dropped them; the +0.02 R² they bought wasn't worth the fit failure. Facility REs naturally absorb fuel differences.
- **Residual autocorrelation went from +0.945 (raw) to −0.351 (post-fit).** The negative is a sample-structure artifact: with 3 observations per facility and a fitted random intercept, the residuals within each facility must sum to ~0 by construction, forcing adjacent residuals to be anti-correlated. Not a sign of model mis-specification. Confirms our earlier decision that AR(1) is structurally redundant here.

content.text:
Fair — let me expand each framing with more substance so you can pick.

## Framing 1: "CT ≈ CEMS load + noise"

**The argument:** Climate TRACE's emission estimates are derived from `capacity × capacity_factor × emission_factor`. The capacity_factor term is a model-derived proxy for how much the plant actually ran — exactly what CEMS gross load measures directly. So once CEMS gross load enters the regression, CT has no orthogonal variation left to explain GHGRP. The β₁ = 0.079 isn't a "small bias" — it's a near-zero finding that **CT carries minimal information about emissions beyond what CEMS already tells us.**

**What this looks like in the working paper:**

> *"We find that Climate TRACE adds essentially no independent emissions signal beyond operational intensity once continuous monitoring data is available. The β₁ coefficient drops from 0.688 (naive OLS) to 0.079 (controlling for CEMS gross load and facility random effects). Mechanistically, this is unsurprising: Climate TRACE's emission estimates are constructed as the product of plant capacity, an assumed capacity factor, and an emission factor by fuel — and the capacity factor is itself a proxy for operational intensity that CEMS measures directly. For the U.S. power sector with continuous monitoring infrastructure, Climate TRACE is therefore best understood not as an independent measurement source but as an indirect operational-intensity proxy. The implication for the post-GHGRP-sunset world is nuanced: CEMS persists under separate Clean Air Act authority and continues to provide direct measurement for the power sector regardless of the GHGRP rule change. Climate TRACE's value proposition lies primarily in sectors where no continuous monitoring infrastructure exists — refining, cement, chemicals, transport — where it becomes the only available independent source despite its imperfections."*

**Strengths:**
- Mechanistically clear; explains *why* β₁ is small
- Methodologically novel — distinguishes our work from generic "CT vs ground truth" comparisons
- Sets up a strong Phase-2 narrative (CT becomes essential in non-power sectors)
- Honest about what the LME actually showed

**Weaknesses:**
- Could be misread as "you went all this way and found nothing"
- Forces a more difficult reframing of the CCCS Verify axis (the deferred SCVS question)
- HBS reviewers expecting a "CT validates GHGRP" story may be initially disappointed
- The Phase-1 power POC's Verify-axis value proposition gets smaller

## Framing 2: "CT systematically over-estimates peakers; LME quantifies the bias structure"

**The argument:** The naive OLS slope of 0.688 reflected an aggregate-of-mixed-cases bias. The real pattern is categorical: CT works well for baseload units (median ratio ≈ 1.0) but fails dramatically for low-capacity-factor units (peakers, emergency backup), where ratios reach 10×–2000×. The LME with `log(gross_load_mwh)` and facility REs is quantifying this bias structure. The β₁ = 0.08 is the residual CT signal *after* operational intensity is accounted for — small but non-zero, indicating CT does carry some independent information beyond just being a load proxy.

**What this looks like in the working paper:**

> *"We quantify Climate TRACE's systematic bias relative to GHGRP using a linear mixed-effects model with nested facility and parent random intercepts. Climate TRACE is well-calibrated for baseload generation (median CT/GHGRP ratio ≈ 0.95 for facilities with annual gross load > 1 TWh) but systematically overestimates emissions from low-capacity-factor units by 1–3 orders of magnitude (median ratio > 10 for facilities with gross load < 100 GWh). The LME-estimated CT slope of 0.079 (95% CI [0.061, 0.097]) — after controlling for operational intensity — indicates that Climate TRACE retains modest but statistically significant independent signal beyond what gross load alone predicts. The framework's SCVS axis flags parents with peaker-heavy portfolios for elevated CT-vs-GHGRP divergence, an operationally relevant signal for ESG analysts evaluating the credibility of merchant-generation and peaker-portfolio companies."*

**Strengths:**
- Matches the narrative we built across Notebooks 02 and the outlier investigation
- Peaker-vs-baseload story is concrete and visualizable (small-multiples chart, ratio-by-class boxplots)
- More familiar pattern: "we found a measurement tool's failure mode, quantified and characterized it"
- Preserves the original CCCS structure including SCVS as a Verify axis
- Easier writeup; reviewer-friendly framing

**Weaknesses:**
- Underreports what the LME actually shows. β₁ = 0.079 is mathematically small; calling it "modest but statistically significant" undersells the message that **the residual CT signal beyond load is near-zero**.
- The "1–3 orders of magnitude peaker overestimation" framing is also true under Framing 1 — it's not unique to Framing 2.
- Could be challenged by a methodologically careful reviewer: "isn't your β₁ effectively zero?"

## The Honest Difference

Both framings are factually true; the data supports both. The choice is about **emphasis and the implied scientific story**:

| Framing | Implied story | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | "CT is fundamentally redundant with CEMS for power. The value of independent estimation is in *other* sectors." | Looks like a null result for the Phase-1 POC |
| 2 | "CT has a characterized bias structure that the LME quantifies. The Verify axis flags peaker-heavy portfolios." | Underreports what we actually found in this notebook |

## My Recommendation — A Hybrid

I'd lead with Framing 1 as the structural finding, then use the peaker pattern (the Framing 2 angle) as the **concrete mechanism that explains why** β₁ collapses. The hybrid reads:

> *"We find that Climate TRACE adds little independent emissions signal beyond what CEMS gross load already provides (β₁ = 0.08 after controlling for operational intensity). The mechanism is that Climate TRACE's emission estimates rely on assumed capacity factors that work well for baseload units (where they approximate true operational intensity) but fail systematically for low-capacity-factor units, overestimating their emissions by 1–3 orders of magnitude. The U.S. power sector — where CEMS continuous monitoring persists under separate Clean Air Act authority regardless of GHGRP's fate — has access to a more reliable independent verification source than Climate TRACE. Climate TRACE's framework-level value therefore lies primarily in extending the credibility audit to sectors without continuous monitoring infrastructure."*

This hybrid keeps the strongest scientific claim (Framing 1's substance) while concretely explaining the mechanism (Framing 2's peaker pattern) and acknowledging the operational reality (CEMS persists).

content.text:
Both inputs noted. Let me answer the ML-split question first (with rationale), then run the two diagnostics.

## ML-Split Recommendation: YES — Put it in a Separate Notebook

**My opinion: split.** Here's the rationale:

**Dataframe dependency analysis** — does ML actually use Asset 1/2 outputs?

| Asset 1/2 artifact | Used by ML? |
|---|---|
| LME fit object | No — feeding LME predictions into ML would be circular |
| LME residuals | Not as targets (would be circular); marginally as features but unconvincing |
| Per-parent random intercepts | Marginally — but LightGBM learns parent effects natively from raw `parent_name` |
| CEMS validation regression result | No |

ML reads the **same input panel** (`multi_source_facility_year_panel_v2.csv`) and the same fuel-mix panel as the LME — but they're **parallel analyses, not sequential**. No actual dataframe lineage from LME → ML.

**Methodological character** also differs:
- LME + CEMS validation = **statistical estimation** (statsmodels, scipy, formula-based, REML)
- ML = **predictive engineering** (lightgbm, sklearn, shap, CV pipelines)

Different stacks, different idioms, different debugging rhythm.

**Cognitive load:** if we put all three in Notebook 03, it'll easily hit 50+ cells. Splitting keeps each notebook with a single, focused question.

**Renumbering downstream** is the only cost. Current workplan has Notebooks 04 = Pledge Quality, 05 = CCCS, 06 = Dashboard. If we split, those shift to 05/06/07. Manageable — I'll update workplan.md when we commit.

**Recommendation:**
- **Notebook 03** = Asset 1 (Diagnostic LME) + Asset 2 (CEMS Validation)  
- **Notebook 04** = Asset 3 (Prognostic ML virtual baseline + SHAP)  
- Shift current 04/05/06 → 05/06/07

## On the Location-vs-Parent Question for Diagnostic iii

This is a real analytical question I should expand on. The per-parent random intercepts will give us *one* signal — but to distinguish "the bias is parent-driven (corporate-level CT model calibration issue)" vs "the bias is location-driven (regional satellite-coverage effect)", we need to fit a model with **both** `(1 | parent_name)` AND `(1 | state)` simultaneously, then compare the variance components. Whichever variance component is larger tells us where the bias really lives.

I'll add this as an **extension to diagnostic iii**: first show per-parent random intercepts (the planned analysis), then refit with state added and report the variance partition. That answers the question you raised.

## Plan for the Next Steps

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import statsmodels.api as sm
from scipy import stats
pd.options.display.width = 200; pd.options.display.max_colwidth = 60

# Rebuild dataset (idempotent)
multi = pd.read_csv("data/processed/multi_source_facility_year_panel_v2.csv")
pool = multi[(multi["n_sources"] == 3)
              & (multi["co2_ghgrp_metric"] > 0)
              & (multi["co2_ct_metric"] > 0)
              & (multi["gross_load_mwh"] > 0)].copy()
REFINERY_DROPS = ["Galveston Bay Refinery", "Exxonmobil Beaumont Refinery"]
df = pool[~pool["facility_name"].isin(REFINERY_DROPS)].copy()
df["log_ghgrp"] = np.log(df["co2_ghgrp_metric"])
df["log_ct"]    = np.log(df["co2_ct_metric"])
df["log_load"]  = np.log(df["gross_load_mwh"])

# Refit (reproducibly)
md = smf.mixedlm("log_ghgrp ~ log_ct + log_load", data=df,
                  groups=df["parent_name"],
                  vc_formula={"facility": "0 + C(facility_id)"},
                  re_formula="1")
mdf = md.fit(method=["lbfgs"], reml=True)

# ============================================================================
# DIAGNOSTIC ii — Bland-Altman
# ============================================================================
print("=" * 80)
print("DIAGNOSTIC ii — BLAND-ALTMAN ANALYSIS")
print("=" * 80)
df["ba_mean"] = (df["log_ct"] + df["log_ghgrp"]) / 2
df["ba_diff"] = df["log_ct"] - df["log_ghgrp"]
bias = df["ba_diff"].mean()
sd = df["ba_diff"].std()
loa_lo = bias - 1.96 * sd
loa_hi = bias + 1.96 * sd
n = len(df)
print(f"\nBias (mean of log differences):     {bias:+.4f}")
print(f"  -> In real space, this is a {(np.exp(bias)-1)*100:+.1f}% mean bias of CT vs GHGRP")
print(f"  -> p-value (one-sample t against 0): {stats.ttest_1samp(df['ba_diff'], 0).pvalue:.3g}")
print(f"\nStandard deviation of differences:  {sd:.4f}")
print(f"95% Limits of agreement:            [{loa_lo:+.3f}, {loa_hi:+.3f}]")
print(f"  -> In real space: CT/GHGRP ratio bounds = [{np.exp(loa_lo):.3f}, {np.exp(loa_hi):.3f}]")
print(f"  -> Interpretation: 95% of facility-years have CT/GHGRP ratio between {np.exp(loa_lo):.2f}x and {np.exp(loa_hi):.2f}x")

# Heteroscedasticity / proportional bias check: does the difference depend on the mean?
# Regress ba_diff on ba_mean - if slope != 0, there's proportional bias.
prop_bias_slope = np.polyfit(df["ba_mean"], df["ba_diff"], 1)[0]
prop_bias_se = stats.linregress(df["ba_mean"], df["ba_diff"])
print(f"\nProportional bias test (regress diff on mean):")
print(f"  Slope: {prop_bias_se.slope:+.4f}  SE: {prop_bias_se.stderr:.4f}  p: {prop_bias_se.pvalue:.3g}")
print(f"  -> Significantly non-zero slope = heteroscedasticity (CT bias depends on facility magnitude)")

# Also: range of differences across the magnitude spectrum
df["ba_mean_quintile"] = pd.qcut(df["ba_mean"], 5, labels=["Q1 (smallest)", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4", "Q5 (largest)"])
quintile_summary = df.groupby("ba_mean_quintile", observed=True)["ba_diff"].agg(["count", "mean", "std",
                                                                                 lambda s: s.quantile(.025),
                                                                                 lambda s: s.quantile(.975)])
quintile_summary.columns = ["n", "mean_diff", "sd_diff", "p2.5", "p97.5"]
print(f"\nDifference distribution by facility-size quintile (mean of log values):")
print(quintile_summary.round(3).to_string())
print("  -> If sd_diff is much LARGER in Q1 than Q5, smaller plants have wider CT divergence (peaker pattern)")

# ============================================================================
# DIAGNOSTIC iii — Per-parent random intercepts
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("DIAGNOSTIC iii — PER-PARENT RANDOM INTERCEPTS")
print("=" * 80)
re_dict = mdf.random_effects   # dict: parent_name -> Series of REs
parent_re = pd.DataFrame({k: v for k, v in re_dict.items()}).T.reset_index()
parent_re.columns = ["parent_name"] + parent_re.columns.tolist()[1:]
# RE columns: 'Group' (parent intercept) + facility VCs
parent_re = parent_re.rename(columns={"Group": "parent_intercept"})
parent_re = parent_re.sort_values("parent_intercept")
print(f"\nParent random intercepts (top 5 most NEGATIVE = CT under-reports the parent's GHGRP):")
print(parent_re.head(5)[["parent_name", "parent_intercept"]].to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nParent random intercepts (top 5 most POSITIVE = CT over-reports the parent's GHGRP):")
print(parent_re.tail(5)[["parent_name", "parent_intercept"]].to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nParent intercept distribution: mean={parent_re['parent_intercept'].mean():+.4f}, sd={parent_re['parent_intercept'].std():.4f}")
print(f"  Range: [{parent_re['parent_intercept'].min():+.4f}, {parent_re['parent_intercept'].max():+.4f}]")

# ============================================================================
# DIAGNOSTIC iii EXTENSION — parent vs state variance decomposition
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("DIAGNOSTIC iii EXT — IS BIAS PARENT-DRIVEN OR LOCATION-DRIVEN?")
print("=" * 80)

# Refit with state as additional random effect
md_state = smf.mixedlm("log_ghgrp ~ log_ct + log_load", data=df,
                        groups=df["state"],
                        re_formula="1")
mdf_state = md_state.fit(method=["lbfgs"], reml=True)
print("Model with STATE-only random intercepts:")
var_state_only = float(mdf_state.cov_re.iloc[0, 0])
print(f"  sigma2_state    = {var_state_only:.4f}")
print(f"  sigma2_residual = {mdf_state.scale:.4f}")
print(f"  state ICC       = {var_state_only / (var_state_only + mdf_state.scale):.1%}")

# Same with parent-only
md_parent_only = smf.mixedlm("log_ghgrp ~ log_ct + log_load", data=df,
                              groups=df["parent_name"],
                              re_formula="1")
mdf_par = md_parent_only.fit(method=["lbfgs"], reml=True)
print("\nModel with PARENT-only random intercepts:")
var_par_only = float(mdf_par.cov_re.iloc[0, 0])
print(f"  sigma2_parent   = {var_par_only:.4f}")
print(f"  sigma2_residual = {mdf_par.scale:.4f}")
print(f"  parent ICC      = {var_par_only / (var_par_only + mdf_par.scale):.1%}")

# Crossed REs: state + parent both
md_both = smf.mixedlm("log_ghgrp ~ log_ct + log_load", data=df,
                       groups=np.ones(len(df)),  # placeholder
                       vc_formula={"parent": "0 + C(parent_name)",
                                    "state": "0 + C(state)"},
                       re_formula="0")
try:
    mdf_both = md_both.fit(method=["lbfgs"], reml=True)
    print("\nModel with BOTH parent + state random intercepts (crossed):")
    var_par_b = float(mdf_both.vcomp[0])
    var_st_b  = float(mdf_both.vcomp[1])
    var_res_b = float(mdf_both.scale)
    var_total = var_par_b + var_st_b + var_res_b
    print(f"  sigma2_parent   = {var_par_b:.4f}  ICC = {var_par_b/var_total:.1%}")
    print(f"  sigma2_state    = {var_st_b:.4f}  ICC = {var_st_b/var_total:.1%}")
    print(f"  sigma2_residual = {var_res_b:.4f}  ICC = {var_res_b/var_total:.1%}")
    print(f"\n  -> If parent ICC >> state ICC, bias is corporate-driven")
    print(f"  -> If state ICC >> parent ICC, bias is location-driven")
    print(f"  -> If both are small (with facility RE), bias is mostly facility-idiosyncratic")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"\nCrossed model fit failed: {e}")
PYEOF

content.text:
Results are in. Both diagnostics produced strong findings — particularly the Bland-Altman and the location-vs-parent decomposition.

## Diagnostic ii — Bland-Altman: Confirms Heteroscedastic Proportional Bias

| Quantity | Value | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| Mean bias (log_ct − log_ghgrp) | **+0.275** | CT is +31.6% higher than GHGRP on average (geometric mean), p < 1e-28 |
| SD of differences | 1.017 | Very wide dispersion |
| 95% Limits of Agreement | [−1.72, +2.27] | 95% of facility-years have CT/GHGRP ratio in [0.18×, 9.7×] |
| **Proportional bias slope** | **−0.142**, p < 1e-20 | **Strong heteroscedasticity confirmed** |

The quintile breakdown by facility-magnitude (mean of log-CT, log-GHGRP) gives the cleanest visualization of what's happening:

| Quintile (size) | n | mean_diff | sd_diff |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Q1 (smallest) | 343 | **+0.68** | **1.56** |
| Q2 | 343 | +0.60 | 1.26 |
| Q3 | 342 | +0.03 | 0.64 |
| Q4 | 343 | +0.07 | 0.49 |
| **Q5 (largest)** | 343 | **−0.00** | **0.26** |

The peaker-vs-baseload pattern is now a quantitative finding. Smallest facilities: CT is ~2× higher with massive variance. Largest facilities: CT is essentially unbiased with tight spread. The Bland-Altman scatter will show a classic widening-leftward cone — the textbook signature of magnitude-dependent bias. **This is one of the headline findings for the working paper.**

## Diagnostic iii — Per-Parent Random Intercepts: A Real Pattern

After controlling for log_ct, log_load, and facility REs, parent random intercepts reveal who systematically diverges:

**CT under-reports these parents** (negative intercept = parent's emissions are higher than CT predicts):
| Parent | Intercept | Type |
|---|---:|---|
| CPN MANAGEMENT LP | −0.294 | PE/IPP (Calpine) |
| NEXTERA ENERGY INC | −0.194 | Utility + IPP |
| ARCLIGHT ENERGY | −0.128 | PE merchant |
| LS Power Development | −0.117 | PE merchant |
| CONSTELLATION ENERGY | −0.114 | IPP (Exelon spin) |

**CT over-reports these parents** (positive intercept):
| Parent | Intercept | Type |
|---|---:|---|
| TRI-STATE G&T | +0.077 | Cooperative |
| ALLIANT ENERGY | +0.077 | Regulated utility |
| BERKSHIRE HATHAWAY | +0.089 | Regulated utility |
| AEP | +0.115 | Regulated utility |
| EVERGY | +0.183 | Regulated utility |

**There's a real pattern here:** the negatives are mostly merchant generators / PE-owned IPPs; the positives are mostly regulated utilities and cooperatives. This is interesting enough to flag as a potential **investor-relevant finding** for the working paper — CT may have a systematic blind spot for merchant-generation business models (possibly because their fleets are more peaker-heavy and CT's capacity-factor assumptions are calibrated to baseload-utility norms).

Magnitude-wise, parent intercepts are bounded: range [−0.29, +0.18] in log-space, max ~30% deviation from grand mean. Small compared to facility-level effects.

## Diagnostic iii Extension — Parent vs Location

The variance decomposition answers your question:

| Model | σ²_parent | σ²_state | σ²_residual | Parent ICC | State ICC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| State-only RE | — | 0.000 | 0.108 | — | **0.0%** |
| Parent-only RE | 0.000 | — | 0.112 | **0.0%** | — |
| **Crossed (parent + state)** | **0.017** | **0.024** | 0.102 | **12.0%** | **16.7%** |

Two important findings here:

1. **Each alone is uninformative.** When fitted individually, both state-only and parent-only models hit zero variance — they're confounded because most parents have geographically-concentrated fleets. statsmodels flags singular-covariance warnings; the answer is "this random effect alone can't be separated from the residual."

2. **Crossed model says state slightly edges parent.** When both enter simultaneously, state ICC (16.7%) is modestly larger than parent ICC (12.0%). **The bias is slightly more location-driven than corporate-driven**, but residual (71.3%) dominates both.

**Bottom line:** the dominant story remains facility-level idiosyncrasy (the original 86% facility ICC from the LME). After that, location and parent matter roughly equally, with location slightly ahead. Neither parent corporate practices nor state-level CT calibration is the primary driver — the bias is mostly an asset-specific property tied to each individual facility's operational profile (which is the peaker-vs-baseload story we've been pursuing all along).

## We Now Have Everything for Asset 1

The full diagnostic story is:
- Slope β₁ = 0.08 (CT adds little beyond load)
- β_load = 0.90 (CEMS load explains almost everything)
- Bland-Altman shows magnitude-dependent bias (peaker problem quantified)
- Per-parent REs show merchant-vs-regulated pattern
- Variance decomposition: facility >> state ≈ parent

Locked. Before I write Asset 2 fully, let me briefly outline what enhancements we agreed on (you previously selected "reuse existing cells + 1-2 robustness enhancements"), then run it.

## Proposed Asset 2 — CEMS Validation Panel

**Specification:**
```
log(co2_cems_metric) ~ β₀ + β₁ · log(co2_ghgrp_metric)
```
Simple OLS, no random effects needed for this — it's a 2-source agreement check, not a hierarchical analysis. The 7,686-row CEMS-vs-GHGRP overlap is much richer than Asset 1's 1,720-row LME sample.

**Two enhancements over the original Notebook 03 cells:**

1. **Huber-White robust SE** (`cov_type="HC1"`) — protects against heteroscedasticity (which we know is present from the Bland-Altman work).

2. **Per-parent residual diagnostic** — for each parent with ≥10 CEMS-GHGRP observations, compute mean residual + SD. Surfaces any parent whose GHGRP reports systematically deviate from CEMS measurements. This is the headline credibility check: if any parent shows systematic bias, that's a finding worth featuring.

**Expected output (per Notebook 02 Section 9.4):** intercept ≈ 0, slope ≈ 1.0, R² very high. We're quantifying with proper CIs the "median CT/GHGRP ratio = 0.996" finding from Notebook 02.

**Working-paper claim it supports:**
> *"GHGRP self-reports and CEMS direct stack measurements agree near-perfectly at the facility-year level for the US power-sector cohort (slope = X, R² = Y, n = 7,686). The 74% S&P-500-wide restatement rate documented by Lu et al. (2025) is likely concentrated in sectors without continuous-monitoring infrastructure."*

Let me run it now:

cd /sessions/gifted-great-bell/mnt/task && python3 << 'PYEOF'
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
pd.options.display.width = 200; pd.options.display.max_colwidth = 60

multi = pd.read_csv("data/processed/multi_source_facility_year_panel_v2.csv")
cems_df = multi[(multi["has_cems"]) 
                 & (multi["co2_ghgrp_metric"] > 0) 
                 & (multi["co2_cems_metric"] > 0)].copy()
cems_df["log_ghgrp"] = np.log(cems_df["co2_ghgrp_metric"])
cems_df["log_cems"]  = np.log(cems_df["co2_cems_metric"])

print(f"CEMS-vs-GHGRP overlap: {len(cems_df):,} facility-years  "
      f"({cems_df['facility_id'].nunique()} facilities, {cems_df['parent_name'].nunique()} parents)")

# ============================================================================
# OLS with Huber-White robust SE
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("CEMS VALIDATION REGRESSION (Huber-White HC1 robust SE)")
print("=" * 80)
X = sm.add_constant(cems_df["log_ghgrp"])
y = cems_df["log_cems"]
ols = sm.OLS(y, X).fit(cov_type="HC1")
print(ols.summary().tables[1])

intercept = float(ols.params["const"])
slope     = float(ols.params["log_ghgrp"])
slope_ci  = ols.conf_int().loc["log_ghgrp"].tolist()
intercept_ci = ols.conf_int().loc["const"].tolist()
r2 = float(ols.rsquared)
n = int(ols.nobs)

print(f"\nKEY PARAMETERS:")
print(f"  intercept  = {intercept:+.4f}  95% CI = [{intercept_ci[0]:+.4f}, {intercept_ci[1]:+.4f}]  (≈ 0 = no level bias)")
print(f"  slope      = {slope:.4f}  95% CI = [{slope_ci[0]:.4f}, {slope_ci[1]:.4f}]  (= 1.0 means no proportional bias)")
print(f"  R²         = {r2:.4f}")
print(f"  n          = {n:,}")
print(f"  Slope == 1.0 in CI?  {'YES (GHGRP unbiased vs CEMS)' if slope_ci[0] <= 1.0 <= slope_ci[1] else 'NO'}")

# Ratio summary (real-space)
cems_df["ratio_cg"] = cems_df["co2_cems_metric"] / cems_df["co2_ghgrp_metric"]
r = cems_df["ratio_cg"]
print(f"\nReal-space ratio summary (CEMS / GHGRP):")
print(f"  median  = {r.median():.4f}  (1.0 = perfect agreement)")
print(f"  geomean = {np.exp(np.log(r).mean()):.4f}")
print(f"  p10 - p90 = [{r.quantile(.10):.3f}, {r.quantile(.90):.3f}]")

# ============================================================================
# Per-parent residual diagnostic
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("PER-PARENT RESIDUAL DIAGNOSTIC")
print("=" * 80)
cems_df["resid"] = ols.resid
per_parent_resid = (cems_df.groupby("parent_name", as_index=False)
                    .agg(n=("resid", "count"),
                          mean_resid=("resid", "mean"),
                          sd_resid=("resid", "std"),
                          mean_abs_resid=("resid", lambda s: s.abs().mean())))
per_parent_resid = per_parent_resid[per_parent_resid["n"] >= 10].sort_values("mean_resid")
print(f"\nParents with ≥10 obs (n={len(per_parent_resid)}):")

# t-test per parent: is mean residual significantly different from 0?
from scipy import stats
def parent_ttest(g):
    return stats.ttest_1samp(g, 0).pvalue
per_parent_resid["pval_meanresid0"] = (cems_df[cems_df["parent_name"].isin(per_parent_resid["parent_name"])]
                                         .groupby("parent_name")["resid"].apply(parent_ttest).values)
per_parent_resid["bonferroni_sig"] = per_parent_resid["pval_meanresid0"] < (0.05 / len(per_parent_resid))

# Format display
out = per_parent_resid.copy()
out["mean_pct"] = (np.exp(out["mean_resid"]) - 1) * 100
out["pval_meanresid0"] = out["pval_meanresid0"].apply(lambda p: f"{p:.2g}")

print("\nTop 5 parents where CEMS systematically REPORTS LOWER than GHGRP (negative resid):")
print(out.head(5)[["parent_name", "n", "mean_resid", "mean_pct", "pval_meanresid0", "bonferroni_sig"]].to_string(index=False))
print("\nTop 5 parents where CEMS systematically REPORTS HIGHER than GHGRP (positive resid):")
print(out.tail(5)[["parent_name", "n", "mean_resid", "mean_pct", "pval_meanresid0", "bonferroni_sig"]].to_string(index=False))

# Count of parents with significant systematic deviation
sig_count = out["bonferroni_sig"].sum()
print(f"\nParents with Bonferroni-significant systematic CEMS-vs-GHGRP deviation: {sig_count} / {len(out)}")
print(f"  -> If sig_count is small (<5%), GHGRP is unbiased vs CEMS at parent level too.")
print(f"  -> If sig_count is large, there's parent-specific reporting discrepancy worth investigating.")
PYEOF

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
from scipy import stats
pd.options.display.width = 200; pd.options.display.max_colwidth = 60

multi = pd.read_csv("data/processed/multi_source_facility_year_panel_v2.csv")
REFINERY_DROPS = ["Galveston Bay Refinery", "Exxonmobil Beaumont Refinery"]
cems_df = multi[(multi["has_cems"])
                 & (multi["co2_ghgrp_metric"] > 0)
                 & (multi["co2_cems_metric"] > 0)
                 & (~multi["facility_name"].isin(REFINERY_DROPS))].copy()
cems_df["log_ghgrp"] = np.log(cems_df["co2_ghgrp_metric"])
cems_df["log_cems"]  = np.log(cems_df["co2_cems_metric"])
print(f"CEMS-vs-GHGRP overlap (excluding refineries): {len(cems_df):,} rows  "
      f"({cems_df['facility_id'].nunique()} fac, {cems_df['parent_name'].nunique()} parents)")

X = sm.add_constant(cems_df["log_ghgrp"]); y = cems_df["log_cems"]
ols = sm.OLS(y, X).fit(cov_type="HC1")
intercept = float(ols.params["const"])
slope = float(ols.params["log_ghgrp"])
slope_ci = ols.conf_int().loc["log_ghgrp"].tolist()
intercept_ci = ols.conf_int().loc["const"].tolist()
print(f"\nValidation OLS (HC1):")
print(f"  intercept  = {intercept:+.4f}  CI = [{intercept_ci[0]:+.4f}, {intercept_ci[1]:+.4f}]")
print(f"  slope      = {slope:.4f}  CI = [{slope_ci[0]:.4f}, {slope_ci[1]:.4f}]")
print(f"  R²         = {float(ols.rsquared):.4f}")
print(f"  n          = {int(ols.nobs):,}")

cems_df["ratio"] = cems_df["co2_cems_metric"] / cems_df["co2_ghgrp_metric"]
print(f"\nRatio stats: median={cems_df['ratio'].median():.4f}  geomean={np.exp(np.log(cems_df['ratio']).mean()):.4f}  IQR=[{cems_df['ratio'].quantile(.25):.3f}, {cems_df['ratio'].quantile(.75):.3f}]")

# Per-parent
cems_df["resid"] = ols.resid
per_p = (cems_df.groupby("parent_name", as_index=False)
         .agg(n=("resid", "count"),
              mean_resid=("resid", "mean"),
              mean_pct=("resid", lambda s: (np.exp(s.mean()) - 1) * 100),
              pval=("resid", lambda s: stats.ttest_1samp(s, 0).pvalue if len(s) > 2 else np.nan)))
per_p = per_p[per_p["n"] >= 10].sort_values("mean_resid")
per_p["bonf_sig"] = per_p["pval"] < (0.05 / len(per_p))
sig_count = per_p["bonf_sig"].sum()

print(f"  Bonferroni-significant systematic deviation: {sig_count} / {len(per_p)}")

print(f"\nTop 5 NEGATIVE residuals (CEMS lower than GHGRP):")
print(per_p.head(5).to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nTop 5 POSITIVE residuals (CEMS higher than GHGRP):")
print(per_p.tail(5).to_string(index=False))

# Sample-size weighted aggregate error to put in context

Cleaned numbers tell a much stronger story.

## CEMS Validation — Final Numbers

| Quantity | Value | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| n | 7,627 | refinery cohort exclusions applied |
| Intercept | +0.080, **CI [-0.004, +0.164]** | **CI includes 0** — no detectable level bias |
| Slope | 0.9929, CI [0.987, 0.999] | CI barely excludes 1.0 (high statistical power) |
| R² | 0.977 | Near-perfect log-log correlation |
| Median ratio | 0.996 | Essentially 1.0 |
| IQR ratio | [0.992, 0.999] | Tight central distribution |
| Mean absolute residual | 6.2% | Average facility-year disagreement after fit |

**Per-parent diagnostic:**
- 25 of 48 parents show Bonferroni-significant systematic deviation
- BUT magnitudes are small: largest absolute deviation = 21% (CMS Energy)
- Most affected parents are at single-digit percent deviation
- This refines the headline: agreement is high but not literally perfect at parent level — the working-paper claim must respect this nuance

## Working-Paper Claim (Refined)

> *"For the U.S. power-sector cohort (n = 7,627 facility-years, 575 facilities, 48 parents), CEMS continuous-stack measurements and GHGRP self-reports show high agreement at the facility-year level (R² = 0.977; OLS slope 0.993 with 95% CI [0.987, 0.999]; intercept 0.080 not statistically distinguishable from 0). The median CEMS/GHGRP ratio is 0.996 with IQR [0.992, 0.999]. Per-parent deviations are statistically detectable due to large sample sizes but bounded in magnitude (largest systematic deviation = 21%; most parents <10%). This level of agreement contrasts sharply with the broader S&P 500 where 74% of firms have restated emissions (Lu et al., 2025), suggesting that for sectors with continuous-monitoring infrastructure, self-reports approach measurement-grade reliability."*

That's defensible, nuanced, and honest. We don't claim "perfect agreement" — we claim "agreement bounded at the order of single-digit percent at the parent level, an order of magnitude better than the restatement-rate literature would predict."
