=== CELL [13] CODE ===
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup, XMLParsedAsHTMLWarning
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=XMLParsedAsHTMLWarning)

CLIMATE_KEYWORDS = re.compile(
    r"\\b(climate|carbon|emission|GHG|greenhouse|decarbon|net.?zero|renewable|"
    r"sustainabilit|ESG|scope\\s+[123]|mitigation|coal\\s+retire|gas\\s+transition|"
    r"electrif|CCS|carbon\\s+captur|methane|biomass|net.?carbon|carbon\\s+neutral)",
    re.IGNORECASE
)


def extract_section(text: str, start_pat: str, end_pat: str, max_chars: int = 200_000) -> str:
    """Pull the LAST occurrence of start_pat (skipping the TOC entry) up to end_pat."""
    matches = [(m.start(), m.end()) for m in re.finditer(start_pat, text, re.IGNORECASE)]
    if not matches: return ""
    start = matches[-1][1]
    end_matches = [m.start() for m in re.finditer(end_pat, text[start:], re.IGNORECASE)]
    end = start + end_matches[0] if end_matches else start + max_chars
    return text[start:min(end, start + max_chars)]


def climate_paragraphs(section_text: str, context: int = 1) -> str:
    """Return paragraphs containing climate keywords plus ±context neighbors."""
    paras = [p.strip() for p in re.split(r"\\n\\s*\\n", section_text) if len(p.strip()) > 50]
    keep = set()
    for i, p in enumerate(paras):
        if CLIMATE_KEYWORDS.search(p):
            keep.add(i)
            for k in range(1, context + 1):
                keep.add(i - k); keep.add(i + k)
    keep = sorted(i for i in keep if 0 <= i < len(paras))
    return "\\n\\n".join(paras[i] for i in keep)


def parse_10k(html_path: Path) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Return (item_1a_climate_text, item_7_climate_text)."""
    html = html_path.read_text(errors="replace")
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "lxml")
    text = soup.get_text(separator="\\n")
    item_1a = extract_section(text, r"item\\s+1a\\.?\\s*risk\\s+factors", r"item\\s+1b\\.?\\s*unresolved")
    item_7  = extract_section(text, r"item\\s+7\\.?\\s*management.?s\\s+discussion", r"item\\s+7a\\.?\\s*quantitative")
    return climate_paragraphs(item_1a), climate_paragraphs(item_7)


def nzt_block_for(parent: str) -> Optional[str]:
    if parent not in NZT_MANUAL_MATCHES: return None
    sub = nzt[nzt["Name"] == NZT_MANUAL_MATCHES[parent]]
    if len(sub) == 0: return None
    d = sub.iloc[0]
    return (
        f"Entity: {d['Name']}\\n"
        f"Industry: {d['Industry']}\\n"
        f"End target: {d['End_target']}  (year {d['End_target_year']}; % {d['End_target_percentage_reduction']}; baseline {d['End_target_baseline_year']})\\n"
        f"  Status: {d['Status_of_end_target']}\\n"
        f"  Description: {str(d['End_target_text'])[:600]}\\n"
        f"Interim target: {d['Interim_target']}  (year {d['Interim_target_year']}; % {d['Interim_target_percentage_reduction']})\\n"
        f"  Description: {str(d['Interim_target_text'])[:400]}\\n"
        f"Published transition plan: {d['Published_plan']}\\n"
        f"Reporting mechanism: {d['Reporting_mechanism']}\\n"
        f"Accountability/governance: {d['Accountability_delivery']}\\n"
        f"Race to Zero member: {d['Race_to_zero_member']}\\n"
        f"Scopes covered: 1={d['Scope_1_coverage']}, 2={d['Scope_2_coverage']}, 3={d['Scope_3_coverage']}\\n"
        f"Source URL: {d['End_target_source_url']}"
    )


def sbti_block_for(parent: str) -> Optional[str]:
    norm = parent.lower()[:20]
    hits = sbti_targets[sbti_targets["company_name"].astype(str).str.lower().str.contains(norm, na=False)]
    if len(hits) == 0: return None
    lines = []
    for _, r in hits.iterrows():
        lines.append(f"action={r.get('action')}, status={r.get('status')}, scope={r.get('scope')}, target_year={r.get('target_year')}, target_value={r.get('target_value')}, classification={r.get('target_classification_short')}")
        lang = r.get("full_target_language")
        if pd.notna(lang): lines.append(f"  full_target_language: {str(lang)[:500]}")
    return "\\n".join(lines)


def build_corpus(parent: str, force_rebuild: bool = False) -> Optional[str]:
    """Return corpus text for a parent (or None if no sources). Cached to scratch."""
    out_path = SCRATCH_CORPUS / f"{safe_name(parent)}.txt"
    if out_path.exists() and not force_rebuild:
        return out_path.read_text()

    parts = []
    tenk_dir = DATA_RAW / "sec_10k" / parent
    if tenk_dir.exists():
        htm_files = list(tenk_dir.glob("*.htm")) + list(tenk_dir.glob("*.html"))
        if htm_files:
            try:
                ia, i7 = parse_10k(htm_files[0])
                parts.append(f"[SOURCE: SEC 10-K Item 1A — Risk Factors (climate-relevant excerpts)]\\n\\n{ia}")
                parts.append(f"[SOURCE: SEC 10-K Item 7 — MD&A (climate-relevant excerpts)]\\n\\n{i7}")
            except Exception as e:
                parts.append(f"[SOURCE: SEC 10-K — PARSE_ERROR: {e}]")
    nzt_text = nzt_block_for(parent)
    if nzt_text:
        parts.append(f"[SOURCE: Net Zero Tracker]\\n\\n{nzt_text}")
    sbti_text = sbti_block_for(parent)
    if sbti_text:
        parts.append(f"[SOURCE: Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi)]\\n\\n{sbti_text}")

    if not parts:
        return None
    corpus = "\\n\\n".join(parts)
    out_path.write_text(corpus)
    return corpus

# --- API client helpers ---
# Install on first use
try: import anthropic
except ImportError:
    import subprocess; subprocess.check_call(["pip", "install", "-q", "anthropic"]); import anthropic
try: import openai
except ImportError:
    import subprocess; subprocess.check_call(["pip", "install", "-q", "openai"]); import openai

CLAUDE_MODEL = "claude-sonnet-4-6"
OPENAI_MODEL = "gpt-4o"

claude_client = anthropic.Anthropic(api_key=ANTHROPIC_KEY) if ANTHROPIC_KEY else None
openai_client = openai.OpenAI(api_key=OPENAI_KEY) if OPENAI_KEY else None

# Cost per 1K tokens (approximate; check current pricing)
COSTS = {
    "claude_in":  0.003,  "claude_out": 0.015,
    "openai_in":  0.0025, "openai_out": 0.010,
}

# Keep requests below org TPM ceilings (large 10-K corpora can exceed limits).
MAX_LLM_CORPUS_CHARS = 18_000


def _compact_corpus(corpus: str, max_chars: int = MAX_LLM_CORPUS_CHARS) -> str:
    if len(corpus) <= max_chars:
        return corpus
    half = max_chars // 2
    head = corpus[:half]
    tail = corpus[-half:]
    note = (
        "\n\n[NOTE: Corpus truncated for API token limits. Preserved beginning and end blocks, "
        f"original_chars={len(corpus)}, kept_chars={len(head) + len(tail)}]\n\n"
    )
    return head + note + tail


def _extract_json_object(text: str) -> dict:
    """Parse a model response into JSON, tolerating code fences/preamble."""
    if text is None:
        raise ValueError("Empty model response (None)")
    t = str(text).strip()
    if not t:
        raise ValueError("Empty model response")

    # Fast path: already valid JSON
    try:
        return json.loads(t)
    except Exception:
        pass

    # Remove markdown fences if present
    if "```" in t:
        t = t.replace("```json", "").replace("```JSON", "").replace("```", "").strip()

    # Extract from first '{' to last '}'
    i = t.find("{")
    j = t.rfind("}")
    if i == -1 or j == -1 or j <= i:
        raise ValueError(f"No JSON object boundaries found. Prefix: {t[:200]!r}")

    candidate = t[i:j+1]
    try:
        return json.loads(candidate)
    except Exception as e:
        raise ValueError(f"Failed to parse extracted JSON: {e}; Prefix: {candidate[:200]!r}")


def score_with_claude(parent: str, corpus: str, max_retries: int = 3) -> tuple[dict, dict]:
    """Returns (parsed_json, usage_dict). Retries on transient errors."""
    if claude_client is None:
        raise RuntimeError("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY not set")
    corpus_llm = _compact_corpus(corpus)
    user_msg = USER_TEMPLATE.format(parent_name=parent, corpus=corpus_llm)
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            msg = claude_client.messages.create(
                model=CLAUDE_MODEL, max_tokens=2000, temperature=0,
                system=SYSTEM_PROMPT, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_msg}]
            )
            text = msg.content[0].text
            parsed = _extract_json_object(text)
            return parsed, {"in": msg.usage.input_tokens, "out": msg.usage.output_tokens,
                                       "cost": (msg.usage.input_tokens * COSTS["claude_in"] + msg.usage.output_tokens * COSTS["claude_out"]) / 1000}
        except Exception as e:
            if attempt == max_retries - 1: raise
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)


def score_with_openai(parent: str, corpus: str, max_retries: int = 3) -> tuple[dict, dict]:
    if openai_client is None:
        raise RuntimeError("OPENAI_API_KEY not set")
    corpus_llm = _compact_corpus(corpus)
    user_msg = USER_TEMPLATE.format(parent_name=parent, corpus=corpus_llm)
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            resp = openai_client.chat.completions.create(
                model=OPENAI_MODEL, max_tokens=2000, temperature=0,
                response_format={"type": "json_object"},
                messages=[{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
                           {"role": "user", "content": user_msg}]
            )
            text = resp.choices[0].message.content
            parsed = _extract_json_object(text)
            return parsed, {"in": resp.usage.prompt_tokens, "out": resp.usage.completion_tokens,
                                       "cost": (resp.usage.prompt_tokens * COSTS["openai_in"] + resp.usage.completion_tokens * COSTS["openai_out"]) / 1000}
        except Exception as e:
            if attempt == max_retries - 1: raise
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)


def score_parent(parent: str, force_rerun: bool = False) -> dict:
    """Score one parent with both APIs. Caches per-(parent, model) results to disk."""
    corpus = build_corpus(parent)
    if corpus is None:
        return {"parent": parent, "status": "talk_na", "claude": None, "openai": None, "cost": 0.0}

    out_claude = SCRATCH_SCORES / f"{safe_name(parent)}__claude.json"
    out_openai = SCRATCH_SCORES / f"{safe_name(parent)}__openai.json"
    total_cost = 0.0

    if out_claude.exists() and not force_rerun:
        claude_j = json.loads(out_claude.read_text())
    else:
        claude_j, usage = score_with_claude(parent, corpus)
        out_claude.write_text(json.dumps(claude_j, indent=2))
        total_cost += usage["cost"]

    if out_openai.exists() and not force_rerun:
        openai_j = json.loads(out_openai.read_text())
    else:
        openai_j, usage = score_with_openai(parent, corpus)
        out_openai.write_text(json.dumps(openai_j, indent=2))
        total_cost += usage["cost"]

    return {"parent": parent, "status": "scored", "claude": claude_j, "openai": openai_j, "cost": total_cost}

Magnitude of reduction commitment + pathway alignment + scope coverage.

Concreteness of target definition — base year, target year, unambiguous numbers.

  4  = Both base year and target year defined, but uses hedging language ("approximately", "around", "up to").

  8  = Multiple targets with distinct base years and target years, all numerically precise.
  10 = Comprehensive disclosure: base year + multiple interim targets each with explicit year + end target, with measurable annual or quinquennial milestones.

## Methodology

My initial plan was to score the 5 pillars from SBTi targets data alone. The cohort coverage probe found **only 2 of 50 cohort parents have SBTi targets** (Vistra, NRG). This finding confirms that SBTi adoption in the U.S. power sector is sparse, and we needed to broaden the disclosure source set.

- **SEC 10-K** Items 1A (Risk Factors) + 7 (MD&A), climate-relevant text only, for the 22 SEC-registered cohort parents.
- **Net Zero Tracker** structured fields (end target, interim target, scopes, published plan, governance, source URL), for the 23 cohort parents NZT covers.

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup, XMLParsedAsHTMLWarning
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=XMLParsedAsHTMLWarning)

CLIMATE_KEYWORDS = re.compile(
    r"\\b(climate|carbon|emission|GHG|greenhouse|decarbon|net.?zero|renewable|"
    r"sustainabilit|ESG|scope\\s+[123]|mitigation|coal\\s+retire|gas\\s+transition|"
    r"electrif|CCS|carbon\\s+captur|methane|biomass|net.?carbon|carbon\\s+neutral)",
    re.IGNORECASE
)


def extract_section(text: str, start_pat: str, end_pat: str, max_chars: int = 200_000) -> str:
    """Pull the LAST occurrence of start_pat (skipping the TOC entry) up to end_pat."""
    matches = [(m.start(), m.end()) for m in re.finditer(start_pat, text, re.IGNORECASE)]
    if not matches: return ""
    start = matches[-1][1]
    end_matches = [m.start() for m in re.finditer(end_pat, text[start:], re.IGNORECASE)]
    end = start + end_matches[0] if end_matches else start + max_chars
    return text[start:min(end, start + max_chars)]


def climate_paragraphs(section_text: str, context: int = 1) -> str:
    """Return paragraphs containing climate keywords plus ±context neighbors."""
    paras = [p.strip() for p in re.split(r"\\n\\s*\\n", section_text) if len(p.strip()) > 50]
    keep = set()
    for i, p in enumerate(paras):
        if CLIMATE_KEYWORDS.search(p):
            keep.add(i)
            for k in range(1, context + 1):
                keep.add(i - k); keep.add(i + k)
    keep = sorted(i for i in keep if 0 <= i < len(paras))
    return "\\n\\n".join(paras[i] for i in keep)


def parse_10k(html_path: Path) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Return (item_1a_climate_text, item_7_climate_text)."""
    html = html_path.read_text(errors="replace")
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "lxml")
    text = soup.get_text(separator="\\n")
    item_1a = extract_section(text, r"item\\s+1a\\.?\\s*risk\\s+factors", r"item\\s+1b\\.?\\s*unresolved")
    item_7  = extract_section(text, r"item\\s+7\\.?\\s*management.?s\\s+discussion", r"item\\s+7a\\.?\\s*quantitative")
    return climate_paragraphs(item_1a), climate_paragraphs(item_7)

        f"Published transition plan: {d['Published_plan']}\\n"
        f"Reporting mechanism: {d['Reporting_mechanism']}\\n"
        f"Accountability/governance: {d['Accountability_delivery']}\\n"
        f"Race to Zero member: {d['Race_to_zero_member']}\\n"
        f"Scopes covered: 1={d['Scope_1_coverage']}, 2={d['Scope_2_coverage']}, 3={d['Scope_3_coverage']}\\n"
        f"Source URL: {d['End_target_source_url']}"
    )


def sbti_block_for(parent: str) -> Optional[str]:
    norm = parent.lower()[:20]
    hits = sbti_targets[sbti_targets["company_name"].astype(str).str.lower().str.contains(norm, na=False)]
    if len(hits) == 0: return None
    lines = []
    for _, r in hits.iterrows():
        lines.append(f"action={r.get('action')}, status={r.get('status')}, scope={r.get('scope')}, target_year={r.get('target_year')}, target_value={r.get('target_value')}, classification={r.get('target_classification_short')}")
        lang = r.get("full_target_language")
        if pd.notna(lang): lines.append(f"  full_target_language: {str(lang)[:500]}")
    return "\\n".join(lines)


def build_corpus(parent: str, force_rebuild: bool = False) -> Optional[str]:
    """Return corpus text for a parent (or None if no sources). Cached to scratch."""
    out_path = SCRATCH_CORPUS / f"{safe_name(parent)}.txt"
    if out_path.exists() and not force_rebuild:
        return out_path.read_text()

    parts = []
    tenk_dir = DATA_RAW / "sec_10k" / parent
    if tenk_dir.exists():
        htm_files = list(tenk_dir.glob("*.htm")) + list(tenk_dir.glob("*.html"))
        if htm_files:
            try:
                ia, i7 = parse_10k(htm_files[0])
                parts.append(f"[SOURCE: SEC 10-K Item 1A — Risk Factors (climate-relevant excerpts)]\\n\\n{ia}")
                parts.append(f"[SOURCE: SEC 10-K Item 7 — MD&A (climate-relevant excerpts)]\\n\\n{i7}")
            except Exception as e:
                parts.append(f"[SOURCE: SEC 10-K — PARSE_ERROR: {e}]")
    nzt_text = nzt_block_for(parent)
    if nzt_text:
        parts.append(f"[SOURCE: Net Zero Tracker]\\n\\n{nzt_text}")
    sbti_text = sbti_block_for(parent)
    if sbti_text:
        parts.append(f"[SOURCE: Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi)]\\n\\n{sbti_text}")

    if not parts:
        return None
    corpus = "\\n\\n".join(parts)
    out_path.write_text(corpus)
    return corpus

OPENAI_MODEL = "gpt-4o"

COSTS = {

}

# Keep requests below org TPM ceilings (large 10-K corpora can exceed limits).
MAX_LLM_CORPUS_CHARS = 18_000


def _compact_corpus(corpus: str, max_chars: int = MAX_LLM_CORPUS_CHARS) -> str:
    if len(corpus) <= max_chars:
        return corpus
    half = max_chars // 2
    head = corpus[:half]
    tail = corpus[-half:]
    note = (
        "\n\n[NOTE: Corpus truncated for API token limits. Preserved beginning and end blocks, "
        f"original_chars={len(corpus)}, kept_chars={len(head) + len(tail)}]\n\n"
    )
    return head + note + tail


def _extract_json_object(text: str) -> dict:
    """Parse a model response into JSON, tolerating code fences/preamble."""
    if text is None:
        raise ValueError("Empty model response (None)")
    t = str(text).strip()
    if not t:
        raise ValueError("Empty model response")

    # Fast path: already valid JSON
    try:
        return json.loads(t)
    except Exception:
        pass

    # Remove markdown fences if present
    if "```" in t:
        t = t.replace("```json", "").replace("```JSON", "").replace("```", "").strip()

    # Extract from first '{' to last '}'
    i = t.find("{")
    j = t.rfind("}")
    if i == -1 or j == -1 or j <= i:
        raise ValueError(f"No JSON object boundaries found. Prefix: {t[:200]!r}")

    candidate = t[i:j+1]
    try:
        return json.loads(candidate)
    except Exception as e:
        raise ValueError(f"Failed to parse extracted JSON: {e}; Prefix: {candidate[:200]!r}")


def score_with_claude(parent: str, corpus: str, max_retries: int = 3) -> tuple[dict, dict]:
    """Returns (parsed_json, usage_dict). Retries on transient errors."""
    if claude_client is None:
        raise RuntimeError("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY not set")
    corpus_llm = _compact_corpus(corpus)
    user_msg = USER_TEMPLATE.format(parent_name=parent, corpus=corpus_llm)
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            msg = claude_client.messages.create(
                model=CLAUDE_MODEL, max_tokens=2000, temperature=0,
                system=SYSTEM_PROMPT, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_msg}]
            )
            text = msg.content[0].text
            parsed = _extract_json_object(text)
            return parsed, {"in": msg.usage.input_tokens, "out": msg.usage.output_tokens,
                                       "cost": (msg.usage.input_tokens * COSTS["claude_in"] + msg.usage.output_tokens * COSTS["claude_out"]) / 1000}
        except Exception as e:
            if attempt == max_retries - 1: raise
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)


def score_with_openai(parent: str, corpus: str, max_retries: int = 3) -> tuple[dict, dict]:
    if openai_client is None:
        raise RuntimeError("OPENAI_API_KEY not set")
    corpus_llm = _compact_corpus(corpus)
    user_msg = USER_TEMPLATE.format(parent_name=parent, corpus=corpus_llm)
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            resp = openai_client.chat.completions.create(
                model=OPENAI_MODEL, max_tokens=2000, temperature=0,
                response_format={"type": "json_object"},
                messages=[{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
                           {"role": "user", "content": user_msg}]
            )
            text = resp.choices[0].message.content
            parsed = _extract_json_object(text)
            return parsed, {"in": resp.usage.prompt_tokens, "out": resp.usage.completion_tokens,
                                       "cost": (resp.usage.prompt_tokens * COSTS["openai_in"] + resp.usage.completion_tokens * COSTS["openai_out"]) / 1000}
        except Exception as e:
            if attempt == max_retries - 1: raise
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)


def score_parent(parent: str, force_rerun: bool = False) -> dict:
    """Score one parent with both APIs. Caches per-(parent, model) results to disk."""
    corpus = build_corpus(parent)
    if corpus is None:
        return {"parent": parent, "status": "talk_na", "claude": None, "openai": None, "cost": 0.0}

    out_claude = SCRATCH_SCORES / f"{safe_name(parent)}__claude.json"
    out_openai = SCRATCH_SCORES / f"{safe_name(parent)}__openai.json"
    total_cost = 0.0

    if out_claude.exists() and not force_rerun:
        claude_j = json.loads(out_claude.read_text())
    else:
        claude_j, usage = score_with_claude(parent, corpus)
        out_claude.write_text(json.dumps(claude_j, indent=2))
        total_cost += usage["cost"]

    if out_openai.exists() and not force_rerun:
        openai_j = json.loads(out_openai.read_text())
    else:
        openai_j, usage = score_with_openai(parent, corpus)
        out_openai.write_text(json.dumps(openai_j, indent=2))
        total_cost += usage["cost"]

    return {"parent": parent, "status": "scored", "claude": claude_j, "openai": openai_j, "cost": total_cost}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Cell 24 — "## 6. Composite PQS"
# Add in-notebook rationale for equal weights and the +5 SBTi bonus.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
i = find_md_cell_starting_with("## 6. Composite PQS")
nb.cells[i].source = """## 6. Composite PQS

For each parent and each pillar, the composite uses the **mean of Claude and GPT-4o scores** when both are available, falling back to the single model when one is missing/null. This is the most defensible single-number per-pillar aggregation given two independent raters of similar capability: it halves the variance of each individual model's noise while not privileging either rater.

**Pillar weighting.** The composite is the **equal-weighted mean of the 5 pillar means**, then scaled ×10 to land on a 0–100 scale. Equal weights are the conservative default in the absence of an external mandate ranking the pillars (Section 7 tests rank stability under three deliberately skewed weight schemes). Notebook 07 will additionally expose interactive weight sliders so stakeholders can re-rank parents under their own priorities.

**SBTi bonus.** Parents whose `sbti_status` is `validated_targets` or `targets_set` receive a **+5 point bonus** (composite capped at 100). The rationale is that SBTi validation is an external, binary credibility signal — the company has subjected its target to independent technical review against a published methodology — which the text-based pillar scoring cannot directly capture. The +5 magnitude is small enough that it cannot flip a low-pillar parent into the top quartile, but large enough to meaningfully separate two parents with otherwise comparable pillar text. `removed` and `committed` statuses do **not** receive the bonus (removed = SBTi rejected the target; committed = pledge without validated target).

Talk-NA parents (no disclosure source) receive `pqs_composite = NaN` and are flagged for Notebook 06 to handle explicitly."""


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Cell 26 — "## 7. Sensitivity analysis on pillar weights"
# Replace "locked Decision" reference with self-contained rationale.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
i = find_md_cell_starting_with("## 7. Sensitivity analysis on pillar weights")
nb.cells[i].source = """## 7. Sensitivity analysis on pillar weights

Section 6 uses equal weights (0.2 each). This section tests how sensitive the per-parent ranking is to that choice by re-computing the composite under three deliberately-skewed weight schemes and reporting the Spearman rank correlation across all four schemes.

Why this matters: if the ranking is robust (Spearman ρ > 0.9 across schemes), the equal-weight default can be defended as informative regardless of stakeholder priorities. If the ranking is weight-dependent (ρ < 0.7), the headline composite must be presented alongside its weighting choice — and the interactive weight sliders in Notebook 07's dashboard become essential context rather than a convenience.

Schemes tested: equal; ambition-heavy (0.4 on Ambition, 0.15 on the others); mechanism-heavy (0.4 on Mechanism Clarity); verification-heavy (0.4 on Verification & Governance)."""


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Cell 30 — "## 9. Summary of Results"
# Tighten language so claims are self-contained (no "real finding, not a
# data acquisition failure" — that phrasing only makes sense if a reader
# was previously challenging the source choice).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
i = find_md_cell_starting_with("## 9. Summary of Results")
nb.cells[i].source = """## 9. Summary of Results

### 9.1 What is delivered

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Cohort parents | 50 |
| Parents with PQS score | (see printout below) |
| Talk-NA parents (no disclosure) | (see printout below) |
| LLM raters | Claude Sonnet 4.6 + GPT-4o, both at `temperature=0` |
| Total API cost | (printed by Sections 4 and 5) |
| Inter-model agreement | (saved as `cohort_pqs_intermodel_agreement.csv`) |

### 9.2 Methodological transparency

- **SBTi coverage gap is itself a finding.** Only 2 of 50 cohort parents have SBTi targets (Section 1 coverage probe). This is the empirical justification for broadening the disclosure source set rather than a data-acquisition shortfall.
- **Multi-source triangulation** (SBTi + Net Zero Tracker + SEC 10-K) brings Talk-axis coverage to 26 of 50 parents. The remaining 24 are cooperatives, public-power authorities, PE-owned holdcos, and government entities for which no public disclosure source we can access exists.
- **Dual-LLM scoring** replaces regex/keyword-density approaches that would conflate hedged with concrete language. Inter-model agreement is reported per-pillar as a reproducibility check.
- **Composite construction** uses equal-weighted 5-pillar mean × 10 = 0–100, plus a +5 SBTi-validation bonus capped at 100 (rationale in Section 6).
- **Audit trail.** Every score carries a 1–2 sentence reasoning and a verbatim quote from the disclosure text, persisted in `cohort_pqs_llm_reasoning.json` for downstream review.

### 9.3 Limitations (what this notebook does NOT do)

- We do not search beyond SEC 10-K, NZT, and SBTi. Company sustainability reports, CDP responses, and proxy statements would add coverage but require additional acquisition work outside this notebook's scope.
- We do not down-weight LLM scores by the models' self-reported `confidence` field, although the field is captured in the saved reasoning JSON and is available for a future-work enhancement.
- The 24 Talk-NA parents inherit `pqs_composite = NaN`. Notebook 06 must decide whether to score them as a partial composite (Walk × Verify only) or carry them with NaN through to the final CCCS.

### 9.4 Next: Notebook 06

Notebook 06 combines `cohort_pqs.csv` (Talk) with the Walk-axis (decarbonization velocity from Notebook 01 + virtual baseline from Notebook 04) and the Verify-axis (SCVS from Notebook 03's LME residuals) into the headline Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS) per parent and the 2×2 quadrant assignment."""

nbformat.write(nb, NB_PATH)
print(f"Patched: {NB_PATH}")
print(f"Cells: {len(nb.cells)}")

content.text:
Comparing the current notebook against what I originally wrote, here are the substantive changes you made and my honest take on each:

## What you changed

**1. Promoted the scoring rubric to the very top of the notebook** (Cells 1-2). My version embedded the full 5-pillar rubric inside the `SYSTEM_PROMPT` string buried in Section 3. You pulled it out into a named `scoring_prompt` variable that sits right after the introduction.

**2. Template-ized the system prompt construction** (Cell 16). You split it into:
- `SYSTEM_PROMPT_TEMPLATE` — the structural / response-format wrapper with a `[SCORING_RUBRIC]` placeholder
- `generate_system_prompt(rubric)` — a one-liner that injects the rubric into the template
- `SYSTEM_PROMPT = generate_system_prompt(scoring_prompt)` — the compiled final

**3. Added two production guards to the API helpers** (Cell 18):
- `MAX_LLM_CORPUS_CHARS = 18_000` + `_compact_corpus()` — head-plus-tail truncation with an inline note when a corpus exceeds the cap
- `_extract_json_object()` — defensive parser that strips ```json fences, locates first-`{` / last-`}`, and only then `json.loads`

**4. Restructured the front matter** — added author email, "Notebook role" bullet list of pillar one-liners, and made the rubric → methodology → schema → section-map order explicit before the code begins.

## My honest take

**The rubric promotion (#1) is unambiguously the right call.** The rubric is the methodological soul of the Talk axis; burying it inside an LLM prompt string was a mistake on my part. A reviewer reading the notebook top-to-bottom now sees the scoring criteria before the LLM machinery, which is correct for a working-paper audience.

**The template split (#2) is a real improvement.** It separates "what we're asking" from "how we want it formatted." If you ever swap a pillar or add an indicator, you touch `scoring_prompt` and leave the structural template alone. This is also how a careful reviewer would expect prompt engineering to be organized — concerns separated, not stringly-coupled.

**The `_compact_corpus` and `_extract_json_object` guards (#3) are essential, and I should have built them from the start.** My version would have crashed mid-bulk on two predictable failure modes: TPM ceilings on long 10-Ks (FirstEnergy's corpus was ~63K tokens in our build stats — that's well over the per-minute throughput on standard Anthropic Tier 1/2), and OpenAI occasionally wrapping JSON in ```json fences. Without your guards the cache would have populated unevenly and you'd be debugging missing parents instead of reviewing scores. Good defensive engineering.

**The front-matter restructure (#4) is right for the audience.**

## Things I'd push back on (small)

**"SCORING RUBIC"** — should be **RUBRIC**. Visible at the top, first impression.

**"Also, please note that you can modify it."** in the intro — this is operator-facing scaffolding leakage. A HBS reviewer isn't modifying the rubric. Either drop the sentence or recast as something like *"(The rubric is centralized in `scoring_prompt` for transparency and easy modification.)"*.

**Pillar names use shell-style quoting in the intro list** — `"Ambition": Magnitude…`. For markdown prose, bold reads more naturally: `**Ambition** — Magnitude…`.

**`MAX_LLM_CORPUS_CHARS = 18_000` is *very* conservative.** That's ~4,500 input tokens. Both models have 100K+ context and even on the lowest-tier rate limits, 40-50K input tokens per call is well within TPM headroom. The downside of aggressive head/tail truncation on an already keyword-filtered corpus: you can drop the single paragraph that contains the only quantified mechanism statement (the difference between a 4 and a 6 on Pillar 4). I'd suggest raising the cap to ~40K chars (~10K tokens). If you want to keep 18K as a safety floor, at minimum print which parents got truncated so it's visible at audit time — `corpus_stats` doesn't currently flag that.

**No `cost_estimate` print before `bulk_cost` is incurred.** Section 5 just runs. For a notebook that calls paid APIs, a one-line "estimated bulk cost based on dry-run avg: $X.XX — proceed?" guard (even just a print + manual eyeball) would be reviewer-friendly. Not a blocker, but a small `if input("Proceed? [y/N]: ").lower() != 'y': raise SystemExit` could go a long way.

If you want, I can apply the typo + pillar-formatting + "modify it" sentence as a single follow-up patch before you run the dry-run, and leave the corpus-cap decision to you.

content.text:
Short answer: yes, I think the rename is a small improvement — but if you're opening the question, I'd argue **"criteria" beats "parameters"** for this framework.

**Why parameters > pillars (your suggestion):**

You already wrote "five structured parameters" in the intro (Cell 0), so renaming everything to "parameters" gives the notebook internal consistency. "Pillars" carries some TCFD inheritance (TCFD has 4 disclosure pillars), but in academic ESG-rating methodology the more common terms are "criteria" / "indicators" / "dimensions" — "pillars" is more of a practitioner-deck word. So moving away from "pillars" is fine.

**Why criteria > parameters (my honest nudge):**

In a notebook that has earlier work involving statistical *parameter* estimation (your LME β coefficients in Notebook 03, the ML model parameters in Notebook 04), reusing the word "parameter" for these scoring dimensions creates a small vocabulary collision. A reader skimming all six notebooks could conflate "PQS parameters" with "LME parameters."

"Criteria" is the standard term in ESG-rating methodology (Net Zero Tracker, SBTi, CDP, ISS-ESG all use *criteria* or *indicators* for exactly this kind of scoring dimension). It also reads as "evaluative dimensions" without any statistical baggage. The singular "criterion" is slightly awkward in code (`CRITERION_KEYS`, `criterion_mean_cols`), but workable.

**If you want me to do the rename:**

This is a global rename — the change cuts across markdown, the rubric, the LLM system prompt's JSON schema, and all consumer code. Specifically:

- The LLM returns `"pillars": {...}` only because the prompt says so. If the prompt key becomes `"criteria"` (or `"parameters"`), the consumer code (`r["claude"]["pillars"]...`) all has to match — otherwise scoring silently breaks.
- The on-disk cached score JSONs in `scratch/llm_scores/` (if you have any from local test runs) would have the old key name and would need either a delete-and-rerun, or a one-time `pillars → criteria` migration.
- `PILLAR_KEYS`, `pillar_mean_cols`, the `pillar` column in the agreement dataframe, the f-string column suffixes (`ambition_mean` stays — pillar names don't change), the dashboard plot labels in Notebook 07 (when we build it), etc.

I can apply the rename as one atomic patch in 5 minutes. **Which term do you want — `parameters` or `criteria`?**

content.text: Several stragglers — my "require=False" guards silently no-op'd when the find string didn't match exactly (e.g. markdown bold `**` got in the way). Let me sweep the remainder with a targeted second pass after seeing the full lines:

--- cell 00 (mark) L14:
  For the detailed structure of each parameter and the scoring method, please see the "SCORING RUBRIC (PILLARS + POINTS) FOR LLM EVALUATION" section below. The rubric is centralized in `scoring_prompt` for transparency and easy modification.
--- cell 03 (mark) L13:
  **Why two LLMs?** Single-model scoring is a black box: we cannot tell whether a score reflects the disclosure or the model's idiosyncrasies. Scoring with two independent frontier models (Claude Sonnet 4.6 + GPT-4o, same system prompt, same `temperature=0`) and averaging pillar-wise gives us (i) noise reduction and (ii) a directly reportable reproducibility statistic — per-criterion Pearson r and mean-absolute-difference between models — which Section 8 saves as `cohort_pqs_intermodel_agreement.csv`.
--- cell 04 (mark) L18:
  | `data/processed/cohort_pqs.csv` | Per-parent composite PQS (0-100) + per-pillar scores (0-10) — the deliverable for Notebook 06 |
--- cell 04 (mark) L19:
  | `data/processed/cohort_pqs_intermodel_agreement.csv` | Per-pillar Pearson correlation and MAD between Claude and OpenAI |
--- cell 05 (mark) L9:
  6. Composite PQS construction (dual-model average + 5-pillar equal-weight)
--- cell 05 (mark) L10:
  7. Sensitivity analysis on pillar weights
--- cell 19 (mark) L7:
  - One parent whose NZT entry says "No target" — a hard case that should pull pillar scores down.
--- cell 22 (mark) L5:
  When this cell finishes, every cohort parent with a corpus has two JSON score files on disk (one per model), each containing pillar scores + reasoning + evidence quotes + supplemental indicators. Parents flagged Talk-NA in Section 1 are correctly skipped (status `"talk_na"`).
--- cell 24 (mark) L3:
  For each parent and each pillar, the composite uses the **mean of Claude and GPT-4o scores** when both are available, falling back to the single model when one is missing/null. This is the most defensible single-number per-pillar aggregation given two independent raters of similar capability: it halves the variance of each individual model's noise while not privileging either rater.
--- cell 24 (mark) L5:
  **Criterion weighting.** The composite is the **equal-weighted mean of the 5 pillar means**, then scaled ×10 to land on a 0–100 scale. Equal weights are the conservative default in the absence of an external mandate ranking the criteria (Section 7 tests rank stability under three deliberately skewed weight schemes). Notebook 07 will additionally expose interactive weight sliders so stakeholders can re-rank parents under their own priorities.
--- cell 24 (mark) L7:
  **SBTi bonus.** Parents whose `sbti_status` is `validated_targets` or `targets_set` receive a **+5 point bonus** (composite capped at 100). The rationale is that SBTi validation is an external, binary credibility signal — the company has subjected its target to independent technical review against a published methodology — which the text-based criterion scoring cannot directly capture. The +5 magnitude is small enough that it cannot flip a low-criterion parent into the top quartile, but large enough to meaningfully separate two parents with otherwise comparable pillar text. `removed` and `committed` statuses do **not** receive the bonus (removed = SBTi rejected the target; committed = pledge without validated target).

prereq_md = """## Prerequisites — API keys

This notebook calls the **Anthropic** and **OpenAI** Chat APIs to score each parent's disclosure corpus on the five rubric criteria. Both providers are required (the inter-model agreement statistic is the only reproducibility check the notebook produces, so a single-model run is not a valid substitute).

To obtain API keys:

- **Anthropic** — create an account at <https://console.anthropic.com/> and issue a key under *Settings → API Keys*: <https://console.anthropic.com/settings/keys>
- **OpenAI** — create an account at <https://platform.openai.com/> and issue a key under *API Keys*: <https://platform.openai.com/api-keys>

Save both keys in the project-root `.env` file (same directory as this notebook's parent `/notebooks/` folder), using **exactly** these variable names:

```env
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
```

The environment cell (Section 0) loads `.env` via `python-dotenv` and prints a presence-check for both keys before any API call is issued. Approximate end-to-end API cost for the full cohort (~26 scored parents × 2 models) is on the order of single-digit US dollars; per-call cost is printed inline in Sections 4 and 5."""

new_cell = nbformat.v4.new_markdown_cell(source=prereq_md)
# Insert at position 1 (after the intro cell)
nb.cells.insert(1, new_cell)

nbformat.validate(nb)
nbformat.write(nb, NB)

# Confirm structure
for i, c in enumerate(nb.cells[:10]):

Notebook is functionally clean. **All 35 cells AST-parse, schema key in the prompt matches consumer code, and all 7 remaining `pillar` string occurrences are legitimate — they're inside the migration logic that detects the legacy key**. Here's the full review.

## What you added

**Cell 20 — `_normalize_model_output()` + helper redefinitions.** A self-healing layer: if a fresh LLM response ever drifts back to `"pillars"`, or if a cached JSON file still has the legacy key, it gets renamed to `"criteria"` on the way in. The new `score_parent()` also writes back to disk on every cached read, so files repair themselves the moment they're touched.

**Cell 34 — eager batch cache migration.** Globs `SCRATCH_SCORES/*.json` and rewrites any legacy file in one pass. Belt-and-suspenders to the lazy version in Cell 20.

Both pieces are well-defended (type-check, dual-key conflict resolution, clear error when `criteria` is missing entirely).

## Two reviewer-readability findings worth fixing before sign-off

**1. Cell 19 is dead code now.** Cell 20 redefines `score_with_claude`, `score_with_openai`, and `score_parent` — Cell 19's versions are shadowed and never called. A reviewer reads Cell 19 carefully (137 lines), tries to understand it, then encounters Cell 20 and realizes Cell 19 was obsolete. This is the single biggest noise source for a cold reader.

Two clean options:
- **(a) Collapse**: delete Cell 19, keep only Cell 20. One canonical definition per function. The `_compact_corpus`, `_extract_json_object`, COSTS dict, `MAX_LLM_CORPUS_CHARS`, and client setup from Cell 19 would need to migrate into Cell 20 (or live in a small standalone "setup" cell). My recommendation.
- **(b) Narrative split**: keep both, but insert a markdown cell between them titled "### 3a. Schema-enforcement wrapper" with a one-sentence rationale ("Wraps the helpers above with a normalization step that handles cached files written under the legacy `pillars` schema."). This frames the duplication as an intentional patch-on-base layer rather than a leftover.

**2. Cell 34 is narratively orphaned at the very end of the notebook.** Right now the sequence reads: `## 9. Summary of Results` markdown → summary printout → `# One-time cache migration` code cell. No header, no section number, sits after the summary. A reviewer would wonder why housekeeping comes after the conclusion.

Two clean options:
- **(a) Move to right after Cell 20** (between helpers and dry-run). import nbformat
import ast
import re

# --- API client helpers (with criteria-schema enforcement) ---
# Install on first use
try: import anthropic
except ImportError:
    import subprocess; subprocess.check_call(["pip", "install", "-q", "anthropic"]); import anthropic

MAX_LLM_CORPUS_CHARS = 18_000


def _compact_corpus(corpus: str, max_chars: int = MAX_LLM_CORPUS_CHARS) -> str:

def _extract_json_object(text: str) -> dict:

        return json.loads(candidate)

        out_openai.write_text(json.dumps(openai_j, indent=2))
    else:
        openai_j, usage = score_with_openai(parent, corpus)
        out_openai.write_text(json.dumps(openai_j, indent=2))
        total_cost += usage["cost"]

    return {"parent": parent, "status": "scored", "claude": claude_j, "openai": openai_j, "cost": total_cost}
'''


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The cache migration cell — adds a one-line header note now that it runs
#    at startup rather than as post-summary housekeeping.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
CACHE_MIGRATION = '''\
# --- One-time cache migration: pillars → criteria ---
# Safety net for runs from before the pillars → criteria rename. Idempotent:
# a no-op on a clean cache or after a previous successful migration.
# Runs at startup so the cache is normalized before the dry-run reads it.
migrated = 0
for fp in SCRATCH_SCORES.glob("*.json"):

    if isinstance(obj, dict) and "criteria" not in obj and "pillars" in obj:
        obj["criteria"] = obj.pop("pillars")
        fp.write_text(json.dumps(obj, indent=2))
        migrated += 1
print(f"Migrated cache files: {migrated}")
'''


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Locate cells by reliable substring (positions are about to shift)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def find_cell_idx(needle: str, kind: str | None = None) -> int:
    for i, c in enumerate(nb.cells):
        if kind and c.cell_type != kind: continue
        if needle in c.source: return i
    raise ValueError(f"No {kind or 'any'} cell containing {needle!r}")


idx_base_helpers   = find_cell_idx("# --- API client helpers ---", "code")
idx_patch_helpers  = find_cell_idx("# --- Criteria schema enforcement patch ---", "code")
idx_cache_migrate  = find_cell_idx("One-time cache migration", "code")

# Sanity: helpers + patch should be contiguous
assert idx_patch_helpers == idx_base_helpers + 1, \
    f"Unexpected layout: base helpers at {idx_base_helpers}, patch at {idx_patch_helpers}"

# Replace the base-helpers cell with the unified version
nb.cells[idx_base_helpers].source = UNIFIED_HELPERS

# Capture migration cell content (we'll re-insert), then delete it at its
# current trailing position
nb.cells[idx_cache_migrate].source = CACHE_MIGRATION
migration_cell_obj = nb.cells.pop(idx_cache_migrate)

# Delete the now-redundant patch cell. NOTE: indices >= idx_patch_helpers may
# have shifted by -1 due to the pop above; idx_patch_helpers itself is unaffected
# because it precedes idx_cache_migrate.
nb.cells.pop(idx_patch_helpers)

# Insert migration cell right after the unified helpers
insert_at = idx_base_helpers + 1
nb.cells.insert(insert_at, migration_cell_obj)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Validation
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
nbformat.validate(nb)

ast_errs = []
for i, c in enumerate(nb.cells):
    if c.cell_type != "code": continue
    try:
        ast.parse(c.source)
    except SyntaxError as e:
        ast_errs.append((i, str(e)))

# JSON-schema coherence check
schema_cell_idx = find_cell_idx("SYSTEM_PROMPT_TEMPLATE", "code")
schema_src = nb.cells[schema_cell_idx].source
assert '"criteria":' in schema_src, "SYSTEM_PROMPT_TEMPLATE missing 'criteria' key"
assert '"pillars":'  not in schema_src, "SYSTEM_PROMPT_TEMPLATE still has 'pillars' key"

# Stray pillar tokens — legitimate ones live only in the migration logic + the
# normalize function (string literals checking for the legacy key)
strays = []
for i, c in enumerate(nb.cells):
    if c.cell_type != "code": continue
    for ln, line in enumerate(c.source.split('\n'), 1):
        if re.search(r'\bpillar', line, re.IGNORECASE):
            strays.append((i, ln, line.strip()[:120]))

# Consumer code must use 'criteria' key — assert no consumer references "pillars"
# outside the migration/normalize logic
illegitimate = [
    s for s in strays
    if 'cache migration' not in nb.cells[s[0]].source.lower()
    and '_normalize_model_output' not in nb.cells[s[0]].source
]

print(f"Total cells: {len(nb.cells)}")
print(f"AST errors:  {len(ast_errs)}")
for i, msg in ast_errs:
    print(f"  cell {i}: {msg}")
print(f"Schema coherence: SYSTEM_PROMPT_TEMPLATE has 'criteria', no 'pillars' — OK")
print(f"Total stray 'pillar' tokens:        {len(strays)}")
print(f"Illegitimate 'pillar' references:   {len(illegitimate)}")
for s in illegitimate: print(f"  ", s)

assert not ast_errs,    f"AST errors found"
assert not illegitimate, "Illegitimate pillar references found"

nbformat.write(nb, NB_PATH)
print(f"\nWrote: {NB_PATH}")

# Final cell map
print("\n=== Final cell map ===")
for i, c in enumerate(nb.cells):
    src = c.source.split('\n')[0][:90]
    print(f"  [{i:02d}] {c.cell_type[:4]} | {src}")

print(f"Migrated cache files: {migrated}")
'''

# Locate cells by reliable substring (positions are about to shift)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

    for i, c in enumerate(nb.cells):
        if kind and c.cell_type != kind: continue
        if needle in c.source: return i
    raise ValueError(f"No {kind or 'any'} cell containing {needle!r}")

idx_patch_helpers  = find_cell_idx("# --- Criteria schema enforcement patch ---", "code")
idx_cache_migrate  = find_cell_idx("One-time cache migration", "code")

# Sanity: helpers + patch should be contiguous
assert idx_patch_helpers == idx_base_helpers + 1, \
    f"Unexpected layout: base helpers at {idx_base_helpers}, patch at {idx_patch_helpers}"

# Replace the base-helpers cell with the unified version
nb.cells[idx_base_helpers].source = UNIFIED_HELPERS

# Capture migration cell content (we'll re-insert), then delete it at its
# current trailing position
nb.cells[idx_cache_migrate].source = CACHE_MIGRATION
migration_cell_obj = nb.cells.pop(idx_cache_migrate)

# Delete the now-redundant patch cell. NOTE: indices >= idx_patch_helpers may
# have shifted by -1 due to the pop above; idx_patch_helpers itself is unaffected
# because it precedes idx_cache_migrate.
nb.cells.pop(idx_patch_helpers)

# Insert migration cell right after the unified helpers
insert_at = idx_base_helpers + 1
nb.cells.insert(insert_at, migration_cell_obj)

schema_src = nb.cells[schema_cell_idx].source
assert '"criteria":' in schema_src, "SYSTEM_PROMPT_TEMPLATE missing 'criteria' key"
assert '"pillars":'  not in schema_src, "SYSTEM_PROMPT_TEMPLATE still has 'pillars' key"

# Stray pillar tokens — legitimate ones live only in the migration logic + the
# normalize function (string literals checking for the legacy key)
strays = []
for i, c in enumerate(nb.cells):
    if c.cell_type != "code": continue
    for ln, line in enumerate(c.source.split('\n'), 1):

# Consumer code must use 'criteria' key — assert no consumer references "pillars"

    s for s in strays

    and '_normalize_model_output' not in nb.cells[s[0]].source
]

print(f"Total stray 'pillar' tokens:        {len(strays)}")
print(f"Illegitimate 'pillar' references:   {len(illegitimate)}")
for s in illegitimate: print(f"  ", s)

assert not illegitimate, "Illegitimate pillar references found"

==============================================================================
# 03 — Diagnostic LME + CEMS Validation Panel

**Project:** Corporate Climate Credibility Audit — power-sector POC

**Author:** Souvik Mandal (drsouvikmandal@gmail.com)

**Notebook role:** This notebook runs two independent checks on U.S. power-plant emissions data. First, it fits a mixed-effects model to quantify how closely Climate TRACE estimates align with EPA GHGRP reported emissions after controlling for plant operating intensity. Second, it runs a direct agreement test between GHGRP and EPA CEMS measurements to assess whether self-reported emissions behave like measurement-grade data. The outputs are model summaries, parent-level bias diagnostics, and publication-ready figures that support credibility claims.

## What this notebook delivers

| Section | Asset | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | **Diagnostic LME** | Quantifies the structural bias of Climate TRACE relative to GHGRP, accounting for facility- and parent-level heterogeneity. Uses CEMS-derived operational intensity as a covariate to disentangle "CT measures something specific about emissions" from "CT is just a proxy for facility size." |
| 3 | **CEMS Validation Panel** | Quantifies the agreement between GHGRP self-reports and CEMS continuous-stack measurements at facility-year level. This is the headline credibility check for the power sector — distinguishing it from the broader S&P-500-wide 74% restatement-rate literature. |


==============================================================================
=== MD CELL [01] ===
==============================================================================
## Methodological framing

We use a "hybrid" interpretation for "Diagnostic LME", the substantive finding (Climate TRACE adds little independent signal once CEMS gross load is controlled for) is supported mechanistically by the peaker-vs-baseload pattern (CT's reliance on assumed capacity factors fails systematically for low-capacity-factor units). For the U.S. power-sector cohort where CEMS persists under separate Clean Air Act authority regardless of GHGRP's fate, Climate TRACE's primary framework-level value lies in Phase-2 generalization to sectors without continuous monitoring infrastructure.

## Decisions consumed here

- **Decision #6:** LME via `statsmodels.MixedLM` with nested random effects (`vc_formula`); AR(1) **dropped**, not deferred (3-year overlap insufficient + facility random intercepts absorb the within-facility correlation that AR(1) would model).
- **Decision #11 (workplan.md):** Climate TRACE GWP horizon mismatch (20-yr vs GHGRP's 100-yr) documented as <3% impact on magnitudes; CCCS rankings invariant.
- **Cluster-aware spatial join:** the v2 multi-source panel uses tightened (1-km) match radius for facilities with another cohort facility within 5 km; 108 cohort facilities affected.
- **Sample restriction:** drop 6 refinery facility-years (Galveston Bay Refinery, Exxon Beaumont) — structural source mismatch (CT cannot see refinery process emissions; CEMS only covers cogeneration portion).

==============================================================================
=== MD CELL [02] ===
==============================================================================

| `data/processed/multi_source_facility_year_panel_v2.csv` | Notebook 02 + walkthrough patch | §2, §3 |

### Outputs

| File | Producer | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| `data/processed/lme_diagnostic_summary.json` | §2 | Working paper §4, dashboard Audit tier |
| `data/processed/cems_validation_summary.json` | §3 | Working paper headline finding |
| `data/processed/lme_per_parent_intercepts.csv` | §2.5 | Notebook 06 (CCCS Verify-axis input — refined SCVS definition) |
| `outputs/figures/03_*.png` | §2.4, §2.5, §3.3 | Working paper figure pack |

## 1. Load and prepare

Load the v2 multi-source panel (cluster-aware Climate TRACE match applied in the Notebook 02 walkthrough patch) and derive the primary fuel per facility-year from `FUEL_DATA`. Fuel is not needed as a LME covariate (collinear with facility random intercepts) but the variable is useful for the per-parent merchant-vs-regulated discussion in §2.5.

==============================================================================
=== MD CELL [10] ===
==============================================================================
## 2. Diagnostic LME

### Goal

Quantify the structural bias of Climate TRACE relative to GHGRP for the U.S. power-sector cohort, accounting for facility- and parent-level heterogeneity. The naive log-log OLS slope (β₁ ≈ 0.69 from preliminary exploration) is uninformative because Climate TRACE's emission estimates are constructed from `capacity × capacity_factor × emission_factor`, and the capacity_factor term is highly correlated with operational intensity that CEMS measures directly. We therefore include `log(gross_load_mwh)` as a covariate and use random intercepts at the facility and parent level to absorb the strong within-facility persistence we observed in the walkthrough (lag-1 correlation r = 0.945).

==============================================================================
=== MD CELL [11] ===
==============================================================================
### 2.1 Exploration recap

Before fitting the LME, the data exploration produced six findings that shaped the specification:

| # | Finding | Modeling implication |
|---|---|---|

# 03 — Diagnostic LME + CEMS Validation Panel

**Project:** Corporate Climate Credibility Audit — power-sector POC

**Author:** Souvik Mandal (drsouvikmandal@gmail.com)

**Notebook role:** This notebook runs two independent checks on U.S. power-plant emissions data. First, it fits a mixed-effects model to quantify how closely Climate TRACE estimates align with EPA GHGRP reported emissions after controlling for plant operating intensity. Second, it runs a direct agreement test between GHGRP and EPA CEMS measurements to assess whether self-reported emissions behave like measurement-grade data. The outputs are model summaries, parent-level bias diagnostics, and publication-ready figures that support credibility claims.

## What this notebook delivers

| Section | Asset | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | **Diagnostic LME** | Quantifies the structural bias of Climate TRACE relative to GHGRP, accounting for facility- and parent-level heterogeneity. Uses CEMS-derived operational intensity as a covariate to disentangle "CT measures something specific about emissions" from "CT is just a proxy for facility size." |
| 3 | **CEMS Validation Panel** | Quantifies the agreement between GHGRP self-reports and CEMS continuous-stack measurements at facility-year level. This is the headline credibility check for the power sector — distinguishing it from the broader S&P-500-wide 74% restatement rate documented by Lu, Liang and Sloan (2025). |


==============================================================================
=== MD CELL [01] ===
==============================================================================
## Methodological framing

The Diagnostic LME (§2) asks whether Climate TRACE — a satellite-and-fuel-inventory-derived emissions estimator that does not depend on facility self-reporting — recovers GHGRP-reported emissions for the U.S. power sector. The substantive finding (Climate TRACE adds little independent signal once CEMS gross load is controlled for) is supported mechanistically by the peaker-vs-baseload pattern documented in §2.4: Climate TRACE's emission estimates are constructed as `capacity × capacity_factor × emission_factor`, and the assumed capacity factor fails systematically for low-capacity-factor (peaker) units. For the U.S. power sector specifically — where CEMS persists under separate Clean Air Act authority regardless of any GHGRP policy change — Climate TRACE's framework-level value lies less in marginal accuracy gains over CEMS and more in generalization to sectors that lack continuous monitoring infrastructure.

## Methodological choices made in this notebook

1. **LME engine.** `statsmodels.MixedLM` with `vc_formula` for nested random effects (facility within parent). `pymer4` / R's `lme4` was considered for richer covariance-structure modeling but was not needed for this specification. AR(1) within-facility errors were considered and **dropped, not deferred** — the 3-year Climate TRACE overlap window is too short to estimate within-facility autocorrelation reliably, and facility random intercepts already absorb the within-facility persistence we see in the raw data (lag-1 r ≈ 0.95; see §2.1 finding D).

2. **GWP horizon caveat.** Climate TRACE reports CO₂-equivalent on a 20-year GWP basis; GHGRP uses 100-year GWP. For the U.S. power sector (overwhelmingly CO₂, minimal CH₄ / N₂O), the difference is <3% on magnitudes and does not affect the qualitative findings or downstream rankings. We retain both series on their native scales rather than rescaling.

3. **Cluster-aware Climate TRACE spatial join.** The multi-source panel uses a tightened 1-km match radius for cohort facilities that have another cohort facility within 5 km, and a 20-km radius elsewhere. The tighter cutoff prevents cross-contamination at densely-clustered sites (e.g., the Astoria Peninsula gas-turbine cluster). 108 cohort facilities fall into the tightened-radius bucket.

4. **Refinery sample restriction.** Six refinery facility-years (Galveston Bay Marathon + Exxon Beaumont) are excluded from both the LME and the CEMS validation. Refineries are a structural source mismatch — Climate TRACE cannot see refinery process emissions, and CEMS only covers the cogeneration portion, so combining them with power-plant facility-years in a single regression would conflate measurement domains.

==============================================================================
  Insuring Against the Dismantling of GHGRP:
  A Predictive Climate Intelligence Framework for Corporate Decarbonization Credibility
  Souvik Mandal
  Candidate for “Senior Data Scientist, HBS AI Institute (formerly D^3 Institute)”; Email: drsouvikmandal@gmail.com
  Problem statement:
  On September 12, 2025, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed to eliminate the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP) for all 47 source categories ( Federal Register, 2025 1, 2, the bedrock of U.S. industrial emissions reporting since 2010, covering ~8,000 facilities and 85–90% of national GHG emissions. If finalized in mid-2026, the rule would dismantle the authoritative public baseline.
  The voluntary reporting by corporates is not reliable: 74% of S&P 500 firms have restated emissions, under-reporting 135 million tons of emissions 3, 4; Nearly one-third of companies that announced 2020 targets never disclosed outcomes 5, 6. Moreover, ESG ratings by major providers, which rely heavily on the EPA GHGRP, correlate poorly on the same companies 7, 8.
  In case of the elimination of GHGRP by EPA, no public framework would exist to reliably assess corporate GHG emissions or evaluate the credibility of voluntary climate claims. This will create a structural gap that will impair ESG capital allocation, regulatory enforcement, and public accountability. Environment, Social and Governance (ESG) factors are considered by 89% of investors when they are deciding where to put their money, according to the Center for Sustainability and Excellence. ESG-focused institutional investments are expected to reach $33.9 trillion globally in 2026, up from $18.4 trillion in 2021, according to the global consulting firm PwC 9. Therefore, without accurate and consistent GHGRP reporting or an alternative assessment system, businesses, investors and the public can't make informed decisions about where to expand, invest, shop and work.
  This project proposes to mitigate that gap through monitoring with dashboard visualization and predictive modeling to assess credibility of the corporate voluntary reporting using other data sources.
  Approach:
  We build an emissions credibility framework for parent companies of facilities producing electricity by combusting fossil fuels and/or biomass. I chose to begin with this sector as a proof-of-concept as
  it is the largest contributor to U.S. stationary emissions, offering a universal baseline of continuous direct measurement to rigorously calibrate satellite-derived proxies,
  the power-sector implementation benefits from a second ground truth (CEMS) that lets us validate the calibration model against an independent measurement.
  The methodology can generalize to sectors where no CEMS analog exists (refining, cement, chemicals);
  and the short execution window of a week for the project.
  The framework integrates five independent data sources across three distinct analytical dimensions:
  Corporate Pledge (Stated Intent). A pledge quality score from voluntary corporate disclosures, scored across five pillars — Ambition, Specificity, Time Horizon, Mechanism Clarity, and Verification — drawn from SBTi commitments and NLP analysis of climate-related disclosures in SEC 10-K filings.
  Empirical Ground-Truth (Direct & Certified Action). A dual physical baseline combining annual EPA GHGRP regulatory reporting (2011–2023) with continuous direct stack measurements of GHG emission from EPA AMPD CEMS, where the GHGRP–CEMS divergence would flag reporting-integrity issues. This step also separates real operational decarbonization of parent companies from accounting effects of mergers and divestitures.
  Satellite Proxy (External Estimation). Independent facility-level emissions estimates from Climate TRACE, derived from satellite imagery and activity data.
  The framework delivers four artifacts:
  Statistical Analysis: A Linear Mixed-Effects Model analysis evaluating how satellite telemetry deviates from empirical ground-truth data across the historical overlap window (2015–2023), establishing how reliably independent remote sensing can substitute for the GHGRP data.
  Predictive Modeling: A supervised machine learning pipeline that predicts a corrected, ground-truth-equivalent emissions baseline for parent companies using satellite telemetry and voluntary corporate reporting from overlapping timelines. In tandem with feature-level explanations, this calibrated baseline enables the systemic categorization of parent companies into distinct performance quadrants (Credible Leaders, Quiet Achievers, Greenwashers, or Laggards).
  A Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS) per parent company, keeping the three underlying analytical dimensions explicitly visible so users see why each score is what it is, ensuring full auditability.
  A live executive-facing dashboard with company, sector, and geographic breakdowns. Companies are additionally labeled by their joint Pledge × Performance position — credible leaders, greenwashers, quiet achievers, or laggards.
  Moreover, unlike proprietary ESG ratings that combine voluntary and authoritative inputs into one opaque score, this framework keeps the three signals inspectable and publishes its full methodology and code.
  Key Findings:
  {Yet to be filled.}
  Limitation of the project and Next steps:
  To ensure absolute data integrity and eliminate entity-matching latency, this framework prioritizes the power sector where continuous physical stack monitoring (CEMS) provides an absolute baseline.
  Future iterations will scale this calibration architecture to less-instrumented sectors (e.g., heavy manufacturing, refineries) as independent remote-sensing methodologies mature.
  {Need to add more.}
  References:
  https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/09/16/2025-17923/reconsideration-of-the-greenhouse-gas-reporting-program
  Jenks & Dewey, EELP, Harvard Law School, 2025: https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/GHG-Reporting-Rule-Proposal.pdf
  Cohen, Rouen. & Sachdeva, 2026: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02494-9
  HBS report, Dec 2025: https://www.hbs.edu/bigs/harvard-study-74-percent-sp-500-companies-revise-emissions-data
  Jiang, Kim & Lu, 2025; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-024-02236-3
  HBS report, March 2025: https://www.hbs.edu/bigs/shirley-lu-corporate-emissions-research-harvard
  Berg et al., 2022: https://academic.oup.com/rof/article/26/6/1315/6590670
  Bheenick et al., 2024: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1059056024005240

content.text:
Read the document. I now have the citation ground truth and I can see exactly where I went wrong.

The 74% S&P 500 restatement finding is **Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026)**, Nature, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02494-9 (reference 3 in your doc, with HBS coverage at reference 4). The name "Lu" *does* appear in your reference list — but as the third author of **Jiang, Kim & Lu (2025)** (reference 5, the "nearly one-third of 2020-target companies never disclosed outcomes" finding), and separately at reference 6 as the subject of an HBS profile on Shirley Lu's corporate-emissions research. So "Lu" is a real person attached to *related* research, but I conflated her work with the Cohen-Rouen-Sachdeva paper and then made it worse by inventing co-authors.

**Citation registry I'll work from going forward** (verbatim from your References section):

| Finding | Source |
|---|---|
| 74% of S&P 500 firms restated emissions; 135 Mt under-reported | Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026), Nature, [s41558-025-02494-9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02494-9) + HBS coverage Dec 2025 |
| ~⅓ of companies that announced 2020 targets never disclosed outcomes | Jiang, Kim & Lu (2025), Nature, [s41558-024-02236-3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-024-02236-3) |
| ESG-rating divergence on the same companies | Berg et al. (2022), Review of Finance; Bheenick et al. (2024), ScienceDirect |
| ESG-focused institutional investments → $33.9T by 2026 | PwC AWM Revolution report |
| Sept 12, 2025 GHGRP-elimination proposal | Federal Register 2025-17923; legal analysis: Jenks & Dewey, EELP Harvard Law, 2025 |

## What needs fixing in Notebook 03

The wrong citation appears in **cell 27** (§3 Goal):

> "where Lu et al. (2025) documented a 74% restatement rate"

This should become (verbatim from your reference list):

> "where Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026) documented a 74% restatement rate among S&P 500 firms (Nature; HBS coverage December 2025)"

The same finding is *paraphrased without a citation* in two other cells:

- **Cell 0** delivery table: "the broader S&P-500-wide 74% restatement-rate literature."
- **Cell 37** §4.2 Working-paper claim #2: "The 74% S&P-500-wide restatement rate documented by Lu et al. (2025) is concentrated in non-power sectors that lack continuous monitoring" — also wrong attribution.

Wait — let me re-verify cell 37 since I'm now in fact-check mode.

=== cell 0 (markdown) ===
  | 3 | **CEMS Validation Panel** | Quantifies the agreement between GHGRP self-reports and CEMS continuous-stack measurements at facility-year level. This is the headline credibility check for the power sector — distinguishing it from the broader S&P-500-wide 74% restatement-rate literature. |

=== cell 27 (markdown) ===
  Quantify the agreement between GHGRP self-reports and CEMS continuous-stack measurements at the facility-year level. This is the *credibility* check for the U.S. power sector. If GHGRP and CEMS agree closely, it tells us that for sectors with continuous monitoring infrastructure, self-reported emissions approach measurement-grade reliability — distinguishing this sector from the broader S&P 500 where Lu et al. (2025) documented a 74% restatement rate, which is concentrated in sectors *without* continuous monitoring.

=== cell 36 (code) ===
          f"This contrasts sharply with the broader S&P 500 where Lu et al. (2025) documented 74% restatement rate, "

=== cell 37 (markdown) ===
  For the 7,627-row cohort overlap (excluding refineries), the OLS regression `log(cems) ~ log(ghgrp)` produces slope = 0.993 with 95% CI [0.987, 0.999], intercept +0.080 not statistically distinguishable from 0, and R² = 0.977. Median CEMS/GHGRP ratio = 0.996. Per-parent deviations are statistically detectable (25/48 Bonferroni-significant) but magnitude-bounded (largest = 21%, most <10%). **This is the headline credibility finding:** for sectors with continuous-monitoring infrastructure, corporate self-reports approach measurement-grade reliability, distinguishing the U.S. power sector from the broader S&P 500's 74% restatement rate.
  | 2 | The 74% S&P-500-wide restatement rate documented by Lu et al. (2025) is concentrated in non-power sectors that lack continuous monitoring | §3 + literature |

content.text:
The Nature page metadata gave me the verified bibliographic data — and surfaced one important nuance the notebook needs to address.

## Verified citation (from publisher metadata)

- **Authors:** Lauren Cohen, Ethan Rouen, Kunal Sachdeva
- **Title:** "Widespread revisions of self-reported emissions by major US corporations"
- **Journal:** *Nature Climate Change*, volume 16, pages 33–36 (2026); published online 26 November 2025
- **DOI:** 10.1038/s41558-025-02494-9
- **URL:** https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02494-9

So the inline form is **Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026)** — first authors are at HBS (Cohen, Rouen), third (Sachdeva) is at Ross.

## The 74% vs 58% nuance — important

Reading the Nature abstract verbatim: *"We find that **58%** of public firms' self-reported emissions were later revised."*

The 74% figure currently in Notebook 03 is **not** the paper's headline number. The 74% comes from the **HBS Business in Global Society (BiGS) coverage** of the same paper — the article URL slug your reference list points to is literally `harvard-study-74-percent-sp-500-companies-revise-emissions-data`. The HBS piece cuts the result to the **S&P 500 subset specifically** (a strict subset of "major US public firms"), where the restatement rate is higher (74%) than across all major US firms (58%).

Your source-doc problem statement is already aware of this — it cites both **[3, 4]** together for the 74% / S&P 500 claim, pairing the Nature paper with the HBS coverage. The notebook should do the same: the underlying scholarship is Cohen-Rouen-Sachdeva, and the 74% S&P-500-specific cut is from the HBS coverage.

## Four surfaces in Notebook 03 to fix

For each I'll show **verbatim current → proposed**, citing both sources to mirror your draft doc's pairing.

### Cell 0 (delivery table, no current citation)

> "This is the headline credibility check for the power sector — distinguishing it from the broader S&P-500-wide 74% restatement-rate literature."

→

> "This is the headline credibility check for the power sector — distinguishing it from the broader 74% S&P-500 restatement rate documented by Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026) in *Nature Climate Change* (HBS BiGS coverage, December 2025)."

### Cell 27 (§3 Goal — wrong attribution today)

> "distinguishing this sector from the broader S&P 500 where Lu et al. (2025) documented a 74% restatement rate, which is concentrated in sectors *without* continuous monitoring."

→

> "distinguishing this sector from the broader S&P 500 where Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026, *Nature Climate Change*; HBS BiGS coverage December 2025) documented a 74% restatement rate, which is concentrated in sectors *without* continuous monitoring."

### Cell 36 (code cell, programmatic summary printout — wrong attribution today)

> `f"This contrasts sharply with the broader S&P 500 where Lu et al. (2025) documented 74% restatement rate, "`

→

> `f"This contrasts sharply with the broader S&P 500 where Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026) documented a 74% restatement rate, "`

### Cell 37 (§4.2 Working-paper-ready claim #2 — wrong attribution today)

> "The 74% S&P-500-wide restatement rate documented by Lu et al. (2025) is concentrated in non-power sectors that lack continuous monitoring"

→

> "The 74% S&P-500 restatement rate documented by Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026, *Nature Climate Change* 16:33–36; HBS BiGS coverage December 2025) is concentrated in non-power sectors that lack continuous monitoring"

---

**One open question for you:**

The Nature abstract says 58% (all major US public firms), not 74% (S&P 500 subset, per HBS). Both numbers describe the same study. Do you want the notebook to:

- **(a)** Keep the **74% / S&P-500** framing throughout (matches your draft problem statement; cite both Nature + HBS as I've proposed); or
- **(b)** Switch to the paper's own headline **58% / major US firms** number (cite Nature only, simpler attribution); or
- **(c)** Present both — "58% across major US public firms (Nature paper); 74% restricted to the S&P 500 (HBS coverage)" — most accurate but more wording.

If (a), I patch what's proposed above and we're done. If (b) or (c), I'll redraft and re-propose.

## 3. CEMS Validation Panel

### Goal

Quantify the agreement between GHGRP self-reports and CEMS continuous-stack measurements at the facility-year level. This is the *credibility* check for the U.S. power sector. If GHGRP and CEMS agree closely, it tells us that for sectors with continuous monitoring infrastructure, self-reported emissions approach measurement-grade reliability — distinguishing this sector from the broader S&P 500 where Lu et al. (2025) documented a 74% restatement rate, which is concentrated in sectors *without* continuous monitoring.

### Specification

Simple OLS with Huber-White HC1 robust standard errors:

$$\log(\text{co2\_cems}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log(\text{co2\_ghgrp}) + \varepsilon$$

If GHGRP is unbiased relative to CEMS, we expect β₀ ≈ 0 and β₁ ≈ 1.0. The HC1 covariance estimator protects against heteroscedasticity (we know it's present from §2.4).

We also perform a **per-parent residual diagnostic**: for each parent with ≥10 observations in the overlap, test whether the mean residual differs significantly from 0 (Bonferroni-corrected). This surfaces parents where GHGRP and CEMS systematically diverge — a useful credibility signal at the corporate level.

# 03 — Diagnostic LME + CEMS Validation Panel

**Project:** Corporate Climate Credibility Audit — power-sector POC

**Author:** Souvik Mandal (drsouvikmandal@gmail.com)

**Notebook role:** This notebook runs two independent checks on U.S. power-plant emissions data. First, it fits a mixed-effects model to quantify how closely Climate TRACE estimates align with EPA GHGRP reported emissions after controlling for plant operating intensity. Second, it runs a direct agreement test between GHGRP and EPA CEMS measurements to assess whether self-reported emissions behave like measurement-grade data. The outputs are model summaries, parent-level bias diagnostics, and publication-ready figures that support credibility claims.

## What this notebook delivers

| Section | Asset | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | **Diagnostic LME** | Quantifies the structural bias of Climate TRACE relative to GHGRP, accounting for facility- and parent-level heterogeneity. Uses CEMS-derived operational intensity as a covariate to disentangle "CT measures something specific about emissions" from "CT is just a proxy for facility size." |
| 3 | **CEMS Validation Panel** | Quantifies the agreement between GHGRP self-reports and CEMS continuous-stack measurements at facility-year level. This is the headline credibility check for the power sector — distinguishing it from the broader 74% S&P-500 restatement rate documented by Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026) in *Nature Climate Change* (HBS BiGS coverage, December 2025). |

# 03 — Diagnostic LME + CEMS Validation Panel

**Project:** Corporate Climate Credibility Audit — power-sector POC

**Author:** Souvik Mandal (drsouvikmandal@gmail.com)

**Notebook role:** This notebook runs two independent checks on U.S. power-plant emissions data. First, it fits a mixed-effects model to quantify how closely Climate TRACE estimates align with EPA GHGRP reported emissions after controlling for plant operating intensity. Second, it runs a direct agreement test between GHGRP and EPA CEMS measurements to assess whether self-reported emissions behave like measurement-grade data. The outputs are model summaries, parent-level bias diagnostics, and publication-ready figures that support credibility claims.

## What this notebook delivers

| Section | Asset | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | **Diagnostic LME** | Quantifies the structural bias of Climate TRACE relative to GHGRP, accounting for facility- and parent-level heterogeneity. Uses CEMS-derived operational intensity as a covariate to disentangle "CT measures something specific about emissions" from "CT is just a proxy for facility size." |
| 3 | **CEMS Validation Panel** | Quantifies the agreement between GHGRP self-reports and CEMS continuous-stack measurements at facility-year level. This is the headline credibility check for the power sector — distinguishing it from the broader 74% S&P-500 restatement rate documented by Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026) in *Nature Climate Change* (HBS BiGS coverage, December 2025). |
