## Methodology

**Why not SBTi alone?** SBTi targets data is the most rigorous and harmonized public corpus of corporate climate targets, so it is the natural first candidate to source the 5-criterion text. However, an initial coverage probe (run programmatically in Section 1) finds **only 2 of 50 cohort parents have SBTi entries** (Vistra, NRG). This is itself a finding — SBTi adoption in the U.S. power sector is sparse — but it means SBTi alone is insufficient as a disclosure source for this cohort. The notebook therefore broadens the source set.

**Disclosure-source design.** Three sources per parent (combined when present):

- **SEC 10-K** Items 1A (Risk Factors) + 7 (MD&A), filtered to climate-relevant paragraphs, for cohort parents that file with the SEC.
- **Net Zero Tracker (NZT)** structured fields (end target, interim target, scopes covered, published transition plan, governance, source URL), for cohort parents NZT covers. NZT-to-cohort matching is hand-curated in Section 1 to filter out false positives that arise from token-overlap matching (e.g., "American Express" colliding with "American Electric Power").
- **SBTi target language** for the parents that do have SBTi entries.

**Why LLM scoring rather than regex / keyword density?** The 5 criteria (Ambition, Specificity, Time Horizon, Mechanism Clarity, Verification & Governance) reward concreteness that text-density cannot capture. Hedging language ("approximately", "we may consider"), conditional commitments, and the difference between "$2B by 2028 to convert coal to gas" vs. "we will continue to invest in clean energy" are exactly the distinctions a keyword counter conflates. An LLM at `temperature=0` produces deterministic scores, reasoning, and verbatim evidence quotes that a human reviewer can audit. The output cost is small (reported per call in Section 4's dry-run printout).

**Why two LLMs?** Single-model scoring is a black box: we cannot tell whether a score reflects the disclosure or the model's idiosyncrasies. Scoring with two independent frontier models (Claude Sonnet 4.6 + GPT-4o, same system prompt, same `temperature=0`) and averaging criterion-wise gives us (i) noise reduction and (ii) a directly reportable reproducibility statistic — per-criterion Pearson r and mean-absolute-difference between models — which Section 8 saves as `cohort_pqs_intermodel_agreement.csv`.

## Interpreting Cell 24 Output

Cell 24 reports inter-model agreement between Claude and GPT-4o on the dry-run criterion scores.

- Pearson r (per criterion): captures directional consistency across parents.
- r near +1.0 means both models rank severity similarly for that criterion.
- r near 0 means weak linear agreement.
- Negative r means inverse scoring patterns and likely disagreement.

- MAD (Mean Absolute Difference): average score gap between models on the 0-10 scale.
- Lower MAD is better.
- MAD = 0 means exact agreement.
- Rough guide: <=1 tight agreement, 1-2 moderate, >2 notable divergence.

Aggregate agreement metrics:
- Exact match: share of criterion-parent pairs with identical model scores.
- Within 1 point: share where absolute difference is <=1.
- Within 2 points: share where absolute difference is <=2.

Interpretation rule of thumb:
- High Pearson r together with low MAD indicates strong rubric consistency across models.
- Low r with high MAD flags criteria where rubric wording or evidence extraction may need refinement before relying on bulk scores.

For each parent and each criterion, the composite uses the **mean of Claude and GPT-4o scores** when both are available, falling back to the single model when one is missing/null. This is the most defensible single-number per-criterion aggregation given two independent raters of similar capability: it halves the variance of each individual model's noise while not privileging either rater.

**Criterion weighting.** The composite is the **equal-weighted mean of the 5 criterion means**, then scaled ×10 to land on a 0–100 scale. Equal weights are the conservative default in the absence of an external mandate ranking the criteria (Section 7 tests rank stability under three deliberately skewed weight schemes). Notebook 07 will additionally expose interactive weight sliders so stakeholders can re-rank parents under their own priorities.

**SBTi bonus.** Parents whose `sbti_status` is `validated_targets` or `targets_set` receive a **+5 point bonus** (composite capped at 100). The rationale is that SBTi validation is an external, binary credibility signal — the company has subjected its target to independent technical review against a published methodology — which the text-based criterion scoring cannot directly capture. The +5 magnitude is small enough that it cannot flip a low-criterion parent into the top quartile, but large enough to meaningfully separate two parents with otherwise comparable criterion text. `removed` and `committed` statuses do **not** receive the bonus (removed = SBTi rejected the target; committed = pledge without validated target).

Talk-NA parents (no disclosure source) receive `pqs_composite = NaN` and are flagged for Notebook 06 to handle explicitly.

# 06 — Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS) composite + quadrant assignment

**Project:** Corporate Climate Credibility Audit — power-sector Proof-of-Concept (POC)

**Author:** Souvik Mandal (drsouvikmandal@gmail.com)

**Notebook role.** This notebook combines three independently-constructed per-parent signals into a single headline credibility score, then assigns each cohort parent to one of four quadrants:

- **Pledge Quality Score (PQS)** — the *Talk* axis. Measures how concrete and verifiable each parent's public climate pledges are. Constructed in notebook 05 by scoring each parent's disclosure corpus (Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) targets + Net Zero Tracker (NZT) structured fields + U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) 10-K filings Items 1A and 7) against a 5-criteria rubric using dual-LLM scoring (Claude Sonnet 4.6 + GPT-4o, both at `temperature=0`).
- **EPA Performance Score (EPS)** — the *Walk* axis. Measures each parent's actual decarbonization trajectory over the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (EPA GHGRP) panel period (2011–2023). Constructed here from per-parent ordinary-least-squares trajectory slopes computed in notebook 01.
- **Satellite Cross-Validation Score (SCVS)** — the *Verify* axis. Measures the agreement between each parent's reported GHGRP emissions and the independent Climate TRACE satellite-derived estimate. Constructed here from per-parent random intercepts of the Linear Mixed-Effects (LME) model fit in notebook 03 §3.6.

The composite Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS) is the weighted geometric mean of the three axes. Each parent is then placed in the 2×2 quadrant defined by Pledge Quality Score × EPA Performance Score, with the Satellite Cross-Validation Score encoded as color.

## What this notebook delivers

| Section | What it produces |
|---|---|
| 1 | Load PQS scores (notebook 05), trajectory slopes (notebook 01), and LME random intercepts (notebook 03 §3.6); merge with the 50-parent cohort |
| 2 | Construct EPA Performance Score (EPS) from trajectory slopes via within-cohort percentile rank |
| 3 | Construct Satellite Cross-Validation Score (SCVS) from "LME random intercept" via within-cohort percentile rank |
| 4 | Compute Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS) composite via weighted geometric mean; carry NaN for Talk-NA parents; provide a partial composite column for them |

--- Cell 1 (markdown) ---
## Significance of this notebook

The three axes — Pledge Quality, EPA Performance, Satellite Cross-Validation — by themselves answer narrow questions:

- *What did the company say it would do?* (notebook 05's Pledge Quality Score)
- *What does the regulator's record show?* (notebook 01's EPA emissions trajectory)
- *What does the independent satellite-derived estimate show?* (notebook 03's Climate TRACE vs GHGRP analysis)

Each axis is interesting individually but incomplete. The accountability question stakeholders actually want answered is sharper: **for each parent company, are these three signals telling a consistent story?**

A parent can score high on one axis and low on others — and which combination they fall into determines whether they should be classified as a *Credible Leader*, a *Greenwasher*, a *Quiet Achiever*, or a *Laggard*. The composite score is the synthesis that lets us answer this question on a single number, while the 2×2 quadrant chart lets us answer it visually.

The two-by-two quadrant chart in §5 is the headline visualization for the working paper: it places every cohort parent on the *Talk* (Pledge Quality) × *Walk* (EPA Performance) plane, color-codes the independent *Verify* (Satellite Cross-Validation) signal, and shows at a glance whether the parents whose pledges and reported emissions look credible *also* survive an independent satellite check.

--- Cell 2 (markdown) ---
## Methodology — choices I made and rationale

### EPA Performance Score (EPS) — rank-based percentile

Each parent has a 2011–2023 trajectory slope (in % change per year of EPA GHGRP reported emissions, normalized by parent baseline) computed in notebook 01 via ordinary least squares with bootstrap confidence intervals. We map these slopes to an EPS in [0, 100] by **percentile rank within the cohort**: the parent with the most negative slope (most aggressive decarbonization) receives EPS ≈ 100; the parent with the most positive slope receives EPS ≈ 0; the median parent receives EPS = 50.

**Why percentile rank, and not absolute % decline or standardized slope?** Three reasons:

1. *Cohort-relative ranking is what the audience cares about.* The question is "how does this company compare to its peers", not "how big is its absolute change". A parent that cut emissions by 30% over 13 years is impressive in isolation; the more useful framing for a credibility audit is "where do they rank against the other 49 in the cohort".
2. *Rank is robust to merger/divestiture outliers.* Several cohort parents (Vistra, Talen Energy spinoff, NRG asset sales) have slopes contaminated by one-time bookkeeping changes that an absolute-% metric would treat as real decarbonization. Rank-within-cohort downweights these.
3. *The median = 50 anchor makes the score directly interpretable.* "Above 50" means above-cohort-median performer. No re-scaling decisions are needed.

### Satellite Cross-Validation Score (SCVS) — rank-based percentile on |random intercept|

Notebook 03 §3.3 fit the Linear Mixed-Effects model `log(GHGRP) ~ log(Climate TRACE) + log(CEMS load) + (1|parent) + (1|facility)` and §3.6 extracted a per-parent random intercept. The magnitude |intercept| measures how much each parent's Climate TRACE-vs-GHGRP relationship deviates from the cohort-wide pattern after controlling for operational scale (CEMS-measured gross load).

We map |intercept| to SCVS in [0, 100] by **percentile rank**: the parent with the smallest |intercept| (best Climate TRACE-vs-GHGRP agreement) receives SCVS ≈ 100; the parent with the largest |intercept| receives SCVS ≈ 0.

**Why percentile rank and not an inverse-magnitude formula?** Symmetry with EPS — using the same construction method across all three axes makes them apples-to-apples comparable, which matters when we compute their geometric mean. Also rank-based scoring is robust to the worst-disagreement parent dominating a formula's denominator.

### Composite construction — weighted geometric mean

```
CCCS = (PQS ^ w_PQS) × (EPS ^ w_EPS) × (SCVS ^ w_SCVS)    where w_PQS + w_EPS + w_SCVS = 1
```

Default weights are **0.2 PQS / 0.4 EPS / 0.4 SCVS** (locked in the project workplan §3). The choice of **geometric** mean rather than arithmetic is deliberate: a low score on any single axis pulls the composite down disproportionately. A parent cannot offset a PQS of 10 with an EPS of 90 — the geometric mean penalizes the imbalance. This reflects the framework's core conviction that **credibility requires consistency across the three signals, not strength on one in compensation for weakness on another**.

### Talk-NA handling — carry NaN, plus a partial-composite column

Notebook 05 produced PQS for 26 of the 50 cohort parents; the remaining 24 are "Talk-NA" — cooperatives, public-power authorities, private-equity-owned holding companies, and government entities with no public disclosure source we can access. For these, the Talk axis is *genuinely unmeasured*, not zero.

Our handling is two-pronged:

1. **The `pqs_composite` column carries `NaN`** for Talk-NA parents. Their full `cccs_composite` is also `NaN`. They appear in the quadrant chart in a separate band along the EPA Performance axis (with Talk = unmeasured), color-coded by Satellite Cross-Validation Score so the missing-Talk status is visible rather than hidden.
2. **A separate `cccs_partial_composite` column** is computed as the geometric mean of (EPS, SCVS) only, with weights renormalized to 0.5 / 0.5. This gives a partial-credibility signal for Talk-NA parents that downstream consumers (notebook 07's dashboard) can display alongside the full composite if they choose.

**Why not impute the missing PQS at cohort median?** Imputation would invent a score we don't have. For a credibility-framework deliverable that argues for methodological honesty, that is the wrong tradeoff. The partial composite is the more defensible alternative.

### Sensitivity analysis — six weight schemes

The default weights (0.2 / 0.4 / 0.4) reflect a specific stance: Walk and Verify dominate Talk because of the 74% S&P-500 restatement rate documented by Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026, *Nature Climate Change*). But different stakeholders would reasonably pick different weights. For this task, I am testing six schemes to see which parents are robustly classified and which are weight-dependent:

| Scheme | PQS | EPS | SCVS | Whose preference this reflects |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Default | 0.20 | 0.40 | 0.40 | Workplan-locked; Walk and Verify dominate Talk |
| Equal | 0.33 | 0.33 | 0.33 | Agnostic / democratic prior across the three axes |
| Action-heavy | 0.10 | 0.45 | 0.45 | Penalize talk-only firms beyond the default |
| Talk-heavy | 0.40 | 0.30 | 0.30 | Pledge-watcher / corporate-strategy weighting |
| Walk-heavy | 0.20 | 0.60 | 0.20 | EPA / regulator-perspective weighting |
| Verify-heavy | 0.20 | 0.20 | 0.60 | Short-seller / post-GHGRP-world weighting |

For each parent we report their CCCS rank under each scheme and whether they remain in the top quartile / bottom quartile across all schemes (a stability flag). The deliverable `cohort_cccs_rank_stability.csv` makes this auditable.

## 1. Load inputs

We assemble a per-parent dataframe by left-joining the 50-parent cohort against the three upstream deliverables. Coverage gaps (Talk-NA parents missing from notebook 05's PQS; parents missing from notebook 03's LME sample) are preserved as `NaN` and reported.

--- Cell 9 (markdown) ---
## 2. EPA Performance Score (EPS) construction

We rank each parent on `pct_per_yr` (the percentage-change-per-year of their EPA GHGRP reported emissions over the 13-year panel) **in descending order**, so the most negative value (most aggressive decarbonization) gets the highest rank. Mapped to 0–100, this gives EPS where 100 = fastest decarbonizer in the cohort, ~50 = median, ~0 = worst (largest emissions increase or smallest decrease).

--- Cell 12 (markdown) ---
## 3. Satellite Cross-Validation Score (SCVS) construction

We take the magnitude |parent_intercept| from notebook 03 §3.6's LME (Linear Mixed-Effects model) and rank in descending order on `-|intercept|`, so the smallest |intercept| (best Climate TRACE-vs-GHGRP agreement) gets the highest rank. Mapped to 0–100, SCVS where 100 = closest agreement in the cohort, ~50 = median, ~0 = largest disagreement.

The sign of the intercept (positive = Climate TRACE over-reports the parent; negative = under-reports) is preserved in `parent_intercept` for downstream auditing but is not used in the SCVS magnitude itself — disagreement-in-either-direction reduces credibility symmetrically.

--- Cell 15 (markdown) ---
## 4. Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS) composite

Two composite columns are computed:

- `cccs_composite` — the full weighted geometric mean across all three axes (PQS, EPS, SCVS) using the default weights 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.4. Returns `NaN` for Talk-NA parents (PQS unavailable).
- `cccs_partial_composite` — for Talk-NA parents, the weighted geometric mean of (EPS, SCVS) only with renormalized weights 0.5 / 0.5. For scored parents this column also reports the EPS×SCVS partial composite, which can be useful for the dashboard to show "what their score would be without the Talk axis."

The geometric-mean formula is implemented in log space for numerical stability:
```
log(CCCS) = w_PQS · log(PQS) + w_EPS · log(EPS) + w_SCVS · log(SCVS)
```
A score of 0 on any axis would map to `log(0) = -inf`, but because EPS and SCVS are constructed via percentile rank with the smallest value getting ~`1/N × 100 ≈ 2`, neither hits exactly 0. PQS could in principle be 0 from a parent with no commitment at all; we floor PQS at 1.0 before the log to keep the composite finite.

--- Cell 21 (markdown) ---
## 5. 2×2 quadrant assignment and headline figure

Quadrant labels are assigned by median splits on PQS (Pledge Quality Score) × EPS (EPA Performance Score). Because EPS is constructed as a percentile rank with median = 50 by definition, the EPS split is exactly 50. The PQS split uses the empirical median of the 26 scored parents (not 50, because PQS is on its native 0–100 scale rather than a percentile rank).

| Quadrant | PQS | EPS | Label |
|---|---|---|---|
| Top right | above median | above median | **Credible Leaders** |
| Top left | below median | above median | **Quiet Achievers** |
| Bottom right | above median | below median | **Greenwashers** |
| Bottom left | below median | below median | **Laggards** |
| (Talk-NA band) | unmeasured | any | **Talk-NA** |

The headline figure has two panels: a narrow left strip showing the 24 Talk-NA parents on the EPS axis alone (color = SCVS, size ∝ 2023 emissions), and the main 2×2 quadrant scatter showing the 26 PQS-scored parents. Dot size is proportional to each parent's 2023 attributed CO₂-equivalent emissions, so the visual weight of each point reflects its share of cohort emissions.

**Note on coverage in the right panel.** Of the 26 PQS-scored parents, 2 are missing their Satellite Cross-Validation Score (SCVS) because they had no facility-years surviving notebook 03's LME sample. In the Plotly chart, these 2 dots have `NaN` for the color channel — Plotly's default behavior is to render them in the lowest color-scale color (rather than dropping them outright). If you spot a discrepancy between this chart and the §6 sensitivity tables (which require all three axes and therefore work on 24 fully-scored parents), the 2 missing-SCVS parents are the explanation. Their full `cccs_composite` is also `NaN` for the same reason.

--- Cell 26 (markdown) ---
## 6. Sensitivity analysis — rank stability under alternative weight schemes

For each of the 6 weight schemes defined in the methodology section, we recompute Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS) for every *fully-scored* parent and record their rank (1 = best). Here "fully-scored" means a parent with all three axes present — Pledge Quality Score, EPA Performance Score, and Satellite Cross-Validation Score. The sensitivity sample is therefore the **24 parents with full CCCS** (a subset of the 26 PQS-scored parents: 2 are missing from notebook 03's LME sample and therefore have no SCVS).

We then characterize each parent's rank stability:

- **`min_rank` / `max_rank`** — best and worst rank across the 6 schemes
- **`rank_range`** — `max_rank - min_rank`; the "stability gap" (smaller = more stable across all weighting choices)
- **`always_top_quartile`** — True if the parent is in the top 25% of scored parents under all 6 schemes (robust Credible-Leader signal)
- **`always_bottom_quartile`** — True if the parent is in the bottom 25% under all 6 schemes (robust Laggard signal)

This is the auditable answer to "does this parent's headline score depend on the weighting choice".

# 07 — Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS) Dashboard

**Project:** Corporate Climate Credibility Audit — power-sector Proof-of-Concept (POC)

**Author:** Souvik Mandal (drsouvikmandal@gmail.com)

**Notebook role.** This notebook produces a single self-contained HTML file (`dashboard/index.html`) that lets a reviewer interactively explore the Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS) framework. The dashboard has three tiers:

- **Macro tier** — the headline 2×2 quadrant chart with three reactive sliders that let the user adjust the (Pledge Quality Score, EPA Performance Score, Satellite Cross-Validation Score) weights and watch the leaderboard reorder live.
- **Drilldown tier** — a parent picker that surfaces the selected parent's component scores, 2011–2023 EPA Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP) emissions trajectory, quadrant assignment, and a "Robust Credible Leader" / "Robust Laggard" badge when applicable.
- **Audit tier** — a sortable table showing each scored parent's rank under all six sensitivity-analysis weight schemes (the same six defined in notebook 06 §6), with min/max rank and stability flags.

The HTML embeds plotly.js inline (≈ 3.5 MB) so the dashboard works offline. A reviewer can open `dashboard/index.html` in any modern browser by double-clicking the file — no server, no installation, no internet required.

## What this notebook delivers

| Section | What it produces |
|---|---|
| 1 | Load the four inputs from notebooks 01 and 06 |
| 2 | Build the embedded JSON data blobs (per-parent components, rank stability, per-parent GHGRP trajectories) |
| 3 | Build the dashboard HTML (HTML structure + CSS + JavaScript) |
| 4 | Write `dashboard/index.html` and report file size |
| 5 | How to view + summary |

--- Cell 1 (markdown) ---
## Significance of this notebook

The headline 2×2 quadrant chart and the per-parent scores are valuable static artifacts (notebook 06's outputs). But a reviewer evaluating the framework wants to *interrogate* it:

- *"What if I cared more about Talk and less about Verify? Does my preferred parent still rank well?"*
- *"For a specific parent — say Vistra — how did their emissions trajectory actually look, and what's their credibility breakdown across the three axes?"*
- *"Which parents are robust top-quartile performers under any reasonable weighting scheme, and which are weight-dependent?"*

A static figure can't answer those interactively. A self-contained HTML dashboard can. The reviewer opens it in their browser, moves sliders, picks parents, sorts tables — exactly the kind of exploration that builds (or erodes) trust in the framework's claims.

The dashboard is also the most defensible answer to the HBS rubric criterion *"Judgment in choosing appropriate methods, NOT just using everything"*: the framework's default weights (0.2 / 0.4 / 0.4) are a *choice*, and the dashboard makes that choice explicit and challengeable rather than hidden inside a CSV.

## Architectural decision — vanilla JavaScript, not a server framework

We use vanilla JavaScript + Plotly.js (not Plotly Dash or Streamlit) for the interactive behavior. The reason is reviewer accessibility: a single `.html` file that opens by double-click has zero friction. A Dash app requires `pip install dash`, running `python app.py`, managing ports, and keeping a terminal open — none of which is reasonable to ask of an HBS reviewer evaluating a take-home submission. Vanilla JS gives us identical functionality (sliders, dynamic tables, reactive charts) with no server.

## Slider behavior — normalize on every change

The three weight sliders (PQS, EPA Performance, SCVS) can be moved independently. On every change, the dashboard reads the three raw slider values, normalizes them to sum to 1.0, and uses the normalized weights to recompute the Corporate Climate Credibility Score (CCCS) for every parent. The displayed weights below each slider show the *effective* (normalized) weight in [0, 1].

This is simpler than a sequential-locking UX (where moving one slider auto-adjusts the others) and delivers the same functional outcome — the user can reach any valid weight combination on the unit simplex. A "Reset to default (0.2 / 0.4 / 0.4)" button restores the workplan-locked default weights.

## What changes when the user moves a slider

**Important methodological note:** the chart's spatial layout does *not* change with weight movement. Position (PQS × EPA Performance), color (SCVS), and size (2023 emissions) all depend on per-parent component scores that are *inputs* to CCCS, not derived from CCCS itself. Quadrant assignment (median splits on PQS × EPA Performance) is similarly weight-independent — quadrant is a structural classification based on the components, not on the composite.

What *does* change:

- **Leaderboard table** — reorders by new CCCS values
- **Hover tooltips on the chart** — show the parent's CCCS under the current weights
- **Drilldown panel** — selected parent's CCCS rank updates

This is the methodologically correct behavior: the user is exploring how *the weighting choice affects credibility ranking*, not how it affects the underlying components.

content.text:
Comprehensive findings by notebook, with each claim sourced to its notebook of origin. I've verified all numbers against the actual saved JSON summaries and CSV outputs.

---

## Findings by Notebook

### `00_Data_Acquisition.ipynb` — Cohort & data source assembly

- **Cohort lock:** Top 50 U.S. fossil-fuel power-generating parents (578 facilities) identified from EPA GHGRP 2023, locked for the entire downstream pipeline.
- **Six independent data sources** stitched into a reproducible acquisition layer: EPA GHGRP, EPA CEMS (via CAMD `streaming-services/emissions/apportioned/annual`), Climate TRACE, SBTi, Net Zero Tracker, SEC EDGAR 10-K. All persisted with a `data_manifest.json` for replay.

### `01_EDA_GHGRP.ipynb` — Cohort EDA on the 13-year EPA GHGRP panel

- **Decarbonization velocity distribution:** 27 of 50 cohort parents are statistically distinguishably *decarbonizing*; 5 are *growing*; 18 are *flat*. Decarbonization is not the universal direction of the cohort.
- **Top decarbonization leaders by absolute slope:** AEP, U.S. Government (TVA), NRG Energy, Duke Energy, Talen Energy.
- **Three "growers" are structural artifacts, not real growth:** Prairie State Energy Campus (Unit 1 online 2012, Unit 2 in 2013 — 2011 baseline near zero), LS Power Development (PE portfolio expanding via acquisitions), Constellation Energy (spun off from Exelon 2022-02-01). Captured in `cohort_young_plant_register.csv`; should be flagged, not featured.
- **Geographic-dispersion finding for Berkshire Hathaway** (cohort rank #4, ~49 Mt 2023): ~99.9% of BHE emissions sit *outside* the top-10 cohort states. Top BHE states are WY (14.6 Mt), IA (11.5 Mt), UT (11.4 Mt), NV (8.6 Mt). A state-level choropleth under-represents BHE; the CCCS (parent-level) captures it correctly.
- **Fuel-mix transition documented:** clear coal→gas shift across the cohort 2011-2023, persisted in `cohort_fuel_mix_panel.csv`.
- **Threshold-effect handling:** EPA's 25 ktCO₂e reporting floor causes apparent "exits" that conflate retirement / sub-threshold drop / rule-change. Top-20 cohort dropouts hand-labeled in `cohort_exit_register.csv` using EIA-860, S&P, press releases; the rest carry `exit_reason="uncertain"`.

### `02_Entity_Resolution.ipynb` — Multi-source alignment

- **CEMS 2023 US-power total: 1.42 Gt CO₂** — within 5% of the EPA-published ~1.5 Gt, validating the short-ton → metric-ton conversion.
- **GHGRP↔CEMS bridge quality (deterministic via ORIS crosswalk):** 577 of 578 cohort facilities matched at least once (99.8%). The one unmatched facility is a Marathon/Exxon refinery cogeneration outlier.
- **Climate TRACE↔GHGRP spatial join (haversine BallTree, 20-km radius):** 568 of 578 cohort facilities matched (98.3%). Match-distance distribution: median 0.66 km, IQR 0.07–8.2 km, p90 14 km, p99 19 km — most matches are tight, long tail captures legitimate coordinate-convention differences.
- **CEMS/GHGRP pairwise ratio (first agreement signal):** median 0.996, mean 1.011, IQR 0.99–1.00 — near-perfect at the facility-year level.
- **Climate TRACE / GHGRP pairwise ratio:** median 0.954 but mean 1.869, IQR 0.81–1.44 — heteroscedastic, with a long upper tail dominated by a small set of outliers. Foreshadows the §3 LME finding.
- **CT temporal coverage is the bottleneck, not spatial:** Climate TRACE spans only 2021–2024, so 10 of our 13 GHGRP years have no CT data. The 1,771 "all-3-sources" facility-year rows are essentially the 2021-2023 overlap × 568 matched facilities. **This is the LME-eligible window.**
- **GWP-horizon documented and bounded:** CT was downloaded at 20-yr GWP; GHGRP/CEMS use 100-yr (IPCC AR4). For CO₂-dominated power-sector emissions the difference is <3%. **CCCS rankings are invariant under GWP-horizon choice** (same horizon applied uniformly to all parents).

### `03_Statistical_Modeling.ipynb` — Statistical-modeling headline (the submission's modeling showcase)

**§2 — CEMS Validation Panel (credibility headline):**

- **GHGRP self-reports near-perfectly track CEMS continuous-stack measurements** for the U.S. power-sector cohort (N=7,627 facility-years, 575 facilities, 48 parents, refineries excluded).
- **OLS regression** `log(co2_cems) ~ log(co2_ghgrp)` with HC1 robust SE: **slope = 0.993 (95% CI [0.987, 0.999])**, **intercept = +0.080 (CI [-0.004, +0.164], zero in CI)**, **R² = 0.977**, **median CEMS/GHGRP ratio = 0.996**.
- **Per-parent residual diagnostic** (1-sample t-test, Bonferroni-corrected for 48 simultaneous tests): **25 of 48 parents show statistically significant systematic deviation**, but **bounded — largest 21.0%, most <10%**. The aggregate-perfect / parent-level-not-uniformly-perfect nuance.
- **Framework-level interpretation:** for sectors with continuous monitoring infrastructure, self-reports approach *measurement-grade reliability* — distinguishing the U.S. power sector from the broader **74% S&P-500 restatement rate** documented by Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026, *Nature Climate Change* 16:33–36). The restatement-rate literature is concentrated in sectors *without* continuous monitoring (oil & gas, refining, manufacturing).

**§3 — Diagnostic LME (Climate TRACE information-content headline):**

- **Specification (Model C, headline):** `log(co2_ghgrp) ~ log(co2_ct) + log(gross_load_mwh) + (1|parent) + (1|facility)` via `statsmodels.MixedLM` with `vc_formula` for nested REs. AR(1) within-facility errors considered and **dropped, not deferred** (3-yr overlap insufficient; facility REs absorb the lag-1 r = 0.945 persistence). N = 1,714 facility-years, 548 facilities, 48 parents, years 2021-2023.
- **The β-collapse — the headline:**

| Model | DV | Predictors | β(log_ct) | What it measures |
|---|---|---|---:|---|
| A | log_ghgrp | log_ct + REs | **0.895** | Naive standalone slope |
| B | log_load | log_ct + REs | **0.901** | CT's slope on CEMS load (proxy strength) |
| **C** | log_ghgrp | **log_ct + log_load** + REs | **0.079** | CT's *partial* contribution after controlling for load |

- **Transitivity decomposition (mass-balance check):** indirect (load-mediated) channel = β_B × β_load = 0.901 × 0.896 = **0.807**; direct = **0.079**; sum **0.886** — reconciles within 1% of Model A's observed 0.895. **Virtually all of CT's apparent emissions signal flows through the operational-load channel that CEMS measures directly.**
- **Variance components (Model C):** parent variance 0.014, facility variance 0.123 (~9× larger), residual 0.0059. Most unexplained heterogeneity is at the facility level.
- **Bland-Altman measurement-agreement diagnostic** (Bland & Altman, 1986, *The Lancet*): bias on log scale +0.275 (CT over-reports by ~31.6% on real scale on average); SD of differences 1.017; 95% LoA on ratio scale **[0.18×, 9.67×]** — wide; **proportional-bias slope = −0.142, p < 10⁻²⁰** → heteroscedasticity confirmed: smaller facilities have wider CT divergence (the peaker pattern).
- **Mechanism (§3.5):** CT estimates emissions as `capacity × capacity_factor × emission_factor`; the assumed capacity factor fails systematically for low-CF peaker units (overestimating their emissions by 1–3 orders of magnitude in the worst quintile).
- **Per-parent random intercepts (§3.6):** merchant / IPP-owned portfolios show consistent CT *under-reporting* (negative intercepts); regulated utilities show consistent *over-reporting* (positive intercepts).
- **Parent-vs-state variance decomposition (§3.7):** residual bias is *slightly more location-driven than parent-driven*; crossed model assigns 12% ICC to parent, 17% to state, 71% to residual (facility-dominated). Both parent and geography contribute modestly; neither alone explains the LME's parent-level variance.
- **Framework-level implication:** for the U.S. power sector — where CEMS persists under separate Clean Air Act authority regardless of GHGRP's fate — Climate TRACE adds little independent emissions signal. Its framework-level value lies in *generalization to sectors without continuous monitoring infrastructure*, where the same β ≈ 0.9 load-proxy strength would make CT the best available substitute.

### `05_Pledge_Quality.ipynb` — PQS (Talk axis)

- **SBTi alone is insufficient cohort coverage** — only **2 of 50** cohort parents have SBTi targets (Vistra, NRG). This sparsity is itself a finding about U.S. power-sector pledge adoption.
- **Multi-source triangulation expands coverage to 26 of 50** (SBTi ∪ Net Zero Tracker ∪ SEC 10-K Items 1A + 7).
- **24 of 50 parents are Talk-NA** — cooperatives, public-power authorities, PE-owned holdcos, government entities (e.g., TVA). They inherit `pqs_composite = NaN`; carried forward with NaN rather than imputed.
- **Dual-LLM scoring** (Claude Sonnet 4.6 + GPT-4o, both at `temperature = 0`) on five criteria (Ambition, Specificity, Time Horizon, Mechanism Clarity, Verification & Governance) — equal-weighted, scaled ×10 → 0–100, with a **+5 SBTi-validation bonus** capped at 100 for parents with validated or set SBTi targets. Inter-model agreement (per-criterion Pearson r + MAD) reported as a built-in reproducibility check.
- **Sensitivity to criterion weights** tested under four schemes (equal, ambition-heavy, mechanism-heavy, verification-heavy); rank-stability reported via Spearman ρ.

### `06_CCCS_Composite.ipynb` — Composite + 2×2 quadrant + 6-scheme sensitivity

- **Composite construction:** CCCS = PQS^0.2 × EPS^0.4 × SCVS^0.4 (weighted geometric mean). The geometric form penalizes parents that score zero on any axis — a parent cannot offset a PQS of 10 with an EPS of 90.
- **EPS and SCVS constructed via percentile rank within cohort** (descending on `pct_per_yr` and `|LME parent intercept|` respectively), so median = 50 by construction; symmetric, robust to outliers, directly interpretable.
- **Coverage:** 50 parents EPS-scored, 48 SCVS-scored, 26 PQS-scored, **24 fully-scored** (full CCCS); the two missing-SCVS parents had no facility-years surviving the LME sample.
- **Quadrant distribution** (median splits on PQS × EPS; Talk-NA excluded):

| Quadrant | Count |
|---|---:|
| Quiet Achiever (low PQS, high EPS) | **10** |
| Credible Leader (high PQS, high EPS) | **7** |
| Greenwasher (high PQS, low EPS) | **6** |
| Laggard (low PQS, low EPS) | **3** |
| Talk-NA (separate band) | 24 |

  Stylized finding: more *Quiet Achievers* than *Credible Leaders*, and more *Greenwashers* than *Laggards*. Credibility is not evenly distributed across the Talk × Walk plane.

- **Top 10 by default-weight CCCS** (PQS / EPS / SCVS components → CCCS, quadrant):

| Rank | Parent | PQS | EPS | SCVS | CCCS | Quadrant |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | American Electric Power | 50 | 90 | 89.6 | **79.87** | Credible Leader |
| 2 | NRG Energy | 63 | 96 | 68.8 | **77.21** | Credible Leader |
| 3 | DTE Energy | 73 | 74 | 75.0 | **74.20** | Credible Leader |
| 4 | Evergy | 24 | 86 | 95.8 | 69.57 | Quiet Achiever |
| 5 | Alliant Energy | 49 | 64 | 81.3 | 66.75 | Quiet Achiever |
| 6 | Vistra | 64 | 50 | 83.3 | 64.44 | Credible Leader |
| 7 | NextEra | 74 | 34 | 97.9 | 60.64 | **Greenwasher** |
| 8 | PPL | 46 | 60 | 54.2 | 54.61 | Quiet Achiever |
| 9 | Dominion | 28 | 56 | 62.5 | 50.94 | Quiet Achiever |
| 10 | Ameren | 66 | 76 | 25.0 | 47.36 | Credible Leader |

  Note the high-PQS / low-EPS Greenwasher case at rank 7 (NextEra) and the high-EPS / high-SCVS but PQS-pulled-down case at rank 4 (Evergy) — exactly the asymmetries the geometric mean is designed to surface.

- **6-scheme sensitivity analysis** (default, equal, action-heavy, talk-heavy, walk-heavy, verify-heavy) — rank-stability flags computed for all 24 fully-scored parents.
- **Robust Credible Leaders** (always_top_quartile across all 6 schemes): **3** — American Electric Power, NRG Energy, DTE Energy. These rankings are weight-independent.
- **Robust Laggards** (always_bottom_quartile across all 6 schemes): **3** — WEC Energy Group, Talen Energy, UNS Energy.

Both fixes — restated so each finding has clear anchoring and an unambiguous quantity-being-measured.

---

### Revised — `03_Statistical_Modeling.ipynb` §2 (CEMS Validation Panel)

**§2 headline (now properly anchored).** To test the credibility of GHGRP self-reports against the regulator's own continuous-stack measurements, an OLS regression of `log(co2_cems)` on `log(co2_ghgrp)` was fit (HC1 heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors; N = 7,627 facility-years, 575 facilities, 48 parents, refineries excluded). The diagnostics establish that **GHGRP self-reports near-perfectly track CEMS at the facility-year level**: slope = **0.993** (95% CI [0.987, 0.999]; the slope of 1.0 lies just outside the CI but within 1% of the point estimate), intercept = **+0.080** (CI [−0.004, +0.164]; zero is in the CI), **R² = 0.977**, and the median CEMS/GHGRP ratio is **0.996**.

**Per-parent residual diagnostic (now disambiguated).** A sharper, parent-level question follows: *does every parent's CEMS-vs-GHGRP relationship sit on the same aggregate regression line, or do individual parents have systematic offsets from it?* For each parent with ≥10 facility-year observations, a 1-sample t-test of the parent's mean OLS residual against zero was run (Bonferroni-corrected for 48 simultaneous tests). **25 of 48 parents show a statistically significant systematic offset between their GHGRP self-reports and the CEMS measurements at their facilities** — i.e., on average their GHGRP either over- or under-reports CEMS by a non-zero amount. The offsets are **detectable but bounded**: the **largest is 21.0%**, and **most are under 10%**. This is the aggregate-perfect / parent-level-not-uniformly-perfect nuance — the framework-level claim of GHGRP reliability for the power sector holds, but individual parent-level claims should carry a ±10% caveat.

---

The two clarifications:

1. **What the t-test measures.** It tests the **mean of each parent's OLS residuals** against zero — i.e., whether the parent's average GHGRP value systematically over- or under-reports its CEMS value, after the aggregate regression line has already been fit. The 21% / <10% magnitudes are on the **real (un-logged) percentage scale**.

2. **What the OLS numbers attach to.** The slope/intercept/R²/median-ratio block is now prefaced by an explicit sentence stating what regression was fit, the sample size, and what question it answers — so the diagnostics no longer arrive context-free.

These are the wordings I'll use in doc-01 unless you want them tightened or rephrased further.

Here's the tight 250–300 word version with notebook anchors for the doc-01 Key Findings section.

---

**Key Findings** (~285 words)

- **Power-sector GHGRP is credible (`03_Statistical_Modeling.ipynb` §2).** OLS `log(co2_cems) ~ log(co2_ghgrp)` on 7,627 facility-years (575 facilities, 48 parents, refineries excluded) returns slope **0.993** [CI 0.987–0.999], intercept indistinguishable from 0, **R² = 0.977**, and median CEMS/GHGRP ratio **0.996**. A per-parent Bonferroni-corrected residual t-test flags **25 of 48 parents** with a statistically significant offset between their reported emissions and CEMS measurements, but magnitudes are bounded (largest 21%, most <10%). The power sector contrasts sharply with the **74% S&P-500 restatement rate** of Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026) — continuous-monitoring infrastructure substantially constrains self-report distortion.

- **Climate TRACE is a load proxy, not an independent emissions measurement (`03_Statistical_Modeling.ipynb` §3).** In a nested LME on the 2021–23 cross-source overlap, CT's standalone slope on GHGRP (**β = 0.895**) collapses to **β = 0.079** once CEMS gross load is controlled. A companion LME confirms CT predicts CEMS load directly with **β = 0.901**. Transitivity mass-balances the collapse: 0.901 × 0.896 + 0.079 = 0.886 ≈ 0.895. Mechanism: CT's `capacity × capacity_factor × emission_factor` formula fails systematically for low-capacity-factor peakers (1–3 orders of magnitude over-estimation in the worst Bland-Altman quintile).

- **SBTi coverage in U.S. power is sparse (`05_Pledge_Quality.ipynb`).** Only **2 of 50** parents (Vistra, NRG) appear in SBTi. Multi-source triangulation (SBTi + Net Zero Tracker + SEC 10-K Items 1A/7) extends Talk-axis coverage to **26/50**; the remaining **24** — cooperatives, public-power authorities, PE-owned holdcos, TVA — are flagged Talk-NA and carry NaN PQS rather than imputed scores.

- **Credibility is unevenly distributed across the cohort (`06_CCCS_Composite.ipynb`).** 2×2 median-split on PQS × EPS: **10 Quiet Achievers, 7 Credible Leaders, 6 Greenwashers, 3 Laggards** (plus 24 Talk-NA). High-Walk-low-Talk outnumbers full Credible Leaders; talk-without-action outnumbers full Laggards.

- **Three robust top performers, three robust laggards (`06_CCCS_Composite.ipynb`).** Default-weight CCCS top 3 — **AEP 79.87, NRG 77.21, DTE 74.20** — remain in the top quartile across **all six** sensitivity weight schemes. Robust bottom-quartile across all schemes: WEC Energy, Talen Energy, UNS Energy.

Here's the rephrased executive-facing version (~285 words). Statistical machinery moved out; the "so what" promoted.

---

**Key Findings**

- **U.S. power-sector self-reports are reliable (`03_Statistical_Modeling.ipynb` §2).** EPA GHGRP self-reports near-perfectly track CEMS continuous-stack measurements at the facility level across the 50-parent cohort. Individual parents can be off by up to ~20%, but most are within 10%. This stands in sharp contrast to the 74% restatement rate that Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva (2026, *Nature Climate Change*) documented for the broader S&P 500 — suggesting that **continuous-monitoring infrastructure, where it exists, substantially disciplines corporate self-reporting**. If GHGRP is sunset, CEMS persists under separate Clean Air Act authority; the ground-truth for U.S. power is durable.

- **Climate TRACE is a noisy load proxy, not an independent emissions check for this sector (`03_Statistical_Modeling.ipynb` §3).** Once CEMS-measured plant output enters the model, CT's apparent emissions signal collapses — virtually all of what looked like "satellite agreement with GHGRP" was CT tracking how hard each plant was running. CT also systematically over-estimates low-utilization "peaker" units by orders of magnitude. The framework implication: **CT's value lies in sectors *without* continuous monitoring** (oil & gas, refining, manufacturing) rather than as a replacement signal for power.

- **Voluntary pledge disclosure has a coverage gap (`05_Pledge_Quality.ipynb`).** Only 2 of 50 cohort parents (Vistra, NRG) appear in SBTi. Multi-source triangulation (SBTi + Net Zero Tracker + SEC 10-K) extends coverage to 26 of 50; the remaining 24 — cooperatives, public-power authorities, PE-owned holdcos, TVA — have no scoreable public pledge and are treated explicitly as **Talk-NA** rather than scored as zero.

- **Credibility is unevenly distributed across the cohort (`06_CCCS_Composite.ipynb`).** Of the 26 fully-scored parents: **10 Quiet Achievers** (decarbonizing without strong pledges), **7 Credible Leaders** (talk and action aligned), **6 Greenwashers** (strong pledges, weak action), **3 Laggards**. Talk-without-action outnumbers full Laggards; quiet decarbonization is the most common pattern.

- **Three robust leaders, three robust laggards (`06_CCCS_Composite.ipynb`).** **AEP, NRG, and DTE Energy** sit in the top quartile under *every* one of the six sensitivity weighting schemes tested. **WEC Energy, Talen Energy, and UNS Energy** sit in the bottom quartile across all six. The headline rankings do not depend on the analyst's prior about which signal matters most.

content.text:
**Limitations of the project and Next steps**

- **No predictive emissions baseline yet → calibrated ML virtual baseline.** The current framework diagnoses the existing data; it does not produce a forward-looking emissions estimate that would survive a GHGRP rollback. The planned **Notebook 04 (Prognostic ML)** — deferred to protect the Day-3 budget — would train a model on Climate TRACE + fuel-mix + parent fixed effects, with calibrated uncertainty intervals (e.g., conformal prediction), to deliver the "Plan B" emissions signal that credibility scoring would need in a post-GHGRP regulatory environment.

- **Talk-axis coverage is incomplete → exhaustive pledge crawling.** Twenty-four of the 50 cohort parents currently carry NaN on the Pledge Quality axis because no scoreable disclosure exists in the three sources we used (SBTi, Net Zero Tracker, SEC 10-K). The Phase-2 cleanup is a targeted crawl of company sustainability reports, CDP responses, proxy statements, investor-day decks, state PUC integrated-resource plans, and FERC filings — most reachable via scripted scraping, the remainder via manual annotation. This should close most of the cooperatives / public-power / PE-holdco gap.

- **Single-source verification and single-sector scope → multi-estimator, multi-sector, cradle-to-grave accountability.** Climate TRACE was the only independent Verify-axis source, and the cohort is restricted to U.S. power. Three layered extensions: (i) add complementary emissions estimators (TROPOMI / Sentinel-5P, MethaneSAT, Carbon Mapper, NASA OCO-2/3, GHGSat) so verification does not depend on any single satellite product; (ii) extend the cohort beyond power to **oil & gas, refining, and manufacturing** — sectors where Cohen, Rouen & Sachdeva's 74% restatement rate likely concentrates and where the verification machinery should add the most value; (iii) build toward a **cradle-to-grave lifecycle layer** that links Scope-1 stack emissions to upstream supply-chain emissions (fuel extraction, transport, processing) and downstream Scope-3 emissions (product use, retirement) for full corporate carbon accountability.

(~285 words.)

Problem framing, storytelling, and a non-technical executive summary carry equal weight to technical depth.

22	2. *Platform & Digital Business Models* — Inside Airbnb listings
23	3. *Future of Work* — LinkedIn job postings (2023–2024)
24	4. *Climate & Sustainability* — EPA Greenhouse Gas Reporting (flagged as the "D^3 bonus")
25	
26	You're also free to bring your own dataset. The "D^3" note on option 4 strongly suggests this is for HBS's Digital, Data, and Design Institute — climate/sustainability angles may score bonus points with that audience.

29	- A well-documented notebook or repo with all code
30	- A log of every LLM prompt used during the project
31	- A 1–2 page written summary covering problem statement, approach, key findings, limitations/next steps
32	
33	**Bonus extensions** (not required, but signal seniority): a deployed app/dashboard, a reproducible pipeline, multiple data sources, error analysis or robustness checks.
34	
35	**My strategic read**
36	The trap here is over-engineering. A senior IC is expected to (a) pick a question with a clear "so what," (b) bring just enough technique to answer it credibly, (c) be honest about limitations, and (d) tell a tight story. I'd recommend we pick one problem with a strong business hook, scope it tight, and invest the saved time in EDA quality, robustness checks, and the executive summary.

39	[assistant] (called AskUserQuestion)

44	[assistant] Clean slate in your project folder. Now to the most important decision — the problem framing. The EPA GHG Reporting Program (GHGRP) contains facility-level emissions for ~8,000 large US facilities (>25,000 tCO2e/year threshold) across 41+ sectors, going back to 2010, with parent company info, lat/lon, and gas-by-gas breakdowns. That richness opens several distinct problem framings, each with different methods, audiences, and "what's new to learn" potential.
45	
46	Here are the strongest framings I'd consider — each genuinely useful in the real world, each fits a 3-5 day scope, each has a clear "so what":
47	
48	**A. "Did the IRA bend the curve?" — Causal policy impact study**
49	*Question:* Has the Inflation Reduction Act (Aug 2022) measurably accelerated emission reductions, and in which sectors? *Methods:* Difference-in-differences or synthetic control comparing treated sectors (those with high IRA exposure like power, manufacturing) vs. controls; facility-level fixed effects. *Audience:* Policymakers, climate-tech investors, ESG analysts. *What's new:* Rigorous causal inference (DiD, synthetic control) — likely new territory and exactly the kind of methodology HBS values. *Risk:* IRA effects are still early; identification is hard. Honest discussion of limitations becomes a feature.
50	
51	**B. "Emissions Risk Scorecard for ESG Investors" — Predictive ML + dashboard**
52	*Question:* Can we build a forward-looking emissions risk score for public companies from their facility disclosures, to help ESG funds screen portfolios? *Methods:* Parent-company rollup, time-series features, gradient boosting to forecast next-year trajectory, SHAP for interpretability, deployed as a simple dashboard. *Audience:* ESG investment funds — direct HBS audience. *What's new:* SHAP interpretability + dashboard deployment. *Risk:* Predictive accuracy may be modest; the real value is the framework, not the score itself.
53	
54	**C. "Environmental Justice Audit" — Multi-source geospatial integration**
55	*Question:* Where is industrial emission concentrated near disadvantaged communities, and is that gap widening or closing? *Methods:* Geospatial join of GHGRP + EPA EJScreen demographic data, equity-weighted emissions index, trend analysis, maps. *Audience:* Regulators, advocacy groups, ESG funds. *What's new:* Geospatial analysis (geopandas, H3 hexagons) + multi-source integration → satisfies the bonus criterion. *Risk:* EJ analysis can drift political — frame carefully and let data speak.
56	
57	**D. "Decarbonization Leaders & Laggards" — Benchmarking + anomaly detection**
58	*Question:* Within each sector, which facilities are decarbonizing fastest, which are stagnating, and what differentiates them? *Methods:* Sector-normalized trend analysis, peer-percentile rankings, clustering to find decarbonization archetypes, outlier detection for unusual reporters. *Audience:* Corporate sustainability teams, investors. *What's new:* Unsupervised clustering + anomaly detection on a real ESG problem. *Risk:* Descriptive rather than predictive — needs sharp narrative to land.
59	
60	**My recommendation:** I'd lean toward **A (causal IRA study) or C (EJ audit with multi-source)** — both have the clearest "wow" factor for an HBS evaluator. A is more methodologically novel (causal inference is rarely done well in takehomes); C nails the bonus criterion (multi-source) and has the strongest visual/storytelling payoff. If you want the absolute best ROI, **a hybrid is doable in 3-5 days**: lead with the IRA causal question, integrate EJScreen as a second lens to ask *"and who bore the burden of slow decarbonization?"* That single-narrative-two-datasets framing is exactly what senior data scientists ship.

content.subject: Section 2: Top-50 cohort identification
content.description: Load GHGRP 2023 panel + parent-company workbook, filter to Subpart D / power generation, attribute by 2023 ownership share, rank by 2023 emissions, write data/processed/cohort_top50.csv.

content.subject: Section 3: EPA AMPD CEMS via CAMD easey API
content.description: Add cells that read CAMD API key from env, fetch facility-annual emissions for 2011-2024, save CSVs to data/raw/cems/, with graceful fallback instructions if key is missing.

content.subject: Section 4: Climate TRACE US power-sector package
content.description: Add cells to download Climate TRACE electricity-generation package (zip), unpack to data/raw/climate_trace/, with version probing.

content.subject: Section 5: SBTi public target dashboard
content.description: Add cells to fetch SBTi companies-excel.xlsx and targets-excel.xlsx, save to data/raw/sbti/, with manual-download fallback instructions.

content.subject: Section 6: SEC EDGAR 10-K fetch for cohort
content.description: Add cells that load SEC ticker→CIK map, fuzzy-match parent names → CIKs with manual override slot, and pull the most recent 10-K (full submission HTML) for each cohort parent into data/raw/sec_10k/{ticker}/.

content.subject: Section 7: data_manifest.json generator
content.description: Final cell that walks data/raw/ and writes a manifest with source URL, retrieved-at timestamp, file size, sha256, and notes for every acquired file.

content.subject: Verify notebook end-to-end (lint, JSON validity, smoke run plan)
content.description: Validate the .ipynb opens as valid JSON via nbformat, do a static read-through, and document which cells the user should run vs which require their API key/credentials.

content.subject: Read current state of 00_Data_Acquisition.ipynb
content.description: Read the notebook end-to-end as it currently exists after the user's fixes. Compare with the original generator script to identify what changed.

content.description: Inspect data/raw, data/processed, and data/external to see exactly what files exist, their sizes, and whether the cohort/manifest/10-K outputs are present and well-formed.

content.subject: Audit user's fixes for impact on plan assumptions
content.description: For each user edit, evaluate whether it violates a locked decision (Power POC, top 50, hybrid velocity, 2023 ownership, tiered NLP, HTML+Plotly, full LME) or is purely a bug fix. Flag anything that needs reversion or follow-up.

content.subject: Report findings + restate work plan

content.subject: Patch notebook 00 — .env loading, orphan exclusion, fuzzy guard, CT URL probe
content.description: Four fixes: (1) explicit .env path resolution in cell 02 so CEMS section sees EPA_CAMD_API_KEY; (2) defensive NO_PARENT_RECORD exclusion + backfill in cell 13; (3) DO_NOT_MATCH set + fuzzy cutoff 0.92 + first-token gate in cell 27 to kill UNS-Energy / GenOn false positives; (4) env-overridable CLIMATE_TRACE_URL with broader candidate list in cell 21.

Verify data/raw/cems and data/raw/climate_trace are populated.
